releases.headline: Sixty-four options a primitive accepts but documented nowhere are written down, five that nothing reads are no longer accepted, three documented names the code refuses are corrected, and a gate holds the two lists equal
releases.summary:
An option an operator cannot find is one they can neither use nor audit, and every primitive stated its option set twice: the list it accepts, which is the array its `validateOpts` call carries, and the list it documents, which is its `@opts` block. Nothing compared them. Sixty-four were accepted, validated with a throw, and discoverable nowhere. Twenty-five turned up on the first comparison, including three proxy-trust flags that are refused rather than honored, the `skip` and `skipPaths` exemptions on two middlewares, `allowPrivateNetwork` on `b.middleware.cors`, `allowUntrustedIssuer` on `b.mdoc.verifyIssuerSigned`, and the whole option list of the `buildLogoutRequestPost` method on the handle `b.auth.saml.sp.create` returns, which pointed at a sibling rather than naming its own. Each is now written out with the default read from the code, and `test/layer-0-primitives/operator-doc-opts-contract.test.js` compares the two lists on every release.

Comparing them surfaced two defects behind the omissions. `b.compliance.aiAct.gpai.adherenceForm`, which builds an unsigned document, accepted a signing key and did nothing with it, because it shared one allowlist with the primitive that signs; it and `declareAdherence` now accept only the options they read.

The other eleven are on `b.db.declareView` and `b.db.declareRowPolicy`, which the gate cannot reach: a block's function is looked up in the block's own file, and these two are documented in `lib/db.js` and implemented in `lib/db-declare-view.js` and `lib/db-declare-row-policy.js`. Both also documented three names their code refuses, so every documented call raised `unknown opt`, including both `@example` blocks. They were caught by narrowing the example-execution gate instead. Sizing that cross-module blind spot needs the export chain resolved rather than a name match, and it is open as issue #834.

The remaining twenty-eight came from reading the validator's whole grammar rather than the two shapes the first version matched, which is what the Detectors entry below describes. They are the tenant scoping, handler overrides and domain screens on the four mail listeners, the NTS endpoints on both `b.ntpCheck` entry points, and the token and proof bounds on `b.auth.oid4vci.issuer.create`.

items.title: Three proxy-trust flags say that they are refused rather than honored
items.body: `trustProxy` on `b.breakGlass.init` and `b.middleware.networkAllowlist`, and `trustForwardedHeaders` on `b.middleware.dpop`, are each accepted only to be refused: passing one raises `breakglass/bad-opt`, `network-allowlist/bad-opt` or `auth-dpop/bad-opt` unless `trustedProxies` or a resolver already peer-gates the decision, and it never contributes to that decision either way. An operator migrating an Express-style configuration meets that refusal with no entry in the documentation explaining it. All three now carry one, in the wording `b.middleware.cors` already used for the same flag: legacy, refused unless paired with `trustedProxies` or a resolver, and spoofable on its own.

items.title: The skip exemptions on csrfProtect and fetchMetadata are documented, including what a throwing predicate does
items.body:
Both middlewares accept `skipPaths`, an array of string prefixes or RegExps the check is skipped for, and `skip`, a predicate consulted after it. Neither appeared in either block. A string entry matches on a segment boundary, so `"/api"` matches `/api` and `/api/x` but not `/apixyz`, and a RegExp entry is asserted ReDoS-safe and stateless when the middleware is built rather than when a request arrives. `skip` skips only on an exact `true`, and a predicate that throws is read as do-not-skip, so a broken exemption can only leave the guard on.

The part worth reading twice is how much an exemption waives. Both options skip the middleware ENTIRELY, so on `b.middleware.csrfProtect` an exempt path loses `checkOrigin` and `requireJsonContentType` along with the token check, and on `b.middleware.fetchMetadata` it loses `deniedDest` and the `Sec-Fetch-Storage-Access` refusal along with the site check. The adjacent `skipStateless` is the one that waives less: it keeps `checkOrigin`. Exempting a tokenless endpoint with `skipPaths` and assuming origin checking survives is the mistake the two entries are written to prevent.

items.title: The GPAI adherence primitives accept only the options they read
items.body:
`b.compliance.aiAct.gpai.adherenceForm` and `b.compliance.aiAct.gpai.declareAdherence` validated against one shared allowlist, so each accepted the other's options. `adherenceForm` builds the UNSIGNED adherence document, and a `privateKeyPem`, `serialNumber` or `audit` handed to it was checked, carried past every validation, and never used: the call looked like it had configured signing and had not. `modalities` was accepted by both and read by neither, being an option of the sibling `b.compliance.aiAct.gpai.trainingDataSummary`.

`adherenceForm` now accepts its own eleven options and refuses the three signing ones with `unknown option`. `declareAdherence` accepts those three plus the eleven it forwards, and forwards only the form's own keys rather than its whole `opts`, by copying that fixed list directly. It does not filter them through `b.pick`: that refuses a prototype-moving key and consults `b.pick.registerPoisonedKeys`, a public registry an application sets for its own object layer, which is the right filter for untrusted input and the wrong one for options that have already passed `b.validateOpts`. Routed through it, an application that registered `provider` made a declaration carrying `{ name: "Acme" }` sign `{ name: null, address: null, contact: null }`, dropping operator data between the validation that accepted it and the signature that attested to it, and one that registered `modelId` made a valid declaration fail. `modalities` is accepted by neither primitive. A call that passed a signing key to the form, or `modalities` to either, now raises instead of being silently dropped; move the signing key to `declareAdherence`, which is the primitive that signs. `generatedAt`, which `declareAdherence` forwards and the form reads as the stamp its validity window runs from, is documented on both.

items.title: Three primitives that documented no options at all now document all fifteen
items.body: `b.fedcm.config` accepted six options and carried no `@opts` section, so the four required endpoint fields, the required `branding` object and the optional `disconnect_endpoint` were discoverable only by reading the function. `b.mail.crypto.pgp.sign` and `b.mail.crypto.pgp.verify` were the same shape, nine options between them: the message and key inputs, `passphrase` for an encrypted private key, `creationTime` for the signature's epoch-second stamp, `armored` for the detached signature, and the `audit` handle both emit through. All fifteen are written out, each with the refusal it raises when absent or malformed (`fedcm/missing-login_url`, `mail-crypto/pgp/bad-armor`, `mail-crypto/pgp/bad-creation-time` and the rest), and with `creationTime`'s default read from the code rather than described.

items.title: The mail listeners document their tenant scoping, handler overrides and domain screen
items.body:
Every SMTP, POP3, IMAP and ManageSieve listener accepted options that appeared in no block, because they validate through `validateOpts.checkOrThrow` and the contract gate read only the plain `validateOpts` call. Twenty-eight options across nine primitives were in that position.

`tenantScope` and `agentTenantId` are now documented on `b.mail.server.submission.create`, `b.mail.server.pop3.create`, `b.mail.server.imap.create` and `b.mail.server.managesieve.create`: a `b.agent.tenant.create()` instance the authenticated actor is checked against, with the tenant this listener belongs to. One without a `.check` function is refused at create rather than at the first login, since a malformed scope would otherwise refuse every authentication as cross-tenant, and supplying a scope without `agentTenantId` is refused too. A mismatch emits `mail.server.submission.cross_tenant_refused`.

`overrides` on `b.mail.server.imap.create` and `b.mail.server.managesieve.create` replaces one verb's handler through `b.mail.serverRegistry`, keeping wire-protocol state, the audit lifecycle and the guard substrate. Each entry must carry both `maxHandlerBytes` and `maxHandlerMs`: one omitted is refused rather than defaulted, so an operator-supplied handler cannot quietly drop its resource ceiling.

`guardDomain` and `allowSmtpUtf8` on `b.mail.server.submission.create` and `b.mail.server.mx.create`, `recipientPolicy` on the submission listener (asked once per RCPT TO, admitting only on an exact `ok: true`, so a policy that throws refuses the recipient), `rateLimit` on the MX listener, and `allowLegacyMUtf7` on the IMAP listener, which decides whether a mailbox name carrying an RFC 3501 modified-UTF-7 escape is accepted at all.

items.title: ntpCheck documents its NTS endpoints, and oid4vci its token and proof bounds
items.body:
`b.ntpCheck.monitor` and `b.ntpCheck.bootCheck` accept `ntsServers`, NTS-KE endpoints tried before the plain `servers` and each written as `"host"`, `"host:port"` or `"[v6]:port"`, with a malformed entry raising `ntp/bad-endpoint`. A reading from one carries `authenticated: true`. They also accept `requireNts`, and what it does is worth stating: with it set, the plain servers are not consulted at all, so if every NTS endpoint fails the result is `{ driftMs: null, authenticated: false }` carrying the last error rather than an unauthenticated reading. `monitor` additionally documents `port` and `timeoutMs`.

`b.auth.oid4vci.issuer.create` documents `accessTokenSingleUse`, which defaults to true so the `/credential` call spends the token and only an explicit false leaves it replayable for its whole TTL; `proofMaxAgeMs`, the holder-proof `iat` bound, default ten minutes, which when supplied must be a positive finite number, so 0 or `Infinity` raises `validate-opts/bad-positive-finite` at create rather than falling back to the default; and `authorizationServers`, advertised in the issuer metadata and defaulting to the issuer URL. `b.auth.saml.sp.create` documents `idpSloUrl`, the default both logout builders fall back on, and `singleLogoutServiceUrl`, this SP's own endpoint in its metadata.

items.title: Options documented on nine more primitives
items.body: `allowPrivateNetwork` on `b.middleware.cors` (default false; left off, a Private Network Access preflight is refused with reason `private-network-not-permitted`). `allowUntrustedIssuer` on `b.mdoc.verifyIssuerSigned` (default false; with it unset, omitting `trustAnchorsPem` raises `mdoc/trust-anchors-required`, because the x5chain signer certificate is attacker-controlled). `guardDomain` and `profile` on `b.mail.create` (the address-domain screen is on by default at the `strict` profile, and a refusal raises `mail/recipient-domain-refused`). `trustedProxies`, `forwardedHeaders` and `clientIpResolver` on `b.middleware.flagContext`, which decide what the anonymous targeting key is derived from. `mountInfoPath` on `b.restore.create`, which the cross-device and mount-point checks read instead of the platform's own table. `now` on `b.auth.jar.parse`, which forwards to `b.auth.jwt.verifyExternal` and is documented there already. And `idpSloUrl` on both SAML logout builders.

items.title: buildLogoutRequestPost names its own options instead of pointing at its sibling
items.body: On the handle `b.auth.saml.sp.create` returns, `buildLogoutRequestPost` accepts the same seven options as `buildLogoutRequest`, and its `@opts` section said "nameId, nameIdFormat, sessionIndex, relayState — same as buildLogoutRequest" with the signing pair described in a second line. A run of names in prose is not something an operator can search for, and a reference to a sibling is not a contract. All seven are written out, with the same meanings the sibling gives them and the fallback order for `idpSloUrl`: the call's own value, then `sp.create`'s `idpSloUrl`, then its `idpSsoUrl`, and `auth-saml/no-idp-slo` when none is set.

items.title: declareView and declareRowPolicy documented option names they do not accept
items.body:
Both blocks named options the implementation refuses. `b.db.declareView` documented `select` and `grants`, which are spelled `source` and `grantTo`, and described `schema` as optional when it is required. `b.db.declareRowPolicy` documented `roles`, an array, where the option is `role`, a single role name, and did not mention `schema` at all, which is also required. Every documented call therefore raised `declare-view/unknown-opt` or `declare-row-policy/unknown-opt`, including the `@example` in each block, and the value each example claimed to return (`spec.kind`) is not a property either primitive returns.

Both now document all nine options they accept, with requiredness and defaults read from the code: for the view, the `source` spellings and the three column-exclusion sets, and that a spec whose exclusions remove every column raises `declare-view/empty-select`; for the policy, that `using` is required, that `permissive: false` emits a RESTRICTIVE policy, and that applying it enables row-level security on the table when it is not enabled already. Both examples now run and assert `spec.description`.

items.title: A signing refusal is not recorded in the audit trail, and the option says so
items.body: `b.mail.crypto.pgp.sign`'s `audit` entry said a refusal is recorded either way. It is not: the primitive's only emit is its `mail.crypto.pgp.sign` success event, and every refusal above it throws first, so a failed sign reaches the caller and not the audit trail. The entry now says that. `b.mail.crypto.pgp.verify` is the one that does emit on failure, as `mail.crypto.pgp.verify_fail`, and its entry already named that event.

items.title: bundleAdapterStorage described a default fs adapter that does not exist
items.body:
`b.backup.bundleAdapterStorage` documented its adapter contract as "an `fs` implementation is the default + ships in `lib/backup/_adapter-fs.js`". Neither half held: `adapter` is required and building the backend without one raises `backup/bad-adapter`, and no such file is in the package. An operator following that sentence would omit `adapter` and meet the refusal, then look for a file that is not there.

The block now names what does ship. Two adapter factories exist, `b.backup.bundleAdapterStorage.fsAdapter({ root })` for a local filesystem and `.objectStoreAdapter(client)` for an object store, so the five-method contract below them is what an operator implements only for a store neither covers; and `b.backup.diskStorage` is the separate filesystem-backed backend that takes no adapter at all. A sweep of every repo path named in a `lib/` comment block found this the only one missing from the tree, out of fifteen.

items.title: Every option a primitive accepts is one its block documents
items.body:
`test/layer-0-primitives/operator-doc-opts-contract.test.js` reads each `@primitive` block's `@opts` section and compares it against the allowlist in that block's own function, and runs in release.js's static-gate block beside the API-name and error-code gates. An injection point for tests is exempt, since publishing one would make it operator surface: the underscore prefix carries itself, and the two seams that do not wear one, `transportFactory` on the mail deliverer and `clock` on the rate limiter, are listed by name with what they inject. Those exemptions are checked for honesty in both directions, so one that stops being accepted, or that becomes documented, fails rather than sitting in the list.

What the gate reads is the validator's grammar, not a list of shapes, and getting that wrong hid options twice. The allowlist reaches the same check four ways: `validateOpts`, `validateOpts.check`, `validateOpts.checkOrThrow`, which is the same key check raising the caller's own error class, and `validateOpts.shape`, whose schema field names are the allowlist because a key outside the schema is refused. The keys themselves arrive either as an array literal or as a name bound to one. Reading one call form and one argument form left 58 of the 413 allowlist sites in `lib/` invisible, and a block the gate cannot read counts as unmeasurable, which reports as a clean verdict rather than as a gap. That is how every mail listener kept its tenant-scoping options undocumented, and how the GPAI adherence primitives kept six through a release whose subject was undocumented options. All four forms are read now, a name is resolved from its literal, and one the gate cannot read fails the run by name instead of joining the unmeasurable pile, since there the keys demonstrably exist and something about the instrument is in the way. Each form carries a fixture, so dropping one fails rather than going quiet.

An `@opts` section documents sub-objects inline, so only its top-level names answer for a top-level accepted option. Counting every `name:` in the section let a nested field stand in for one: `b.mail.server.submission.create` accepts and reads a top-level `rateLimit`, the connection admission control for the listener, and the only documented `rateLimit` was `auth`'s nested one, which budgets authentication failures. The gate called it documented and the operator was told about a different option. Depth now comes from the indentation, with the top level being the shallowest depth at which a name appears rather than a fixed column, which is also what handles the brace-wrapped form several blocks use.

A block with no `@opts` section at all is measured rather than skipped, since documenting nothing is the most complete form of the omission. That one takes a fixture to hold, because once such a block is documented it carries a section again and an assertion made against the tree would pass either way; the named-array case takes a fixture for the same reason.

What the gate had to get right is which function a block describes, because both obvious rules are wrong in one direction. A body that ends at the first closing brace in column zero ends at the enclosing `create()` factory rather than at the primitive, which credits a block with every later allowlist in that factory: measured that way, `b.auth.oauth.parseCallback` appeared to accept eight options while calling no `validateOpts` at all. Requiring the function to carry the primitive's own name misses `b.middleware.cors`, which is implemented by `function create(opts)`, and preferring that name finds a different function of that name in the same file. The gate tries the adjacent declaration and the named one, keeps whichever validates its own options parameter, and delimits it by matching its own braces. It also asserts that a useful share of blocks remain measurable, so a regression that empties the comparison fails here rather than reporting a clean verdict over nothing.

items.title: An options object is not forwarded through the poison-aware filter
items.body: `b.pick` refuses a prototype-moving key and consults `b.pick.registerPoisonedKeys`, a registry that only ever grows and that an application sets for its own object layer. That makes it right for untrusted input and wrong for forwarding a primitive's own options, whose key list is a fixed literal that has already passed `b.validateOpts`: the forwarding question does not depend on that policy, and consulting it lets unrelated application configuration change what a primitive does with data it already accepted. A `codebase-patterns` rule refuses a direct `b.pick` filter call on an options object, and leaves the `assertSafeKey` and `isPoisonedKey` helpers and genuine untrusted-input filtering alone.

items.title: A documented example that passes an option the primitive refuses fails the release
items.body:
`test/layer-0-primitives/jsdoc-example-execution.test.js` runs every `@example` and treats a framework typed error as illustrative, on the grounds that the API resolved and threw its own refusal, which is what a precondition or input demo is written to show. That exemption also covered an example that is simply wrong: both `b.db.declareView` and `b.db.declareRowPolicy` raised `unknown opt` on the option names their own blocks documented, and the gate passed over both.

An unknown-option refusal is now a failure rather than a skip. It is the one refusal a documented example has no reason to demonstrate, since the example documents that very API, and it says the call shape in the documentation does not exist. Both spellings in the tree are covered: `unknown option 'x'. Allowed keys:` from the shared validator, and `unknown opt 'x'. Allowed:` from a hand-rolled key loop. Run against the two broken blocks it reported exactly those two failures out of the examples that execute and nothing else, and with both corrected the count of executing examples rises by two, to 1,149, with none failing. An example that demonstrates such a refusal deliberately catches it, so it never reaches the classifier.

items.title: The vendored @blamejs/pki bundle moves to 0.8.48, which hardens three verification verdicts
items.body:
`lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` carried 0.8.31. 0.8.48 fixes verification verdicts that were assembled through `Promise.all` read from the global binding at the call rather than from an operation captured at load. A replacement whose `all` resolves an array without awaiting the component verifications therefore handed its own values back as the verdict: `pki.crmf.verifyPop` reported an unverified proof of possession as `verified: true`, and the composite-signature arm reported a signature whose ML-DSA and traditional halves were never checked as verified, reachable through `pki.cms.verify` and `pki.path.validate` wherever a composite algorithm is in use. `pki.webauthn.verify` returned its refusals as rejected promises and folded its attestation trust-path checks over a seed built the same way. In this framework that surface is `b.mtlsCa` and the WebAuthn attestation and assertion verification behind `b.auth.passkey`.

Refreshed through `scripts/vendor-update.sh`, which is the only bundler for `lib/vendor/`. The count of `Promise.all` references in the bundle falls from nine to one, and the process, network, dynamic-evaluation and filesystem-write surface is unchanged: `child_process` 1, `spawn`/`exec` 1, `net`/`tls`/`http` requires 7, URL literals 5, `process.env` 2, and no `eval`, `new Function`, `fetch` or write call in either version. `dependencies` stays empty, as the framework ships no npm runtime dependencies.

releases.headline: A stored password hash no longer dictates what a login attempt costs, and every Argon2id derivation waits behind one bounded gate
releases.summary: `b.auth.password.verify` read the memory, passes and lanes out of the PHC string it was handed and ran Argon2id at those parameters, so a row carrying `m=4194304` spent 4 GiB and about three seconds on one login attempt. A ceiling now bounds what a stored hash may ask for, `hash` refuses to write a credential above it, and `needsRehash` reports a row above it as needing re-derivation. The concurrency gate those derivations wait on moved into the Argon2id entry point, so the vault's passphrase wrapping and the backup key derivation are counted alongside the login path instead of running on top of the limit; the queue behind it can be bounded in depth and in waiting time, and `b.auth.password.stats` reports both counts. Alongside that: `b.promisePool` honors a `queueLimit` of 0 instead of refusing every task, `b.session` deletes expired rows in batches and gained `purgeStale` for rows past an idle or absolute limit, `b.localDb.thin` applies the pragmas an operator passes after the fixed ones rather than before, and a route that throws a typed 4xx refusal no longer writes an error-level line with a stack trace.

items.title: A ceiling bounds the Argon2id cost a stored hash can ask verify to spend
items.body:
`b.auth.password.verify` decodes `m`, `t` and `p` from the stored PHC string and derives at those parameters, so whatever wrote the row decides the cost of every attempt against it. A row carrying `m=4194304` was measured at 4 GiB and about three seconds. `b.auth.password.costCeiling(opts?)` reads or sets that bound, defaulting to 512 MiB of memory, 24 passes and 16 lanes, which is eight times the hash defaults for memory and time. A hash above the ceiling answers `false` and reports `auth.password.cost_over_ceiling` through observability with the three parameters, rather than raising, because `verify` stays safe to call without a `try`. `b.auth.password.needsRehash` reports such a row as needing re-derivation, and `hash` raises `argon2/cost-over-ceiling` rather than writing a credential this process would then refuse to verify. Raise the ceiling where a deployment deliberately runs more expensive parameters; a raw key derivation, which nothing later reads a cost out of, is not bound by it.

That `false` means "not verified" to a login, which is a failed sign-in, but it means "not one of the old passwords" to a password-history check, which approves the very password the check exists to refuse. A history entry hashed above the ceiling, which is what a ceiling lowered or restored after those hashes were written leaves behind, therefore let the exact previous password through. `reuseProhibited` raises `auth-password/history-over-ceiling` for such an entry instead of answering: it cannot be checked without spending the work the ceiling refuses, and an answer it cannot compute must not read as a pass. Rehash that entry, or raise the ceiling to cover it.

items.title: The Argon2id concurrency gate counts every derivation in the process
items.body: `b.auth.password.gate(n)` wrapped two functions, `b.auth.password.hash` and `b.auth.password.verify`, so `n` bounded those two and nothing else. The passphrase wrapping in `b.vault`, the backup key derivation in `b.backup` and the reuse check a `b.auth.password.policy` runs over stored history each reached Argon2id without passing the limit, and each held 64 MiB or more while it ran, so the memory a deployment sized `n` to bound was exceeded by however many of those were in flight. The gate moved into the Argon2id entry point every one of those paths goes through, so `n` now bounds the process. Lowering `n` below the number already running takes effect as those finish: the old limiter handed a freed slot straight to the next waiter without rechecking the limit, so a lowered `n` did nothing until the waiter list emptied.

items.title: A derivation past the gate limit can be refused or timed out instead of queued without bound
items.body:
Every derivation past the limit joined an unbounded queue and waited for as long as it took, so a burst of sign-in attempts grew a queue that held each request open with no way to shed it. `b.auth.password.gate(n, { maxQueued, waitTimeoutMs })` bounds the queue in depth and in waiting time: a derivation arriving with the queue full raises `argon2/busy`, and a waiter past `waitTimeoutMs` raises `argon2/queue-timeout`. Both propagate out of every entry point that derives: `hash`, `verify` (which otherwise answers `false` rather than raising), a policy's `reuseProhibited`, `b.credentialHash.hash` and `verify`, and the passphrase derivations in `b.vault` and `b.backup`. A credential check that read them as a mismatch would report a correct API key as invalid and audit `bad-secret` against the caller, and a vault unseal that read them as a bad passphrase would report an intact key file as corrupt.

A refusal is only useful if the caller can act on it, which takes two things: the code has to survive the consumer, and the consumer must not have done something irreversible first. `b.backupBundle.create` created its output directory and the `files/` subdirectory before deriving, so a refusal left both behind and the retry it invites failed permanently with `backup-bundle/outdir-exists`. It derives first and claims the directory afterwards, with a single non-recursive `mkdir`, at mode `0700`, rather than a tolerant one. That also closes a window the old order had hidden: the existing-directory check runs before the derivation awaits, so two calls naming one `outDir` both passed it and both wrote their files and manifest into the same directory, and the second replaced the first operator's backup without saying so. One call creates the directory now and the other is refused. The derived key is wiped on every path out of the call, including a filesystem failure while claiming the directory. The same question applies one level down: `b.vaultWrap.wrap` copies a string plaintext into a buffer it owns, which is how the vault key and a generated audit-signing private key reach it, and its cleanup began after the derivation, so a refusal left that copy in memory. Each buffer is zeroed from the point it exists now rather than from the point the encryption starts.

On the first point, a consumer that wraps the derivation in a catch-all re-labels whatever comes out. Eleven such catches now let a capacity refusal through before translating: `b.archive.unwrapWithPassphrase` reported a valid archive as `archive-wrap/decrypt-failed`, `b.keychain`'s fallback file read answered "passphrase rejected or file corrupted" for an intact file, `b.restoreBundle.extract` answered `restore-bundle/vault-key-recovery-failed` for an intact backup whose manifest predates the bundle key scheme, and `b.auditSign`'s boot unseal and all four of the vault passphrase operations said the passphrase was rejected. Each is permanent, so a caller reading one looks for a wrong passphrase or a damaged file instead of retrying. The rotation check was the opposite shape and the more serious one: it confirms a rotation took effect by requiring the OLD passphrase to fail against the new sealed bytes, and it accepted any failure as that confirmation, so a refusal under load read as proof. It now requires the one failure it is looking for, a passphrase rejection, and propagates everything else, removing the staged `vault.key.sealed.tmp` on its way out: `preflightRotatable` refuses while that file exists and tells the operator to remove it by hand, so a refusal that left one behind could not be retried.

They also carry `transient: true`, so `b.retry.withRetry` retries them and `b.retry.withBreaker` counts them, and a loaded process can answer 503 instead of blaming the input. `b.auth.password.stats()` reports `running`, `waiting` and the three limits. Both bounds default to off, so a queued derivation still waits indefinitely unless one is set.

items.title: Two config accessors no longer reset a security bound on an absent argument
items.body: `b.cryptoField.configureUnsealRateCap()` called with no argument turned off the unseal rate cap, the brute-force bound on the KEM-decapsulation oracle, because an absent argument shared the disable branch with the documented `null`. A call written against a config value that turned out to be absent therefore disabled the cap silently. It raises `crypto-field/bad-rate-cap-opt` now; `null` and `{ disabled: true }` remain the opt-out. `b.auth.password.costCeiling` reads the same way: calling it with no argument reports the ceiling in force and leaves it alone, and only `null` restores the default.

items.title: promisePool accepts a queueLimit of 0 and runs a task when a slot is free
items.body: `b.promisePool.create({ concurrency: 8, queueLimit: 0 })` refused every task with `promise-pool/queue-full`, including the first one offered to an idle pool, because each task was queued before the pool started it and the queue length was compared against the limit before the free slot was consulted. `queueLimit` bounds how many tasks may wait, not how many may run, so 0 now means run it when a slot is free and refuse it when none is. The refusal also quotes the value the caller passed: a `queueLimit` of -1 was reported as `0` and a `"3"` as `"31"`.

items.title: localDbThin applies the pragmas an operator passes after the fixed ones
items.body: `b.localDb.thin` applied `opts.pragmas` after its own fixed set, which starts with `journal_mode=WAL`. `auto_vacuum` only takes on a database with no tables yet, and setting the journal mode writes the header, so `pragmas: { auto_vacuum: "INCREMENTAL" }` left `PRAGMA auto_vacuum` reading 0 and a store built on it could not reclaim pages with `incremental_vacuum`. Measured on node:sqlite: WAL then auto_vacuum reads 0, the other order reads 2. The pragmas now apply in three steps. The caller's go first, so one that must precede the journal mode takes effect. The framework's tuning defaults, `synchronous=NORMAL` and `busy_timeout=5000`, go second and only for a key the caller did not set, so an operator who raised `busy_timeout` for a contended store or chose `synchronous=FULL` for durability keeps that value instead of having it quietly restored. The fixed set goes last: `journal_mode=WAL`, `foreign_keys`, `secure_delete`, `trusted_schema` and `cell_size_check` are not the caller's to lower, and naming one of them in `pragmas` raises `localdb-thin/pragma-not-overridable` rather than being accepted and discarded.

items.title: session.purgeExpired deletes in batches, and purgeStale removes rows past an idle or absolute limit
items.body:
`b.session.purgeExpired()` deleted every expired row in a single statement, which holds a write lock for as long as the delete takes and grows without bound against a table that has not been purged in a while. It takes a `batchSize` now and deletes in batches until the table is clear, returning the same total. Each batch selects the keys it will remove and deletes them under the same condition, so a session refreshed between the two statements keeps its row rather than being revoked for an expiry it no longer has. The sweep runs until nothing matches rather than stopping at a batch count, and one that keeps matching the same rows while deleting none raises `session/purge-stalled` with the count it did remove. That judgement reads the set of keys the select returned rather than their order, so a backend free to return the same matching set in a different order does not read as progress; sixteen consecutive passes that match rows and remove none raise it too, which covers a backend whose ordering ties differently at the batch boundary each time. That second count reads an explicit zero only: a store that deletes rows and does not report how many is terse rather than stalled, and counting its silence as no progress would stop a sweep partway through a table it was clearing.

Each pass re-runs the select, so bounding what one statement writes is only half of it: the read has to be bounded as well. Each sweep orders by the column it filters on, which is the column the table indexes for expiry. Ordering by the primary key instead made every pass walk the whole table to find the matching rows, and on the first-party SQLite store the plan was a full scan of the key index rather than a range over the expiry index. Measured on 200,000 rows with 10% expired, in batches of 500: 1,574ms ordered by the key against 44ms ordered by `expiresAt`. The idle and absolute sweeps read `lastActivity` and `createdAt`, and the session table now indexes both, so those sweeps search a range instead of scanning what is left of the table and sorting it. Measured on the same shape, the idle sweep is 81ms indexed against 245ms unindexed, and the two indexes cost about 19% on the update that bumps `lastActivity`, which is a microsecond per touch. Existing deployments pick the indexes up at the next boot. The table is declared in three places and all three carry them: the default single-node schema, the external-database schema, and the dedicated `b.session.stores.localDbThin` file, which creates them with its table. The count is what the deletes reported: a store that reports no row count for a delete contributes nothing to it rather than having the batch size assumed. Each pass yields to the event loop, so the sweep does not hold the process for its whole duration. A `batchSize` that is not a positive integer, or is above 10000, raises `session/bad-batch-size`; the ceiling is there because each key is a bound parameter and the backends cap how many a statement may carry.

items.title: A route that throws a typed 4xx refusal is logged at debug level
items.body: The router wrote `log.error("route error: ...")` with five stack frames for every error a route threw, before handing it to the error handler, so an authentication failure or a validation refusal produced an error-level line with a stack trace for an expected outcome and a burst of failed sign-ins produced one per request. An error carrying a status in [400, 500) on either `statusCode` or `status` is written at debug level with its code and message and no frames. A 5xx, and an error carrying no status at all, still reach error level with their frames. Every property it reads off the thrown value is read defensively and the whole line is drop-silent, because this logger runs ahead of the error handler and the last-resort 500: a thrown value whose `statusCode` is an accessor that raises, or whose `code` will not coerce to a string, would otherwise have thrown out of the logger and left the request with no reply at all.

items.title: promisePool.fire contains a failing task instead of exiting the process
items.body: `fire` is the variant for a caller that does not hold the returned promise, which is how the module documents it for fan-out from event handlers. It was `run` under another name, so a task that threw became an unhandled rejection and took the process down: one failing background job ended the server. `fire` now contains the rejection, and a new `onFireError` on `b.promisePool.create` receives it where an operator wants it reported. `run` is unchanged, since its caller holds the promise, and both still raise `promise-pool/bad-task`, `promise-pool/queue-full` and `promise-pool/closed` to the caller.

items.title: b.session.purgeStale(opts?) removes sessions past an idle or absolute limit
items.body: `purgeExpired` removes rows whose own expiry has passed, which leaves a session that is still inside its expiry but has not been touched for days, and one that has been continuously refreshed since it was created. `purgeStale({ idleTimeoutMs, absoluteTimeoutMs, batchSize })` removes both, deleting in batches and returning the count. The two timeouts default to the same 30 minutes idle and 12 hours absolute the session middleware enforces, so calling it with no options sweeps to the policy already in force. Passing 0 for one of them leaves that limit unenforced, and a timeout that is neither 0 nor a positive integer raises `session/bad-timeout`.

items.title: defineClass takes transientCodes, so a class can name the failures a retry can clear
items.body: `b.frameworkError.defineClass` offered `alwaysPermanent` for a class whose failures are all configuration and `permanentClassifier` for one that has to read a status, and nothing in between. A class whose failures are a mix, such as the Argon2id gate's full-queue refusal next to its bad-configuration refusal, had to take `alwaysPermanent` and mark a capacity failure permanent, which tells `b.retry.withRetry` not to retry it and the breaker behind `b.retry.withBreaker` not to count it. `transientCodes: ["argon2/busy", "argon2/queue-timeout"]` names the codes a retry can clear and leaves every other code of the class permanent. An instance carrying a named code also reports `transient: true`, which is what `b.retry.isRetryable` reads: `permanent === false` cannot stand in for it, because that is also what a call site passing no third argument gets. So a retry around one of these now retries, where before it gave up after one attempt. `b.network.dns`, `b.network.tls` and the local HTTP client, which each wrote the same classifier by hand, now declare their transient codes this way; their `permanent` classifications are unchanged, and their transient codes become retryable by the default classifier. `b.wsClient` keeps its own classifier, because its decision reads the HTTP status alongside the code.

items.title: b.auth.password has a documentation page
items.body: The namespace shipped without one, so `hash`, `verify`, `needsRehash`, `policy`, `params`, `gate`, `stats` and `costCeiling` were reachable and undocumented. Each now carries its signature, its options, the errors it raises and a worked example, including the eleven `policy/` refusal codes `policy().check` returns and the four methods a built policy exposes.

items.title: An Argon2id derivation can now raise where it previously waited or succeeded
items.body:
`b.auth.password.hash` raises `argon2/cost-over-ceiling` for parameters above the ceiling, which previously wrote a hash this process would not verify. `verify` answers `false` for a stored row above the ceiling: raise the ceiling with `b.auth.password.costCeiling` where those parameters are deliberate, since re-deriving a row needs a successful `verify` first and the remedy is otherwise a password reset.

The gate's own refusals, `argon2/busy` and `argon2/queue-timeout`, appear only once `maxQueued` or `waitTimeoutMs` is set through `b.auth.password.gate`; both default to off and the previous behavior of waiting indefinitely is unchanged. When one is set, the refusal reaches every path that derives, not only the login path: `b.auth.password.hash` and `verify`, a policy's `reuseProhibited`, `b.credentialHash.hash` and `verify`, and through those the `verify` on a handle from `b.apiKey.create`, and the passphrase derivations in `b.vault` and `b.backup`, including the unseal `b.vault.init` performs at boot. What arrives is an `Argon2Error`, not a `VaultError`, a `BackupError` or a `false`, so a handler that catches one of those classes needs a branch for it; `b.retry.isRetryable` recognizes both codes. The bound an operator sets to shed a flood of sign-ins therefore also sheds a vault unseal and a backup run, which is the reason to set it on the paths that need it rather than process-wide at boot.

Five other calls can refuse where they did not before. `b.promisePool.create` with `queueLimit: 0` ran nothing before and runs tasks now. `b.cryptoField.configureUnsealRateCap()` with no argument raises instead of disabling the cap, so a deployment calling it that way has been running with no unseal rate cap and should pass `null` if that was intended. `b.auth.password.gate` and `costCeiling` refuse an unknown option, a non-object and a non-integer with `auth-password/bad-gate` and the new `auth-password/bad-ceiling`, where a second argument used to be ignored; `costCeiling` also refuses a value below what `hash` writes by default, which would have left the module refusing every credential it produces. `b.auth.password.hash` and `needsRehash` refuse a fractional `memoryCost`, `timeCost` or `parallelism` with `auth-password/bad-params`, which previously reached the caller as node's own `RangeError`. And `b.localDb.thin` refuses a `pragmas` key that names one of its fixed settings with `localdb-thin/pragma-not-overridable`, where such a key was accepted and then overwritten; a tuning pragma the fixed set does not claim, such as `busy_timeout` or `synchronous`, is kept rather than overwritten, which restores what 0.20.36 did with it.

Finally, `b.session.purgeExpired` and `purgeStale` refuse a `batchSize` above 10000 with `session/bad-batch-size`, where a larger value reached the driver and failed the sweep with its own untyped error after removing nothing.

releases.headline: An audit chain stops recording its own writes, a multi-signer S/MIME envelope validates every signer's certificate chain, and a primitive that names one of its error codes names them all
releases.summary: In cluster mode the audit chain is written through `b.externalDb`, which audits every query it issues, so appending a row emitted an event that appended another row: one `b.audit.record` call produced 164 rows, and a chain nothing recorded to grew from 80 rows to 5,105 across four idle seconds. Audit's own reads and writes of its own tables no longer emit, which also stops `b.audit.verify` appending to the chain it walks and `b.audit.checkpoint` appending past the counter it anchors. `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` verifies every SignerInfo's signature but validated only the first signer's certificate chain, then returned `chainVerified: true` for the whole envelope. A second signer whose certificate chained to nothing the caller supplied was accepted. It now validates every signer's chain. `b.tsa.verifyToken` reads one SignerInfo, and RFC 3161 allows a timestamp token the TSA's signature and no other, so a token carrying a second signature is refused rather than judged on its first. Alongside that, 110 primitives documented some of the error codes they throw and not the rest, which left operators writing a catch for a list that was never complete; 592 of the 594 omitted codes are documented, the other two deleted because the primitive built them and threw them away before raising, and a gate holds the lists complete from here.

items.title: Recording one audit event appends one row, not a cascade of them
items.body:
In cluster mode the audit chain is written through `b.externalDb`, which audits every query it issues. Appending a row therefore emitted an audit event, and writing that event appended another row, which emitted again. One `b.audit.record` call produced 164 rows against a cluster backed by SQLite, and the growth did not need an operator: a chain holding 80 rows after boot reached 5,105 across four idle seconds with nothing recording to it, each window larger than the one before. Reads had the same shape: `b.audit.verify` appended rows to the chain it was walking, so `rowsVerified` described a chain that had moved under it, and `b.audit.checkpoint` appended rows past the counter it had just anchored, leaving the anchor stale as it was written.

Audit's own storage calls now run with audit emission suppressed: the chain append, the checkpoint's reads and writes, the reads behind `verify`, `verifyCheckpoints` and `query`, the slice reads in `b.auditTools`, and the hand-off to a store registered with `b.audit.useStore`, in both its shadow and its redirect mode. The suppression covers those calls and stops there, so work an operation performs around its storage keeps its own audit: a read that cannot unseal the rows it returns still records `system.crypto.unseal_failed`, and a tuple that trips the unseal rate cap still records the `denied`-outcome `system.crypto.unseal_rate_exceeded`. It is scoped to the call tree of that storage work, so an emission from a request running at the same time is unaffected, and a connection the pool opens during a chain write is built outside it rather than carrying it for the connection's whole life. The scope is inherited by what runs inside it, which is what a store's own persistence needs: a store that writes through `b.externalDb` would otherwise emit `system.externaldb.query` on every write, have that handed back to it, and write again. The same inheritance reaches a keepalive, listener or retry timer a store arms inside its own `record`, which is then suppressed for the life of the process, so arm one when the store is constructed, or through the new `b.audit.outsideSelfEmitSuppression`. That covers the purge paths as well: the anchor read was already inside the suppression while the anchor write and the row delete were not, so every purge and every anchor repair still queued a `system.externaldb.query` of its own into the chain it had just trimmed. All nineteen calls that reach audit's own tables are inside it now, and a detector refuses the twentieth that arrives without it. A suppressed emission is counted as the observability event `audit.self_emit_suppressed` carrying the action that was dropped. `b.audit.query` still records its `audit.read` self-log, which is a write rather than an emission, so reading audit data still leaves exactly one row (PCI DSS 10.2.3). A single-node deployment, where the chain does not go through `b.externalDb`, is unaffected, and so is a deployment that never calls `b.cluster.init`.

items.title: verifyAll validates the certificate chain of every signer, not the first
items.body: `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` is the multi-signer entry point: it verifies each SignerInfo against its own key in `signerPublicKeys` and reports `valid: true` only when every one verified. When `trustAnchorCertsPem` was supplied it validated one chain, the first signer's, and returned `chainVerified: true` as a property of the envelope. So a two-signer message whose second certificate chained to no supplied anchor passed `valid && chainVerified`, which is the check an operator writes. Every signer's chain is validated now, and the first failure refuses the envelope. A single-signer envelope and a multi-signer envelope whose signers all anchor behave as before.

items.title: A chain check is bound to the certificate its SignerInfo names
items.body: Validating each signer's chain was not enough on its own: the chain walk picked its leaf by matching the public key that verified the signature, and took the first certificate in the bundle that matched. Two SignerInfos naming different certificates that carry the same key therefore validated the same chain twice, so an envelope holding one anchored certificate followed by an unanchored one with the same key returned `chainVerified: true` with the second certificate never walked. A SignerInfo's sid names its certificate by issuer and serial together, and that pair now picks the certificate whose chain is walked. Matching the serial alone would not do: a serial is unique only within an issuer (RFC 5280 section 4.1.2.2), so a bundle may legitimately hold two certificates with one key and one serial under different issuers, and the sid says which is meant. When no certificate in the bundle both carries the verifying key and is the one the sid names, the envelope is refused with `mail-crypto/smime/signer-cert-not-named`, because a chain validated for any other certificate describes an identity the SignerInfo never claimed. A sid that identifies its certificate by subject-key identifier instead names no issuer and serial, so it cannot be bound to a bundle entry at all: chain validation refuses it with `mail-crypto/smime/unbindable-sid`, and verifying that envelope without `trustAnchorCertsPem` is unaffected.

items.title: A timestamp token carrying a second signature is refused
items.body: RFC 3161 §2.4.2 gives a time-stamp token the TSA's signature and no other. `b.tsa.verifyToken` reads one SignerInfo, so a token carrying two was verified on the first and accepted, leaving the second read by nothing. Such a token now raises `tsa/multiple-signers`. A token with no SignerInfo still raises `tsa/no-signer`, and a conformant single-signer token is unaffected.

items.title: b.audit.outsideSelfEmitSuppression(fn) lets an external store arm something long-lived
items.body: While audit writes its own chain it suppresses emissions, and that suppression is inherited by whatever runs inside it. A store registered with `b.audit.useStore` has its `record` called in there, which is what its own persistence needs, and it is also why a keepalive, listener or retry timer the store arms inside `record` is suppressed for the life of the process: every audit event that resource emits afterwards is dropped with no error and no row. Arm it when the store is constructed, which is outside any chain write, or arm it inside this wrapper, which runs `fn` with the suppression lifted and returns what it returns. Wrap only the arming: a store's writes belong inside the suppression, because a store that persists through `b.externalDb` emits `system.externaldb.query` on each one, has it handed back, and writes again.

items.title: b.x509Chain.canonicalNameKey compares two distinguished names as names
items.body:
`b.x509Chain.canonicalNameKey(nameNode)` returns one comparable string for an X.501 `Name`, the shape a certificate's issuer and subject fields carry. Distinguished-name equality is not DER equality: RFC 5280 section 7.1 compares the attributes after normalization, with the one deliberate narrowing described below. Two encodings of one name, in `PrintableString` or `UTF8String`, in either case, or with repeated inner spaces, give the same key, and attribute order inside a single relative distinguished name does not change it. A case-insensitive attribute is prepared per RFC 4518: the soft hyphen, the combining grapheme joiner, the variation selectors, the zero width space and the control and format code points Unicode 3.2 defined are removed, the separators become one space, and the value is case folded rather than lowercased, so `Straße CA` and `STRASSE CA` are one name and so are the final and medial forms of sigma. The mapping, the folding and the normalization run to a fixed point rather than in a fixed order, because no single order settles every name: case mapping can hand back a decomposed sequence that only a later normalization recomposes, and folding U+0345 turns a combining mark into a base letter, so a mark run folded before it is canonically ordered puts the accent on a different letter for good. Folding stops at the default Unicode rules, leaving U+0131 alone, since folding it onto an ASCII `i` is Turkic-only and would let one issuer read as another.

Case mapping is the runtime's, so a character Unicode assigned after 3.2 folds onto its case partner as that version defines: U+1C90 GEORGIAN MTAVRULI CAPITAL AN keys as U+10D0, the Mkhedruli letter it capitalizes. RFC 4518 would prohibit the newer character outright, which needs the Unicode 3.2 repertoire to implement, so this matches the pair instead. It does not merge two DIFFERENT letters: every set of code points sharing a key is one Unicode case class, which is what a case-insensitive attribute is defined to do, and that is asserted over every code point rather than argued.

Normalization is to form C, not the form KC that RFC 5280 section 7.1 reaches through RFC 4518, and that narrowing is deliberate. Compatibility normalization maps one character onto a DIFFERENT one, which under form KC gave 24,355 pairs of unrelated code points the same key: every superscript, subscript, circled, fullwidth and mathematical variant collapsed onto its ASCII base, so an issuer `A<U+1D2C>B` took the key of `AAB` and a SignerInfo could be bound to a certificate it never named. U+1D2C is a modifier letter, so no category test excludes it. The RFC bounds the same hazard by prohibiting every code point unassigned in Unicode 3.2, which needs that repertoire to implement. Canonical normalization only composes and reorders, so it never maps a character onto another one: case, encoding type, whitespace, precomposed and decomposed spellings and canonically reordered marks all still compare equal, and only compatibility variants no longer do.

A `PrintableString`, `IA5String` or `TeletexString` is read only within its own repertoire, printable ASCII and for `PrintableString` the letters, digits and `'()+,-./:=?` that type permits. Decoding bytes outside it as Latin-1 fed preparation characters that were never in the input, so the bytes `41 00 42` became A, NUL, B, the NUL was removed, and the result took the key of the valid `AB`. Such a value now keys by its bytes, which can only equal an identical byte sequence.

The removed set is a fixed table rather than a category test against whatever Unicode version the runtime ships, and any other code point in category Other refuses the whole name with `null`. Removing a character is the one mapping that can make two DIFFERENT names equal, so a character the RFC never listed must not be removed because a later Unicode gave it a format category: U+061C, added in Unicode 6.3, made an issuer `A<U+061C>B` take the key of `AB`. RFC 4518 section 2.4 prohibits the code points unassigned in Unicode 3.2, and refusing is the safe answer for one the preparation cannot classify, since no conformant peer sends it. An empty `RDNSequence` keys like any other name, since RFC 5280 section 4.1.2.6 permits an empty subject when the identity is in `subjectAltName`. A structure that only resembles a name returns `null`: every node is checked for its tag, its class and whether it is constructed, so a relative distinguished name written as a `SEQUENCE`, one holding no attribute, an attribute that is not exactly a primitive object identifier and one value, or a value whose tag number matches a string type under another class refuses rather than keying, each of which would otherwise key the same as the well-formed encoding. A value that does not read as text keys by its bytes together with its full tag identity. Two `null`s are not a match, so check for `null` before comparing. The S/MIME chain check uses it to decide which certificate a SignerInfo names.

items.title: Primitives that document an error code document all of them
items.body:
An error code is what an operator writes in a catch, and 110 primitives named some of theirs and left the rest undiscoverable, 594 codes in all, of which two turned out to be codes nothing could ever raise. `b.csp.build` named one of nine, so `csp/header-injection`, `csp/unsafe-keyword`, `csp/catch-all-source` and `csp/data-source` reached nobody. `b.mail.crypto.smime.checkCert` attributed the SHA-1 and short-RSA refusals to `mail-crypto/smime/bad-cert` when they arrive as `mail-crypto/smime/refused-hash` and `mail-crypto/smime/rsa-too-small`. `b.problemDetails.create` named one of eight, `b.guardManageSieveCommand.validate` one of 27, and the `parseNotification` method on the handle `b.auth.ciba.client.create` returns one of seven. The `pollToken` method on that same handle named the two codes an operator polls through and none of the four that end the request, so a poll loop had nothing to tell it to stop. Others wrote their list as a run of bare suffixes after one full code, so `b.safeDns.parseResponse`, `b.safeIcal.parse`, `b.safeIcap.parse` and `b.safeVcard.parse` listed sixteen, sixteen, eleven and twelve codes with only the first of each written in full, which no operator can search for. Each code is now written out with the condition that raises it. `b.guardMarkdown.render` named one of six and omitted the size and amplification budgets, `b.fileType.assertOneOf` named one of five and called a second `EMPTY`, which is not a code the framework raises, and `b.auditSign.rotateSigningKey` named one of four. Another group documented only what the handle a factory returns throws, and not what building it refuses: `b.auth.fal.requireFal` named the code its guard raises and not `auth/bad-fal-band` for a band it cannot build a guard for, `b.deprecate.warn` said it throws in error mode without naming `deprecate/used-in-error-mode`, and `b.wsClient.connect` said every failure arrives on the `error` event when eight of its eleven refusals are thrown before the client is returned. `b.backup.create`, `b.backup.bundleAdapterStorage`, `b.cluster.init`, `b.dev.create`, `b.mail.scan.create`, `b.middleware.idempotencyKey`, `b.time.monotonicClock` and `b.workerPool.create` stated their bounds in prose and left every code for them unnamed.

The largest group is a primitive that raises a code through a helper it calls rather than from its own body, which reaches the caller just the same and was documented nowhere. `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` now lists the eighteen further refusals its per-signer verification and its chain walk make; `b.safeUrl.canonicalize` lists the seven its `parse` makes; `b.db.init` lists the 29 its boot checks and config validation make, each with the check that raises it, and names the three the encrypt-to-disk path raises instead so a caller does not catch for them here; and `b.storage.exists`, `listVersions` and `presignedUploadPolicy` list the six that picking a backend can raise. Where a code is reached but cannot actually arise, the block says so rather than claiming it: `b.safeJson.jsonCopyUnderCap` takes no `schema`, so it names the schema-validation refusals as ones that cannot occur in a copy, and `b.network.dns.discoverEncrypted` says `dns/no-result` does not reach the caller because it translates that into `dns/ddr-not-discovered`. No behavior changed in any of these.

items.title: guardImapCommand describes the per-verb checks it performs
items.body: `b.guardImapCommand`'s documentation described a per-verb argument-shape check refusing with `guard-imap-command/bad-shape`. No such check and no such code exist. What the verb selects is which caps run: a zero-argument verb refuses arguments with `guard-imap-command/unexpected-args`, a mailbox-first verb has the name measured against the mailbox cap, a sequence-set-first verb has its element count measured, and a SEARCH-family verb has its parenthesis nesting measured. Argument arity beyond the zero-argument verbs is not checked, which the documentation now says, so a listener that needs `LOGIN` to carry exactly two arguments checks that itself.

items.title: S/MIME trust anchors are documented on the primitives that read them
items.body: `trustAnchorCertsPem` turns on certificate-chain validation in `b.mail.crypto.smime.verify` and `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll`, and appeared only in the namespace's prose, so an operator reading either primitive could not find how to enable it. Both now document it, including that omitting it verifies the signature and leaves the chain unchecked. `b.mail.crypto.smime.checkCert` documents `certPem`, which until now appeared only inside its example.

items.title: atomicFile.read honors allowShortRead instead of accepting and dropping it
items.body: `b.atomicFile.read` and `b.atomicFile.readSync` built the descriptor read's options without carrying `allowShortRead` across, so the option was accepted and then ignored: `allowShortRead: true` still threw `atomic-file/short-read` on a file that shrank between the stat and the read, and a value of the wrong type reached nothing that could refuse it. It is forwarded now, which also makes the refusal the documentation promised reachable: the option suppresses a check, so it is accepted only as a real boolean and anything else raises `atomic-file/bad-opt`. Both primitives document it, as does `b.atomicFile.readJson`, which reads through them.

items.title: A missing file reports the code the primitive actually raises
items.body:
`b.atomicFile.read` and `b.atomicFile.readJson` said a path that does not exist throws `atomic-file/not-found`. It does not, and never did: the error was built with that code and `code` was then assigned `ENOENT` before the throw, so an operator catching the documented code never matched, while `b.atomicFile.readSync` documented `ENOENT` and was right. `ENOENT` is the code all three raise, it is the code they now build, and all three blocks say so. `ENOENT` is also what the retry predicate reads to decide a filesystem failure is transient, and what a caller already reads from `fs` for a missing file, so nothing changes for code written against the behavior rather than against the sentence.

The `send` method on the handle `b.notify.create` returns had the same shape: a transport timeout built `notify/timeout` and overwrote it with `ETIMEDOUT`, which is the code it raises and now the code it builds. An errno-shaped code is a deliberate choice in both places, as it is for `b.httpClient` and the OTLP gRPC sink; what was wrong was building one code and delivering another, which left two of the 594 codes above documented and unreachable.

items.title: Envelopes and chains that used to pass now refuse
items.body:
A multi-signer S/MIME envelope passed to `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` with `trustAnchorCertsPem` refuses when any signer's certificate does not chain to a supplied anchor, including the case where two signers name different certificates carrying the same key. A bundle whose certificates carry the signer's key but do not include the one the sid names raises `mail-crypto/smime/signer-cert-not-named` from both `verify` and `verifyAll`, and an envelope whose sid is a subject-key identifier raises `mail-crypto/smime/unbindable-sid` when trust anchors are supplied; verifying it without anchors is unchanged. An issuer name carrying a code point RFC 4518 prohibits, such as one of the control or format characters added to Unicode after 3.2, cannot be canonicalized, so it binds only when the sid's issuer field and the certificate's are byte-identical, which is what a conforming producer emits. Two different encodings of such a name do not match each other and reach `mail-crypto/smime/signer-cert-not-named`. A DN of letters, digits, spaces and punctuation is unaffected, and so is a certificate whose subject and issuer bytes are equal, which still counts as self-issued for the path-length exemption. A `PrintableString`, `IA5String` or `TeletexString` holding bytes outside its own repertoire is no longer decoded as Latin-1 and compared as text; it is compared by those bytes. Two such values that are byte-identical still match, which is the ordinary case, but a malformed one no longer matches the well-formed spelling of the same name, and that reaches the same refusal.

If one of these starts refusing, the envelope was being accepted on one signer's chain: supply the anchors for every signer, or verify the signer you care about through `b.mail.crypto.smime.verify` with that signer's key.

A timestamp token carrying more than one SignerInfo raises `tsa/multiple-signers` from `b.tsa.verifyToken`; a conformant RFC 3161 token carries one and is unaffected.

`b.mail.deploy.autoConfigXml` refuses an `opts` key it does not accept with `mail-deploy/bad-opts`, which its documentation already described and only `requireObject` enforced, so a key outside `domain`, `displayName`, `imap`, `pop3`, `smtp` and `jmap` was accepted and ignored. A caller passing an extra key now gets the refusal instead of a configuration document silently missing what that key was meant to set, which is what a misspelled `displayName` produced. Remove the key, or spell it as the list spells it.

`b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` refuses a CMS structure it cannot read with `mail-crypto/smime/parse-failed`, the code `verify` has always used. It parsed outside any catch before, so a malformed envelope escaped as the CMS layer's own code, which varied with how the envelope was malformed. A caller matching on `parse-failed` now sees it from both entry points.

Two distinguished names that differ only by a Unicode COMPATIBILITY variant are no longer one name, because the comparison normalizes to form C rather than form KC. `b.x509Chain.pathLenSatisfied` therefore counts a self-issued rollover that re-encoded its own name into such a variant, for instance a full-width `ＣＡ` against `CA`, where it previously exempted it. Case, encoding type, whitespace, and precomposed against decomposed spellings are unaffected, so a rollover that re-encodes between `PrintableString` and `UTF8String`, or changes case, is exempt as before. If a chain starts failing on path length, compare the DNs byte for byte: the rollover is re-encoding its name into a compatibility form, and re-issuing it with the name spelled as the predecessor spells it restores the exemption.

`b.atomicFile.read`, `b.atomicFile.readSync` and `b.atomicFile.readJson` raise `atomic-file/bad-opt` for an `allowShortRead` that is not a boolean, where the value used to be ignored. A caller that was passing `allowShortRead: true` and relying on the throw it did not suppress will now get the short buffer instead; drop the option to keep the refusal.

items.title: A framework error's code is not reassigned after it is built
items.body: A framework error's `code` is its contract, and assigning over it after construction leaves the first code reachable by nobody while any block naming it promises a failure the caller can never receive. `test/layer-0-primitives/codebase-patterns.test.js` refuses the shape across `lib/`, carrying the binding from the declaration into the assignment so only the error's own `code` counts. It fires on the two sites that had it, `b.atomicFile.read`'s missing-path error and the transport timeout in the handle `b.notify.create` returns, and on neither of the shapes next to it: setting `code` on a plain `new Error` to hand a caller a Node-shaped failure is what the SPF and DMARC evaluators behind `b.mail.spf`, the DNS resolver and `b.wsClient.connect` do for callers that read dns and lookup errors, and an errno-shaped code is fine when it is the code that was built.

items.title: One record, one row, and a chain nothing records to does not grow
items.body: `test/layer-0-primitives/audit-query-self-log.test.js` already covered the read path's self-log, where a query for audit data records exactly one `audit.read`. The write path asks the same question and had no test. It now brings up cluster mode over a SQLite-backed external backend and pins four things: one `b.audit.record` call appends exactly one row, the chain does not grow across an idle window, a checkpoint appends no row past the counter it anchors, and `b.audit.verify` appends nothing to the chain it walks. The three read assertions already in the file are the control for the fix, since a suppression that reached too far would stop `b.audit.query` recording the read it is required to record.

items.title: Two different letters cannot take one distinguished-name key
items.body: `test/layer-0-primitives/x509-chain-canonical-name.test.js` groups every code point in the BMP and the first two supplementary planes by the key `b.x509Chain.canonicalNameKey` gives it, and requires each group to be a single Unicode case class. 145,921 of the 194,527 scanned code points reach a key, and 2,388 keys are shared by more than one, all of them case variants. Unifying case variants is what a case-insensitive attribute is defined to do; merging two different letters is the defect, and this is the assertion that distinguishes them over the whole space rather than over the examples anyone thought of. Run against a build that normalizes to form KC instead of form C, the same scan reports 24,355 pairs that share a key without being case variants, because a compatibility variant is not a case variant of what it maps to, so it also pins the normalization form. It checks that most of the scanned code points reach a key at all, so a prohibition that grew to refuse most of Unicode could not make it vacuous.

items.title: A block that names an error code must name every code its function throws
items.body:
`test/layer-0-primitives/operator-doc-error-codes.test.js` reads each documented primitive's error codes out of its comment block and compares them against the codes its function raises, whether from its own body or through a helper it calls. A block that names none is out of scope, since it documents nothing to be partial about. A code built inside a nested function is thrown when that function runs, so a body that runs LATER is removed from the comparison, which is a returned handle or a registered listener, while the throws the outer function makes itself are kept. A callback runs into the caller unless the call it was handed to defers it, which listing the synchronous ones got backwards: that list has to grow for every API anyone uses, and it was missing `new Promise`, `.then`, `.catch` and every comparator or replacer handed to something else, so `b.backup.runInWorker`'s two rejections and the seven transport failures behind `b.network.dns.querySvcb` were invisible. The constructs that genuinely defer are few and do not grow, so those are named instead, and everything else counts: `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` raises `mail-crypto/smime/bad-chain-cert` and `mail-crypto/smime/bad-trust-anchor` inside `Array.map` callbacks, and removing every nested body hid both. A function whose shape the scan cannot read is held back whole rather than read wrongly. The bodies come out whether they are written with the `function` keyword, as a shorthand method or as an arrow, which matters because reading only the keyword had attributed every method of a returned handle to the factory that built it. A literal on the far side of an equality test is a code being recognized rather than thrown, so it is not demanded.

Which literals count as error codes is decided by reading every `throw` and `reject`, not by matching call shapes. Anchoring on an error class beside the literal is precise and blind by construction: `lib/guard-markdown.js` builds every error through `var _err = GuardMarkdownError.factory`, `lib/a2a.js` through `errorClass.factory(...)` on a parameter, and `lib/sql.js` passes the code as a trailing argument, so all three had an empty vocabulary, every code was filtered out, and their documented blocks went unchecked while the gate reported clean. Every code reaches an operator by being thrown, so that is the construct read; the ten IANA top-level media types are excluded, since a media type is written exactly like a code. This surfaced `b.queue.enqueueFlow`, which documented its two graph refusals and not `queue/bad-flow` or `queue/flow-unsupported`.

A code raised by a local helper the primitive calls is the primitive's to document, so the comparison follows those calls transitively rather than reading one lexical body: `b.archive.unwrap` reaches `_tenantKey`, which throws `archive-wrap/no-tenant-id`, and `b.mail.crypto.smime.verifyAll` reaches the refusals its per-signer verification and its chain walk make. Call detection reads a body whose strings and comments are masked, and skips member calls, because neither `"db.init() must be awaited"` nor `JSON.parse(` is a call to a local function of that name; without both, `b.db.stream` was asked to document `db/bad-at-rest`, which it does not throw. A code the primitive's own body compares against is one it HANDLES, so a helper raising it is not propagated: `b.network.dns.discoverEncrypted` catches `dns/no-result` from the SVCB query and throws `dns/ddr-not-discovered` instead, and demanding the caught code would put a failure in the documentation that an operator can never receive. Only propagation is suppressed, so a primitive that compares a code and also builds it still documents it. Whether comparing a code handles it depends on what that branch does next, and one catch answers that both ways: a backup object-store adapter returns on `objectstore/not-found` and re-raises everything else, while the `pollToken` method on the handle `b.auth.ciba.client.create` returns reads `auth-ciba/expired_token`, `auth-ciba/access_denied`, `auth-ciba/invalid_grant` and `auth-ciba/transaction_failed` only to drop its polling state and then re-raises the error it caught. A branch that returns, or that throws a different error, handles the code; a branch that re-raises leaves the caller holding it, so it stays in the contract. Reading the catch whole answered eleven catches in `lib/` the first way wrongly and `pollToken` the second, and all four of its codes are now in the block.

The body a block describes is the function it NAMES, not whichever function follows it. A module-local helper sitting between the two had its codes read as that primitive's: the block for `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties` is followed by a concurrency validator belonging to `jmap.create`. The gate names the function it is looking for and finds it, rather than taking whatever follows the block, and it counts how often that lands somewhere other than the adjacent function so the number is visible rather than asserted.

A code written in quotes counts as documented as well as one in backticks, in the prose above the block's first multi-line tag. A block that spelled all of its codes in quotes extracted none, and a block that names no code is out of scope, so the gate reported clean over a block it had never judged. Counting quotes anywhere in the block instead produced 23 further demands that came from examples rather than from prose, since `@opts` and `@example` carry quoted profile names, sample inputs and illustrated outputs, and one sample output line read as a claim about every code `b.guardMessageId.validate` raises. A block on a factory method is not adjacent to its function either: `pollToken`'s block is followed by two unrelated declarations and the method itself sits sixty lines below it and indented, so seven blocks that name a code were compared against nothing while 254 were judged. The lookup finds an indented declaration and delimits its body by matching its own braces, because an indented function's closing brace is indented too. A code's suffix can carry an underscore, which none of the three patterns describing a code admitted, so the six `auth-ciba` codes carrying the CIBA and OAuth wire names were invisible in a backtick and in prose alike.

The gate reports how many blocks were narrowed and how many were held back, so the scope cannot quietly shrink, asserts that most of `lib/` contributes a vocabulary at all, so a regression that empties the filter fails here instead of passing quietly, and asserts that the helper call graph is readable, so coverage cannot silently shrink to the bodies it can parse. A code is counted as documented wherever it is written inside a backticked span, not only when the span is the bare code, since `VaultError("vault/not-initialized")` names the code an operator greps for. What counts as a code the function raises is the part that took the most getting right, and each shape came from a site in the tree rather than from a guess. A code reaches a caller through a `throw` or a `reject`, through an error assigned and thrown a few lines later, through one returned for a caller to throw, through a validator carrying an error class beside it, and through a local helper whose body throws. An error handed straight to another call is not raised here, because `b.workerPool.create` builds `workerpool/task-failed` and hands it to the function that rejects a TASK's promise; nor is a code written as an audit event's `reason`, which reports it. A nested function the body calls is part of the contract, while one reached only from a method on the returned object is not, so a factory is not asked for its handle's codes. The grammar reads a code as the option it names is spelled, so `mail-deploy/bad-displayName` is no longer invisible. Each shape is pinned by a fixture, and `b.httpClient.downloadStream`, `b.httpClient.uploadMultipartStream`, `b.mail.deploy.autoConfigXml`, `b.openapi.create`, `b.safeJson.canonical`, `b.workerPool.create` and `b.regexLinear.compile` gained the sixteen codes this reading found. The full list of omissions goes to `.test-output/operator-doc-error-codes.log`. It is registered in the static-gate block, where it takes about a second, so an incomplete list is reported before a test run rather than after one; it also runs inside smoke, as every file under `test/layer-0-primitives/` does.

releases.headline: A flag that loosens a check is refused unless it is a boolean, on every path that sets it
