releases.summary: A guard reads a loosening flag truthily, which is correct for a boolean, so a value of the wrong type reads as ON while the operator wrote the word false. Calling a guard with the flag directly already refused that, because the shared option resolver validates every flag its profile declares as a boolean. Two other ways in did not: `buildProfile` merged an override without consulting that declaration, and a `profile` supplied as an object was accepted and then half-read, its keys never reaching the resolver that would have checked them. Both are refused now, and two primitives that own their own options, `b.network.dns.dnssec.verifyDenial` and `b.cbor.encode`, validate the loosening flag they each read.

items.title: A profile override that loosens a guard must be a boolean
items.body: `buildProfile({ baseProfile: "strict", overrides: { ... } })` merged an override into the resolved profile without checking its type, and the guards read a loosening flag truthily because the profiles declare it as a boolean. So `allowImageData: "false"` under the strict profile turned `data:` URI acceptance ON while reading as though it were off, and the same held for `allowComments`, `allowAnimation` and `allowExternalRefs`. Calling the guard with the flag directly was never affected: `b.gateContract.resolveProfileAndPosture` validates every flag the declared defaults give a boolean value, so `b.guardSql.validate(sql, { allowLiterals: "false" })` already raised `sql/bad-opt`. The profile is the declaration, so the merge judges an override against it and raises `gate-contract/bad-override`, naming the key and the type it received. A real boolean still overrides either way, and a key the profile does not declare as a boolean is not judged by this rule.

items.title: A guard profile is named, so an object is refused rather than half-read
items.body: Every guard documents `profile` as one of its own profile names. An object was accepted and then read in part: the overlay the resolver builds is only populated for a string, so an object's keys never reached the resolved options and never met the validation applied there, yet the values still took effect further down. A profile built with `allowLiterals: "false"` and passed as `b.guardSql.validate(sql, { profile: built })` was accepted, and the embedded string literal that profile exists to refuse went through. A non-string `profile` now raises `<guard>/bad-profile` and says where a deliberate delta belongs, which is `overrides` on `buildProfile`. Passing a profile name is unchanged.

items.title: An Opt-Out NSEC3 denial is accepted only on a real boolean
items.body: `b.network.dns.dnssec.verifyDenial`'s `allowOptOut` accepts an Opt-Out NSEC3 proof, which shows only that no SIGNED record exists rather than that the name does not exist, so it widens what counts as a valid denial. The call validated its option names but not their types, and the flag was read truthily, so `allowOptOut: "false"` accepted an Opt-Out proof the operator had written `false` to refuse. Measured against a real Opt-Out NSEC3 chain. A non-boolean now raises `dnssec/bad-opt`; omitting the option still refuses such a proof, and `true` still accepts it.

items.title: NaN and Infinity reach CBOR bytes only on a real boolean
items.body: `b.cbor.encode`'s `allowNonFinite` permits NaN and Infinity into the encoding, and those bytes are what `b.cms`, `b.mdoc`, `b.eat` and content credentials sign. The option was read truthily and never type-checked, in a file that already validated `requireDeterministic` beside it, which tightens rather than loosens and is harmless when mistyped. A non-boolean now raises `cbor/bad-input`; omitting it still refuses a non-finite number with `cbor/non-finite`.

items.title: A mistyped guard flag or a profile object now raises instead of being ignored
items.body: Three calls that used to be accepted now refuse. A `buildProfile` override of a flag the profile declares as a boolean must be a boolean, so `overrides: { allowImageData: "false" }` raises `gate-contract/bad-override` where it used to loosen the guard. A `profile` passed as an object raises `<guard>/bad-profile`; pass the profile name, and express a delta through `overrides`. And `b.network.dns.dnssec.verifyDenial`'s `allowOptOut` and `b.cbor.encode`'s `allowNonFinite` raise on a non-boolean. In each case the previous behavior was to read the value as true, so a deployment that hits one of these errors was running with the protection off.

releases.headline: A bot-challenge ladder counts an API key as a caller, and an identity hook can no longer end the process
releases.summary: The adaptive bot-challenge ladder named its caller from `req.user` and `req.actor` but not from `req.apiKey`, where `b.middleware.requireBoundKey` stores the principal it verified, so a route authenticated by key alone and carrying no body credential counted every key behind one address on one ladder. Each rung of that key now carries its own namespace, so the value one rung reads cannot spell another's, and a carrier names a principal only when it is an object, because a raw key string is the secret itself. Separately, `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` and `b.requestHelpers.actorDisplayName` call an operator-supplied `actorKey` hook without awaiting it, so an `async` hook that threw returned a rejected promise that nothing handled and Node ended the process on it.

items.title: A bot-challenge ladder counts an API key as a caller, not its address
items.body: `b.authBotChallenge`'s default key names the caller from the body credential, then the authenticated principal, then the client address. It read `req.user` and `req.actor` only, and `b.middleware.requireBoundKey` stores the principal it verified on `req.apiKey`, so a route authenticated by key alone that carries no credential in its body named no principal and fell to the address. Every key behind one NAT or one reverse proxy then advanced a single ladder: one key reaching the escalation threshold challenged or locked out the rest, and one key's failures were spent on the others' budget. Measured before the fix: two distinct keys from one address both keyed on `198.51.100.9`. `req.apiKey` resolves through `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` now, under its own prefix, so a user and an API key carrying the same id remain two callers. An API-key record is named by its `id`, or by its `ownerId` when it carries none, which is the shape `requireBoundKey` stores when a resolver returns a record without an id. The owner fallback keys under `apikey-owner:` rather than `apikey:`, and keeps the record's `tenantId` binding, so a key whose `id` is another key's `ownerId` is still a different caller, and one owner in two tenants is two callers. A deployment whose routes carry a body credential, or whose callers are named on `req.user`, counts the same principals as before.

items.title: A raw API key never becomes a cache key, an audit value or a lockout counter
items.body: The ladder key is written to `req.botChallengeKey`, used as the lockout key, stored in the session store for the challenge TTL, and emitted as the audit `resource.id`. `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` folds a primitive actor into the key verbatim, so a credential carried as a bare string, which is what `req.apiKey = req.headers["x-api-key"]` holds, would put the key itself in all four places. The credential carrier now names a principal only when it is an object, matching the guard the idempotency scope already applied, and a request carrying a bare string is counted per address instead. Operators who set `req.apiKey` to a record object are unaffected, and `req.user` and `req.actor`, which are not credentials, still name a principal when they are a string or a number.

items.title: One rung of the challenge key cannot spell another rung's
items.body: The body credential was returned raw and lowercased with no namespace of its own, so it shared one key space with the authenticated rungs. An unauthenticated request could therefore name its body credential after a real principal's ladder and drive that ladder to the escalation threshold from an unrelated address, locking the principal out; measured end to end to a 423. Every rung now carries a namespace: `body:<field>:<credential>`, `actor:<key>`, `apikey:<key>`, `apikey-owner:<key>` and `addr:<ip>`, so the spaces are disjoint. The body rung names the field as well as the value, because it reads `email` then `username` and a username that reads like someone's address is not that person. The address needed one too, because the caller partly chooses it: a request from inside a declared proxy range selects which forwarded hop is read, so without a namespace it could present a named principal's ladder as its own address and lock that principal out. **`req.botChallengeKey` changes value for a request named by a body credential or by the address**: it reads `body:email:user@example.com` and `addr:198.51.100.7` where it read `user@example.com` and `198.51.100.7`. Pass `req.botChallengeKey` to `recordFailure` and `check` rather than rebuilding the key, which is what the documented pairing has always been. Ladder state is held in the operator's store under a TTL, so existing counters age out rather than needing migration.

items.title: An async identity hook no longer ends the process
items.body: `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` and `b.requestHelpers.actorDisplayName` call an operator-supplied `actorKey` hook synchronously and read its return value. An `async` hook returns a promise, which can never name a principal, and when its body threw the rejection reached nothing: Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` then ended the process, so one flag evaluation on one request took the listener down. Both now detect a promise return, attach a handler to it, and treat the hook as having named nobody. A synchronous hook behaves exactly as before, including a synchronous throw, which the caller still sees.

items.title: An actorKey hook that is not a function is refused instead of ignored
items.body: `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` reads an `actorKey` hook only when it is a function and otherwise falls back to the identity fields it knows. `b.flag.context.fromRequest` forwarded the option without checking its type, so a hook supplied as a string or an object was dropped silently: an actor carrying only the custom field it was meant to name became unnameable, and the call returned the address-derived `anon:<ip-hash>` targeting key. Behind a shared proxy that merges unrelated callers into one percentage rollout and one cached flag decision. The option now raises `flag/bad-context` at the call, naming the type it received. Passing a function is unchanged, and so is omitting the option; `null` and `undefined` still mean no hook, while `false`, `0` and `""` are refused rather than ignored.

items.title: The vendored Public Suffix List is refreshed
items.body: `lib/vendor/public-suffix-list.dat` moves from the 2026-09-24 snapshot to 2026-10-01_23-02-52_UTC. One rule changes: the retired `juniper` gTLD is no longer a public suffix, so a hostname under it is now treated as an ordinary registrable name by `b.safeUrl`, `b.guardDomain` and cookie-scope checks. The rest is upstream's gTLD import timestamp and two registry-operator renames in comments.

items.title: A forwarded actorKey hook is validated as a function
items.body: A module that forwards an operator-supplied `actorKey` into `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` has to refuse a non-function at the call, because the resolver's fallback is an identity the operator did not ask for rather than an error they can see. A check covers `lib/` for the forward and is satisfied by the validation beside it.

items.title: Only a tag something reads keeps a comment block in lib
items.body: The rule that preserves a documented block from the comment stripper asked whether a line began with an at-sign word, not which word, so inventing a tag kept any prose beside it. The recognized set is now explicit, every tag in `lib/` is in it, and a block whose only tag is unrecognized is reported like any other narrative.

items.title: Pass req.botChallengeKey rather than rebuilding the ladder key
items.body: A request named by a body credential now keys on `body:<field>:<credential>` instead of the bare credential, and one named by its address on `addr:<ip>` instead of the bare address, so code that rebuilds the key by hand, such as `recordFailure(req.body.email.toLowerCase())` or `recordFailure(clientIp)`, advances a different ladder than the middleware counted. Pass `req.botChallengeKey`, which the middleware writes for exactly this. Existing ladder entries expire under `challengeTtlMs`, 30 minutes by default, so there is nothing to migrate.

releases.headline: One resolver names the principal, a type check does not read which realm made a value, and a limit must be a number
releases.summary: Four kinds of check were reading something other than what they were written to read. `instanceof` compares against one realm's constructor, so bytes, patterns and dates built in a worker, a `vm` context or another copy of the framework read as the wrong type. A walker classified values by type name and missed `Map`, `Set`, `Promise`, `ArrayBuffer` and `DataView`, each of which a `JSON.stringify` reads as an empty object. A limit taken from options was compared without being checked as a number, and every comparison with a non-number is false, so such a limit allowed everything. Identity was resolved per module by reading whichever field a caller happened to use, so principals that `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` separates were folded into one key. The entries under Security are the ones where the wrong reading skipped a check instead of refusing the input.

items.title: A CSV export under a redacting posture redacts
items.body: `b.guardCsv.serialize` read `piiPolicy: "redact"` as "redact if the caller also passed `opts.redact`", and the HIPAA, PCI-DSS and GDPR postures all set that policy. An operator who selected a posture and wrote no redactor of their own got the rows back whole: measured under the HIPAA posture, a Social Security number and a Luhn-valid card number both reached the output. The policy now scrubs every emitted string cell with `b.redact.redactText`, which removes SSNs, card numbers, JWTs, PEM blocks, AWS keys and URL passwords and leaves the surrounding text. `opts.redact` still replaces it, and a value carrying no `string(value)` method is refused rather than ignored.

items.title: An idempotency key cannot answer two principals from one cache entry
items.body: The default scope read `actor.userId` and folded every other actor onto the literal `"anon"`. `extractActorContext` fills `userId` from `req.user.id`, `req.user.userId` or `req.apiKey.ownerId` only, so a bearer token carrying `sub`, the ordinary OIDC shape, left every principal on that literal. Two authenticated users sending the same idempotency key were answered from one cache entry: measured, the second received the first's status, headers and body verbatim. An actor the request carries is now scoped by `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey`, which tags the key with the field it came from so `id:"x"` and `sub:"x"` cannot collide, and refuses an actor it cannot name rather than folding it onto a shared literal. A request carrying no actor keeps the shared anonymous scope, because the middleware cannot tell two anonymous callers apart by construction.

items.title: A step-up grant binds to the principal that holds it, not to one field's text
items.body: `b.middleware.requireStepUp` matches a grant's subject against `req.user.id`, then `userId`, then `claims.sub`, then `sub`. A grant carried only the text, so every principal named by any of those four fields with the same text held the same grant: measured, one grant minted for `"collide"` elevated all four of `{ id }`, `{ userId }`, `{ claims.sub }` and `{ sub }`. `b.auth.stepUp.grant.create({ actor: req.user })` mints a grant bound to the field that names the principal as well as to the value, and the middleware passes the request's actor so the check runs against that binding. Such a grant is refused for a principal named by a different field, and refused outright when the caller checks it without naming an actor, rather than falling back to the text. `create` refuses an actor and a subject together, and refuses an actor that names no principal. `{ subject: "..." }` is unchanged and keeps matching the resolver's chain.

items.title: A break-glass grant, an unseal-rate bucket and a static quota window each name one principal
items.body: Four per-actor buckets derived identity by reading fields inline, and each folded principals that `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` separates. `b.breakGlass` records a grant's holder as `user:<userId>` or `apikey:<keyId>`; a user whose `userId` spelled an API key's id produced the same holder text, so `listActive` returned each of them the other's live grant ids, and `unsealRow` redeems a grant from its id alone. That same text keyed the factor lockout and the TOTP replay-step reservation. `revokeAll` now takes either prefix to target one holder and a bare id to reach both, and refuses when the grants table carries no derived owner hash, where it previously dropped the actor criterion and revoked by table alone, or revoked every active grant when no table was named.

items.title: A sealed-column read names the principal its unseal-failure cap counts for
items.body: `b.cryptoField.configureUnsealRateCap` is armed by default and counts unseal failures per (actor, table, column). No shipped read named an actor, so every read shared one bucket: once a forged value in a sealed column tripped the threshold, the framework refused that column to every reader for the whole cooldown, five minutes by default. `b.db.from(table).asActor(actor)` names the principal a read is for, and `first()`, `all()` and `stream()` carry it. The chain refuses an actor that names no principal, and refuses null or undefined, since a read with no actor is what happens when the call is omitted. `b.breakGlass.unsealRow` counts against the grant's holder, and `unsealRowAsService` against the API key that opened the bypass.

items.title: A step-up audit row names the principal the decision was about
items.body: `b.middleware.requireStepUp` decides which principal a step-up applies to by reading `req.user.id`, then `userId`, then `claims.sub`, then `sub`, so it serves a principal named by any of the four. The two audit emitters read `req.user.id` alone, so a decision about a principal named by one of the other three was recorded with a null actor: the row said a step-up was required or satisfied and named nobody it was about, which is the unattributed state `b.audit.bindActor` refuses. The four-field chain now lives in `b.auth.stepUp`, which owns the question, and both the matcher and the emitters read it, so a future edit cannot narrow what the audit names while leaving what the matcher matches. `b.auth.stepUp.emitAuditRequired` and `emitAuditSatisfied` take an optional audit sink as a trailing argument, the shape every other audited primitive here already accepts.

items.title: An agent audit row carries its actor whichever field names it
items.body: `b.agent.saga`, `b.agent.eventBus`, `b.agent.orchestrator`, `b.agent.idempotency`, `b.agent.postureChain`, `b.agent.snapshot`, `b.agent.stream`, `b.agent.tenant`, `b.agent.trace` and `b.mail.agent` share one actor normalizer, and it read `actor.id` into both the row's `id` and its `userId`. An actor written as `{ userId }`, `{ username }`, `{ sub }`, `{ principalId }` or `{ email }` produced a row with no actor at all, which `b.audit.bindActor` refuses and which leaves the action unattributed everywhere else. It now reads the fields `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` reads, in that order, and a string or number actor keeps its own name instead of becoming the system actor.

items.title: Redaction recognizes bytes it did not construct, and a byte body is scanned
items.body: `b.redact.redact` replaced a byte value with its marker only when this realm's `Uint8Array` had built it. A byte array built anywhere else fell past that branch to the plain-object walk, which found no properties to copy and wrote each byte as a numbered key: a six-byte secret came out as `{"0":115,"1":101,"2":99,"3":114,"4":101,"5":116}` where the same bytes built here collapse to `[REDACTED]`. A classifier from `b.redact.classifyDefaults` decided the same way whether a body was bytes, so a body built elsewhere skipped the text scan and returned `verdict: "clean"` for a payload carrying a Social Security number. `b.redact.installOutboundDlp` gates egress on that verdict, so the payload left as clean. Values like these come from operator code that evaluates anything in a `node:vm` context; the framework's own worker boundary does not produce them, because structured clone rebuilds a typed array with the receiving realm's constructor.

items.title: A write-once record stores the bytes it was given
items.body: `b.worm.put` decided whether its input was bytes the same way, so three bytes from another realm were stored as the nineteen bytes of `{"0":1,"1":2,"2":3}` and the record's digest covered that instead. A WORM record is write-once and retained, so a second put cannot repair it.

items.title: A mail filter cannot be walked past its own refusals
items.body: `b.guardMailQuery.validate` refuses a `RegExp` in a filter with `mail-query/regex-not-allowed` and refuses an invalid `Date` with `mail-query/bad-date`. Both refusals tested the realm, so a pattern or a date built elsewhere walked past them, reached the key walk, which is empty for those values, and validated clean.

items.title: A serializer refuses a value it would otherwise write as empty
items.body: A `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, `RegExp`, `ArrayBuffer`, `SharedArrayBuffer` or `DataView` keeps its data outside its own properties, so JSON writes `{}` for it and CBOR writes a one-byte empty map. `b.canonicalJson.stringify` refused the first three by name and wrote the empty object for the rest, and callers sign those bytes. `b.safeJson.stringify` wrote `{}` for all of them and raised nothing, which is how such a value reached storage empty through every caller that routes through it; it now raises `json/no-form`, naming the key, at the root and at any depth including inside an array. `b.cbor.encode` wrote an empty map for all of them and for a bare `Date`; `b.cose`, `b.cwt`, `b.mdoc`, `b.scitt` and `b.contentCredentials` sign its output. `b.safeJsonPath.validateContainment` accepted every one of them, after which `b.db` serialized the value to `{}` for the query, and every JSON object satisfies a containment predicate against `{}`, so `where({ col: { contains: aMap } })` returned every row rather than the intended ones.

items.title: A limit that is not a number is refused instead of binding nothing
items.body: A limit is enforced by comparing against it, and every comparison with a non-number is false: `entries.length > "abc"` never trips, and `(maxAgeSec || 300) * 1000` is `NaN`, against which every age test is false too. A limit supplied as a string therefore imposed nothing while the configuration said it was set, which is what happens when a limit is read from an environment variable or parsed from JSON without being coerced. Refused at the call now, naming the option: the `maxEntries`, `maxEntryDecompressedBytes`, `maxTotalDecompressedBytes` and `maxExpansionRatio` of `b.archive.read.zip`'s `bombPolicy` and of `b.guardArchive.zipBombPolicy`, which together bound a zip bomb; `maxHeaderCount` and `maxValueBytes` on `b.middleware.headers`, which bound what a client may send; `maxAgeSec` on `b.dbsc.verifyBindingAssertion`, which bounds how long a device-bound session assertion may be replayed and was never type-checked; and `maxResults` on the local `b.objectStore` `list`, which bounds how much of the tree the walk reads. `b.redact.redact`'s `maxDepth` bounds recursion over a log payload and runs where raising is not allowed, so a value it cannot use falls back to the documented default and the bound applies again.

items.title: The vendored-artifact check is documented as what it does, and the checklist reads its verdict
items.body: `b.configDrift.verifyVendorIntegrity` re-hashes every file under `lib/vendor` against `MANIFEST.json` and returns `{ ok, checkedCount, mismatches }`. It does not stop the process, and the framework does not call it. `SECURITY.md` said in two places that it "runs at boot" and that "mismatches abort start", and the operator checklist said to call it "so a tampered artifact aborts start". An operator following that literally calls the function, ignores the verdict, and keeps serving on a swapped crypto bundle with only an audit row to show it. The checklist now carries the lines that read `ok` and stop the boot, the threat model says what the call returns instead of what it aborts, and the assurance case points at the checklist rather than implying the framework acts. That checklist line also passed an `audit` option the call has never had; the audit is emitted on every invocation regardless. The primitive's own documentation named its two throws as `VENDOR_MANIFEST_MISSING` and `VENDOR_MANIFEST_SHAPE` when the codes are `config-drift/vendor-manifest-missing` and `config-drift/vendor-manifest-shape`, so an operator matching on what was written caught nothing; both are corrected and asserted by a test now. A `files` entry carrying no hash was skipped without being counted, which is the silent zero-files-checked pass those throws exist to prevent one entry at a time, and is now reported as a mismatch. Every entry in the shipped manifest carries a hash, so a stock install is unaffected.

items.title: A DKIM "self" requirement names the authenticated identity's domain, not the envelope's
items.body: `b.mail.server.submission.create`'s `dkimRequireMode: "self"` requires a message to carry a `DKIM-Signature` whose `d=` tag names a domain the authenticated identity holds, which is what separates it from `"any"`. The listener resolved that domain from the actor's `domain` field, then from an `id` spelled as an address, and then from the envelope sender. That last fallback let a connection whose actor carried neither field have its `d=` tag compared against its own `MAIL FROM`. The listener reads the tag and does not verify the signature, so a client could write `DKIM-Signature: v=1; d=attacker.example` beside `MAIL FROM:<x@attacker.example>` and satisfy the mode. An unauthenticated connection and one authenticated as `{ id: "u-1042" }` both had such a message queued. `"self"` now means a domain the connection may send as: the actor's `domain`, the domain of an address-shaped `id`, the domain of any assigned mailbox, or the domain of an alias `senderPolicy` approved for the transaction being sent. That last one is scoped to its own transaction, so an approved alias does not sign for the rest of the session. An actor holding none of those, and a connection with no authenticated actor, have no domain for `"self"` to name, so the message is refused. Under the default `identityBinding: "strict"` the envelope sender is already either in the actor's mailbox set or approved by `senderPolicy`, so those listeners behave as before. A listener running `"self"` under `identityBinding: "permissive"`, or under a permissive profile where `MAIL FROM` needs no `AUTH`, refuses mail it previously queued: give the actor a `domain`, an address-shaped `id`, or a mailbox set. `dkimRequireMode` is now described in the option list beside `requireDkim`, where it was accepted but never documented.

items.title: A CalDAV or CardDAV URL is authorized by one declared principal field
items.body: `b.mail.dav`'s `caldavHandler` and `carddavHandler` compare the first path segment of the URL against the principal they resolve from the request and refuse it when the two differ. That principal was resolved from `req.user.principalId`, then `req.user.id`, then `req.user.username`, all into the single namespace the URL addresses, so two actors named through different fields were one principal. A caller authenticated as `{ username: "alice" }` requested `/caldav/alice/cal1/ev1` and received the calendar event belonging to the principal whose `principalId` is `"alice"`, with the same reach for `PUT` and `DELETE`. Each of those requests is well formed on its own, so no per-request check separates them and the field has to be settled for the deployment. The handlers now read `principalId` alone, and `opts.actorPrincipalId(actor, req)` names the field where a deployment carries it elsewhere; when that hook is set it is the only thing consulted. An authenticated request whose actor yields no principal is refused with 401 rather than served under a shared name, and a hook that throws is treated the same way. `dispatchCaldav` and `dispatchCarddav` are unchanged, since a caller on a non-Express transport passes the principal itself. The module also described per-tenant URL isolation as something it provides while never reading a tenant: it isolates by principal ID, and a deployment whose tenants can hold the same ID returns the tenant as part of the hook's value.

items.title: A cached flag decision belongs to the whole evaluation context, and an authenticated caller is named
items.body:
A targeting rule reads any path through the evaluation context, so `attribute: "role"` resolves `role`. `b.flag.cache` keyed an entry on the flag key, the `targetingKey` and the context's `attributes` alone, and `b.flag.context.fromRequest` builds no `attributes`: it carries `userId`, `role`, `email`, `tenantId`, `locale` and `userAgent` at the top level. Every field a rule could decide on was therefore outside the key, and a context asking with `role: "guest"` was answered with the decision computed for `role: "admin"` without the provider being consulted. The key now covers the whole context, as a SHA3-512 digest so it stays a fixed length whatever a client puts in its agent string, and a context that cannot be canonicalized goes straight to the provider instead of being cached.

The key that separates one principal from another was also narrower than the actors reaching it. `fromRequest` read a string `user.id` and nothing else, so an actor carrying `sub` (what `b.middleware.bearerAuth` assigns from a JWT) or a numeric id fell through to the anonymous bucket, `anon:` plus a hash of the client address, shared with every other such caller behind that address. It now names the actor through `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey`, which reads `id`, `userId`, `username`, `sub`, `principalId` and `email`, tags the field the name came from and scopes by `tenantId`. `opts.actorKey(actor)` names an actor whose shape is the deployment's. An actor carrying none of those fields, and an unauthenticated request, are still keyed by the address. The raw identity also reaches the context as `userId` now, so a rule can target an actor named by `sub`.

items.title: A bot-challenge ladder counts one caller, not one address
items.body:
`b.authBotChallenge`'s default key read `body.email`, then `body.username`, then the client address. Every auth route that carries no credential in its body, which is every token refresh, step-up confirmation and OTP check, therefore fell to the address, and an address is shared by everyone behind one NAT or one reverse proxy: a single caller reaching the escalation threshold locked out all of them, and the traffic from everyone else diluted that caller's failures. The key now names the authenticated principal, through `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` and tagged so it cannot be spelled by an email or an address, before it falls back to the address.

The address came from the socket alone, which is right against a forged `X-Forwarded-For` and wrong behind a real proxy, where every request carries the proxy's address and the whole internet shares one ladder. `trustedProxies`, `forwardedHeaders` and `clientIpResolver` are accepted now and resolve the client through `b.requestHelpers.trustedClientIp`, so a forwarded header is honored only where the operator declared the proxy it arrives through. With no proxy declared the key is the socket address, exactly as before.

`middleware()` writes the key it counted on to `req.botChallengeKey`. The post-verify path passes that to `recordFailure`, rather than deriving a second key by hand and advancing a ladder the middleware never reads.

items.title: A principal named by claims.sub is named everywhere, not refused
items.body:
`b.auth.jwt.verify` and its siblings in `b.auth.jar`, `b.auth.oauth`, `b.auth.oid4vp` and `b.auth.openidFederation` all answer with the token payload under `claims`, so an operator whose `b.middleware.bearerAuth` `verify` returns one of those results has `req.user = { claims: { sub } }`. `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` read top-level fields only and answered `null` for that actor, which its own contract defines as refuse-the-operation: `b.fileUpload` ownership, `b.cryptoField`, `b.db` unseal-failure scoping and idempotency scoping refused, while flag evaluation, `b.staticServe` quotas and the `b.authBotChallenge` ladder folded the actor onto the anonymous bucket. `b.auth.stepUp` named the same actor through a `claims.sub` rung of its own.

The drift ran both ways: the shared resolver named an actor carrying only `username` or `principalId` and step-up did not, so `b.middleware.requireStepUp` refused a principal the rest of the framework names. Both now read one list. `claims.sub` is appended last, so no actor an ownership record already names is re-keyed, and every step of a nested read is an own-property read so a prototype cannot supply an identity. `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityFields(actor)` is the reader a primitive uses to ask what names a principal; indexing the field list cannot see a nested entry, and a gate now requires it.

A step-up grant held for an actor carrying both `claims.sub` and a top-level `sub`, `username`, `principalId` or `email` binds to a different principal than before and needs re-elevating once. Grants are short-lived, and no other primitive's keys change.

items.title: The documentation-site validator reads its snapshot through the framework
items.body: `examples/wiki/lib/source-comment-block-validator.js` resolves every `@related` reference against `api-snapshot.json`. It read that file with a bare `JSON.parse` and reported an unreadable snapshot by throwing a plain `Error`, which the wiki's own pattern gate refuses on both counts: a parse without a size bound or prototype screen, and an error a caller cannot dispatch on. It parses through `b.safeJson.parse` now, with an explicit 32 MiB bound because the snapshot is past the 1 MiB default at 1.6 MiB, and raises a typed error carrying `wiki/comment-block-snapshot-unreadable` or `wiki/comment-block-snapshot-shape`. The framework modules are required by path rather than by package name, so the root static gate that loads this engine keeps working without the documentation site's dependencies installed.

items.title: A mistyped trusted-proxy list is refused instead of read as no proxies
items.body: `b.requestHelpers.trustedClientIp` takes `trustedProxies` as one CIDR string or an array of them, and normalized anything else to the empty list. An empty list means no proxy is trusted, so a value of the wrong type left every forwarded header ignored while the configuration said a proxy was trusted, with nothing reported. Its sibling `forwardedHeaders` already refused the same value, so one function answered the same question two ways. A `trustedProxies` that is neither a string nor an array is refused now, naming the caller, and the same applies to `trustedIdentityHeaders`, `trustedProtocol` and `trustedHost`, which share the normalizer. An empty array still means no proxies, which is what omitting it means. `b.authBotChallenge.create` raises these under its own `auth-bot-challenge/bad-opt` rather than letting a bare `TypeError` escape a call that documents that code.

items.title: An audit export does not name an unattributed row after a principal
items.body: `b.auditTools.exportCadf` set the CADF `initiator.id` to `"unknown"` for a row carrying no actor, and `target.id` to `"n/a"` for one carrying no resource. Both are values real data can hold, so a row whose `actorUserId` is literally `unknown` exported the same initiator as every unattributed row, and an auditor grouping by that id read one principal as having performed all of them. The placeholders are `blamejs:unattributed` and `blamejs:unidentified` now, which an actor id cannot be, and an unattributed initiator is no longer typed `service/security/account/user`, since there is no user account to describe. A row that does name an actor or a resource exports exactly what it did before.

items.title: A break-glass grant from an earlier release is not claimed by a current lookup
items.body: Grant owners are recorded as `user:<id>` or `apikey:<id>`, and releases through 0.20.33 recorded them bare. The two spellings meet where a bare id spells a prefixed one: a grant belonging to the user whose literal id is `user:alice` carries the owner hash an ordinary user `alice` now derives, so `listActive` returned that other principal's grant id and `revokeAll({ actorId })` revoked it. A grant id is redeemable, so the exposure is the grant itself and not only its listing. The grants table gains an `ownerKeyVersion` column, added in place on an existing install, and both owner-scoped queries require the current format, so a grant written under either format is reachable only by the lookup that wrote it. `revokeAll({ table })` does not read the owner hash and still reaches any grant, and every grant expires within the policy's `grantTtl`.

items.title: A sealed-column read under an unnameable actor is refused instead of pooled
items.body: `b.db.from(table).asActor(actor)` accepts an object, a string or a number, and refuses a value that names no principal so that `b.cryptoField.configureUnsealRateCap` counts unseal failures per principal. That refusal ran only for objects, so `asActor("")`, `asActor(NaN)` and `asActor(Infinity)` were accepted although the resolver returns no key for any of them, and `b.cryptoField.unsealRow` counted their failures in the shared bucket it uses for reads that name nobody. Those reads spent one rate-cap budget and entered one cooldown together with every other unnamed reader, which is what naming an actor is supposed to prevent. An empty string and a non-finite number now raise `db-query/bad-actor`; `"alice"`, `42` and `0` are accepted as before.

items.title: A valid value is no longer refused for having been built elsewhere
items.body: The same realm test rejected values that were correct. `b.time.toParts` refused a `Date` with `time/bad-input: got object`. `b.safeBuffer.toBuffer`, which nearly every primitive that takes bytes routes through, refused a byte array, and so did `b.acme.revokeCert`, `b.archive.gz`, `b.archive.wrap`, `b.auth.passkey`, `b.auth.saml`, `b.backup`, `b.cms`, `b.contentCredentials`, `b.crypto.xwing`, `b.cwt.verify`, `b.fileType`, `b.mail.bimi`, `b.mail.crypto.pgp`, `b.mail.crypto.smime`, `b.mcp`, `b.objectStore`, `b.sessionDeviceBinding` and `b.vaultWrap.wrap`. `b.safeBuffer.secureZero` returned without wiping, and nothing in its return value distinguished that from a wipe. `b.safeBuffer.byteLengthOfIfMeasurable` answered `null`, which a caller reads as having no size to cap, for 1024 bytes.

items.title: A date, a map and a pattern are read for what they are
items.body: `b.compliance.aiAct.logging` recorded a null timestamp for a date it did not recognize. A `b.db` collection filter keyed on a date matched every row, because the date was read as an operator map and a map with no operators in it constrains nothing. `b.mdoc` read a map's members as undefined. `b.middleware.spanHttpServer` left an `ignorePaths` entry inert, so a path it names stopped matching and nothing rejected the entry either; `b.mail.helo` dropped an `extraPatterns` entry instead of adding it; and `b.dev` never matched a redaction or ignore pattern.

items.title: A rejection carrying an error keeps that error's stack
items.body: `b.appShutdown` hands `onUncaught` the value an unhandled rejection carried, wrapping anything that is not an error. The test was realm-bound, so an error built elsewhere reached an operator's crash-reporting hook as a replacement with the same message and a stack pointing into the framework rather than at the throw site. The check also accepted an object that claims `Error.prototype` and carries no stack, passing it through as a real error; such a value is now wrapped like any other non-error. `b.selfUpdate`'s rollback path replaced the error it then audited, for the same reason.

items.title: A boxed primitive serializes as the value it wraps
items.body: `b.canonicalJson.stringify` wrote `{}` for `new Number(1)`, which has no own properties, and `{"0":"x"}` for `new String("x")`, whose own properties are indices. `b.cbor.encode` wrote an empty map for both. Each now writes the primitive, which is what JSON does.

items.title: A stale binding assertion names the bound that refused it
items.body: `b.dbsc.verifyBindingAssertion`'s `dbsc/stale` refusal reported the bound the caller passed rather than the one it applied, so whenever the default was in force the message read `iat is more than undefineds old`. It now reads the bound in force.

items.title: The requireBoundKey example returns a key record that names its principal
items.body: `b.middleware.requireBoundKey`'s documented example returned a record with no `ownerId`, and the paragraph above it states that a key without one leaves an audit row naming nobody, because `b.requestHelpers.extractActorContext` reads the principal from `req.apiKey.ownerId`. An operator copying the example got the shape the text warns against. The example carries one now, and the middleware no longer drops the `ownerId` a resolver record supplies.

items.title: A filename overlay is checked against what it does
items.body: `b.guardFilename`'s GDPR overlay was verified by reading the overlay object back, which reports what it declares rather than what it does. It is compared against the default now, where a bidi name is refused and the overlay strips it.

items.title: An API key sharing a user's id is a separate idempotency scope
items.body: `b.middleware.idempotencyKey` scopes a cached response to the principal that made the request. Keying it through the identity resolver named the credential's `id` without naming which credential it was, so a user and an unrelated API key that happen to share an `id` produced the same scope: a request carrying `apiKey = { id: "alice", ownerId: "someone-else" }` was served user `alice`'s cached private response and its own handler never ran. The scope now carries the credential it came from, `u:` for a user and `k:` for an API key, which is what `b.staticServe` already did. Each still replays its own slot, so idempotency is unchanged for either caller.

items.title: A step-up grant carrying a bare subject refuses an actor check it cannot answer
items.body: `b.auth.stepUp.grant.verify` compares `opts.actor` against a grant minted with `opts.actor`, and `opts.subject` against one minted with `opts.subject`. A caller who passed only `opts.actor` against a bare-subject grant matched neither branch, so nothing was checked and a grant issued for `alice` verified under `{ actor: { id: "bob" } }`. Such a grant has no actor binding to answer that question with: its subject is an operator-chosen string, not a tagged identity key. It is refused now with `subject_mismatch`, naming both ways forward, mint the grant with `opts.actor` or name the principal with `opts.subject` as well. Passing both, which is what `b.middleware.requireStepUp` does, is unchanged.

items.title: A break-glass grant belongs to the credential that took it out
items.body:
Break-glass grant owners are recorded as `user:<id>` or `apikey:<id>` so a user and an API key cannot be confused. The owner id was read from the audit context, which resolves an API key to its `ownerId`, so a grant taken out with a key was filed under `user:<ownerId>`: it appeared in that owner's own user-session `listActive`, and `revokeAll({ actorId: "apikey:<id>" })` did not reach it. The credential is now resolved from the request, so a key's grant is listed and revoked as the key's.

A grant persisted before those prefixes existed records the earlier ownership format and is not reachable by `actorId`. Revoke such grants by `table`, which does not read the owner hash, or let them expire within the policy's `grantTtl`.

items.title: A DKIM body-length opt-out takes a boolean, not anything truthy
items.body: `b.mail.dkim.verify`'s `acceptBodyLengthLimit` accepts a signature whose `l=` tag covers less than the canonical body, which is the RFC 6376 §8.2 hole where anyone can append to the bytes past that length after the fact. It was read as a bare truthy value, so `acceptBodyLengthLimit: "false"` or `"0"` turned the protection off while reading as though it kept it on. A value that is not a boolean is refused at the call now, with `dkim/bad-accept-body-length-limit`, and the check reads an explicit `true` rather than anything truthy. Passing `true` or `false` is unchanged. The option is one of six on that verifier that had no documentation at all; the block now records each, including that `minRsaBits` defaults to 2048 above the 1024 RFC 8301 §3.2 permits, that `maxSignatures` defaults to 8 with a ceiling of 16, and that the call resolves an array with one entry per signature.

items.title: b.auth.jwt.verifyExternal documents the policy it verifies against
items.body: The verifier for another party's JWT accepted eleven options and documented none of them, so the whole verification policy was undiscoverable: `algorithms`, which is required and has no default because the accepted set is the security of a verifier; `jwks` / `jwksUri` / `jwksCacheMs` / `keyResolver` for key sourcing; `allowKidlessJwks`, which accepts a single-key set for a token carrying no `kid`; `audience`, `issuer` and `subject`, each checked only when given, so a verifier naming none of them takes any issuer's token for any audience; and `clockSkewMs`, 30 seconds by default. The block records each one, what it defaults to, and that `none` and the symmetric `HS*` family are refused outright so an issuer cannot downgrade a token to a key the verifier already holds.

items.title: Thirty namespaces that shipped without a documentation page now have one
items.body: The documentation site generates a page per namespace from the comment block above it, and thirty namespaces had no block, so they had no page: `b.cli`, `b.seeders`, `b.wsClient`, `b.parsers` and its two body readers, `b.secCyber`, `b.sessionDeviceBinding`, `b.otelExport`, `b.websocketChannels`, `b.pick`, `b.lazyRequire`, `b.validateOpts`, `b.frameworkError`, `b.flag.context`, `b.flag.cache` and the rest. Seventy primitives within them gained a signature, an options contract and a runnable example at the same time.

items.title: An explicit limit of zero is honored
items.body: A limit read as `opts.x || DEFAULT` treats zero as absent, and for a cap zero is usually the strictest setting rather than an unset one. `maxEntries: 0` became 65535, `maxHeaderCount: 0` became 100, and `maxAgeSec: 0` became five minutes, so the tightest configuration could not be expressed. `b.archive.read.zip` already honored `maxEntries: 0`, so the builder disagreed with the reader it builds for. A limit of zero now reaches the comparison it was written for.

items.title: b.cbor.encode names the tag to use for a date
items.body: RFC 8949 spells a date as a tag, and this module already supports tags, so a bare `Date` is refused with `cbor/unencodable` and the message names `new b.cbor.Tag(1, epochSeconds)` for the epoch form and `new b.cbor.Tag(0, isoString)` for the string form.

items.title: A grant-owner query pins the ownership format it reads
items.body: The break-glass grants table is matched on a hash of the owner id, and that id's format changed, so a query pinning the hash alone can match a row written under the other format. A check requires every query on `issuedToActorHash` to pin `ownerKeyVersion` too.

items.title: An identity check is not narrowed to objects
items.body: `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` answers the same question for a string or a number as for an object, so a gate that consults it under a `typeof x === "object"` test admits every primitive the resolver rejects. A check covers `lib/` for that shape.

items.title: Nothing in lib decides whether a value is bytes by which realm built it
items.body: Deciding that a value is bytes has no correct form that tests the realm, so a check covers the whole of `lib/` for `instanceof` against a typed-array view, with no allowlist. Asking the same question about a date or a map does have a correct form, since `x instanceof Date ? x : new Date(x)` handles the other branch, so the existing per-module check keeps the wider set of built-ins and now names every module that decides a type and then stores, signs, redacts, refuses or timestamps the value. Run against the tree before this release, the two report 64 and 42 sites.

items.title: No serializer answers a value it cannot represent with the empty encoding
items.body: Each of the four serializers was corrected separately, each by its own list of named types, and each list was missing a different member. A check now asserts the property across all four instead: for every value whose data lives outside its own properties, the answer must be a refusal and must never be the encoding of an empty container. It carries the differences between the formats rather than flattening them, so a `Map` is encoded by CBOR and refused by JSON, and it asserts the accept side too, so a serializer that refuses everything does not pass it. Adding a serializer means adding one line.

items.title: Four byte parsers that nothing fuzzed now have harnesses
items.body: The fuzz gate requires a harness for every `lib/safe-*.js` and `lib/guard-*.js` primitive, with an allowlist for the ones that are not parsers and a second list for untrusted-byte parsers whose filename does not match. `b.guardImage.inspectMagic` and `b.guardPdf.inspectMagic` each walk a signature table over the leading bytes of an upload, and both were excused as "magic-byte detection covered by safe-buffer" when the signature tables are in the guards themselves and `safe-buffer` does no magic-byte detection. `b.safeBuffer` was excused as having no operator-facing parse path, while `normalizeText` decodes UTF-8 and strips a BOM and the base64 / base64url / hex readers parse text a peer controls. `b.fileType.detect` and `assertOneOf` read the leading bytes of an upload body, a mail attachment or a decoded MIME part, and sat outside both lists because the filename is not `safe-*` or `guard-*`; it is in the byte-parser list now, and both fuzzing workflows carry the target. Each harness was driven over 61 buffers before shipping, covering every signature, every truncation of each, polyglots carrying two signatures, malformed UTF-8 and a megabyte of one repeated byte, with no escape.

items.title: An API name written in lib prose resolves against the framework
items.body: A primitive's prose names other primitives, and nothing checked that those names exist. A check resolves every `b.`-prefixed name written in a `lib/` comment block against what the framework exports, so a renamed or imagined primitive is caught where it is written rather than by a reader who tries it. `@related` references are held to the same rule, and a primitive whose `opts` is the object under test is exempt from carrying an options contract, because there is nothing to document.

items.title: An API name in lib prose is checked without a one-segment wildcard
items.body: The gate that requires every `b.<namespace>.<member>` written in `lib/` prose to resolve allows the house shorthand for a handle member, `b.cache.update` for `b.cache.create().update`, by accepting one leftover segment when the resolving prefix has a `create` function. That holds for a namespace which is also a container of sub-namespaces, so any member name under `b.mail` passed and three comment blocks in shipped source, which are what the documentation site publishes, named primitives that do not exist. Those three blocks now name `b.mailBounce`, `b.mail.rbl` and `b.mail.server.submission`. A prefix that holds a sub-namespace no longer gets the wildcard, where a sub-namespace is an object carrying functions so a data bag such as `DEFAULTS` does not count and the sixty-one leaf factories keep their shorthand. Under a container the shorthand is declared by name in the same list the operator-doc half of the gate has always used, which both halves now read.

items.title: An actor's identity is read through the shared reader, not by indexing the field list
items.body: A `lib/` file holding `b.requestHelpers.ACTOR_IDENTITY_FIELDS` must call `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityFields(actor)`. An entry may name a nested field, `claims.sub`, and `actor["claims.sub"]` is not it, so a consumer that indexes the list directly cannot see that principal at all. Naming the list in an error message satisfies the gate through `.join(`, and the allowlist is empty.

items.title: A resolver named for a principal may not take a peer-supplied parameter
items.body: A function named `_actorDomain`, `_principalX`, `_ownerX`, `_tenantX`, `_subjectX`, `_grantX` or `_accountX` answers what the authenticated identity carries. Accepting a peer-supplied parameter alongside that identity gives it a rung to fall back to when the identity carries nothing, and the caller then compares the answer against another field of the same peer input, so the check passes on whatever the peer chose. The gate refuses the shape, with an empty allowlist.

items.title: Revoke outstanding break-glass grants by table when upgrading
items.body: A break-glass grant issued before this release records its owner as a bare id, where a new one records `user:<id>` or `apikey:<id>`. The grants table gains an `ownerKeyVersion` column recording which of the two a row holds; the column is added to an existing table on the first connection after the upgrade, and rows already present take the earlier format. `revokeAll({ actorId })` and `listActive` require the current format, so they do not reach an older grant, including one whose bare id spells a prefixed one. `revokeAll({ table })` does not read the owner at all and reaches any of them; otherwise they expire within the policy's `grantTtl`, 15 minutes by default. A grant taken out with an API key is now owned by `apikey:<id>` rather than by its owner's user id, so revoke it as the key.

items.title: Pass req.botChallengeKey to recordFailure, and re-point anything grouping CADF initiators
items.body:
`b.authBotChallenge`'s middleware keys its ladder by the authenticated principal on a route that carries no credential in the body, where it previously used the client address. A post-verify path that derived the key itself, `recordFailure(clientIp)` on a token-refresh route, now advances a different ladder from the one the middleware reads, and the two never meet. `middleware()` writes the key it used to `req.botChallengeKey`; pass that. A route whose body carries `email` or `username` is unchanged, so the documented `recordFailure("user@example.com")` still pairs.

`b.auditTools.exportCadf` emits `blamejs:unattributed` and `blamejs:unidentified` where it emitted `"unknown"` and `"n/a"`. A dashboard or SIEM rule grouping initiators by those literals needs the new values. Rows that name an actor or a resource are unchanged.

items.title: Authenticated callers land in new flag rollout buckets once
items.body: `b.flag.context.fromRequest` derives `targetingKey` from `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` rather than from the raw `user.id`, so the key that places an authenticated caller in a percentage rollout changes value. Each caller keeps a stable key from then on, but a partial rollout re-draws its membership at upgrade: a caller inside a 10 percent rollout may fall outside it, and one outside may fall in. Pin the assignment across the upgrade by passing `userKey`, which is still used exactly as given. Nothing changes for an unauthenticated caller, or where the context is built by hand and carries its own `targetingKey`. A caller whose actor the framework could not name moves the other way, out of the shared anonymous bucket and onto its own key, which is the point of the change.

items.title: A CalDAV or CardDAV deployment naming its principal outside principalId sets a hook
items.body: `b.mail.dav.create`'s Express-style `caldavHandler` and `carddavHandler` accepted `req.user.id` and `req.user.username` for the URL's principal segment. They now read `req.user.principalId`, or `req.actor.principalId`, and nothing else. A deployment carrying the principal under another name passes it: `b.mail.dav.create({ storage: ..., actorPrincipalId: function (actor) { return actor.id; } })`. Without that, an authenticated request is refused with 401 rather than served under a name another identity can also reach. When the hook is set it is the only thing consulted, so it also covers a multi-tenant deployment: return the tenant as part of the value and two tenants holding the same principal ID address different URLs. `dispatchCaldav` and `dispatchCarddav` are unchanged, since a caller on a non-Express transport passes the principal itself.

items.title: Name the principal on a sealed-column read and a step-up grant
items.body: Two per-actor mechanisms now ask which principal an operation is for, and refuse rather than sharing one bucket. A read of a table carrying sealed columns takes `b.db.from(table).asActor(actor)`, and the chain refuses an actor that names no principal or is null. A step-up grant minted with `b.auth.stepUp.grant.create({ actor: req.user })` is bound to the field that named the principal, is refused for a principal named by a different field, and is refused when checked without an actor; `create` refuses an actor and a subject together. The existing `{ subject: "..." }` form is unchanged and keeps matching the resolver's chain, so a deployment that does not adopt the binding keeps its current behavior.

items.title: Check that every limit you configure is a number
items.body: A limit supplied as a string, as a negative number, or as a fractional value where a whole one is required is now refused where the call is made rather than ignored. A limit read from an environment variable needs `Number(...)` or `parseInt(..., 10)` around it. The options affected are named under Security above. A limit you leave unset is unaffected, and its default is what it always was.

items.title: Convert a Map, a Set or a Promise before serializing it
items.body: `b.safeJson.stringify` raises `json/no-form`, `b.canonicalJson.stringify` raises, `b.cbor.encode` raises `cbor/unencodable`, `b.safeJsonPath.validateContainment` raises `safe-jsonpath/containment-bad-type`, and a `b.db` collection refuses such a value in a `jsonColumns` column or folded into an overflow column. Each previously wrote or stored an empty object. Convert to a plain object or an array first: `Object.fromEntries(map)` for a map, `Array.from(set)` for a set. A value defining its own `toJSON` is unaffected, so a `Date` still writes its ISO string everywhere except `b.cbor.encode`, which needs the tag named under Changed.

items.title: Verify the vendored artifacts at boot and stop on a bad verdict
items.body: `b.configDrift.verifyVendorIntegrity` reports; it does not exit. If you already call it at boot, read `ok` and stop the boot yourself, and drop the `audit` option if you pass one, because there is none. If you match on its throws, the codes are `config-drift/vendor-manifest-missing` and `config-drift/vendor-manifest-shape`, not the upper-case names its documentation used to give.

releases.headline: A release page is rendered to fit the size a release body holds
releases.summary: 0.20.32 is tagged but was never published: its release page rendered 148,498 characters, GitHub refuses a release body over 125,000, and the call that creates the release failed once the tag was already public. This release carries everything 0.20.32 carries, and renders the page to fit. Upgrading from 0.20.31 lands every change both releases describe.

items.title: A release page is rendered to fit, and keeps the entries that name an action
items.body: The page a release is published with is generated from the same notes as the changelog entry, and nothing bounded its size. GitHub refuses a release body over 125,000 characters, so a release large enough to pass that ceiling failed at the call that creates it, after its tag was public and could not be re-cut. The page is now rendered within a budget below that ceiling. A release carrying more entries than the body holds drops the ones that describe a change before the ones that name something to do, so `Security`, `Migration`, `Added`, `Changed`, `Deprecated` and `Removed` survive ahead of `Fixed`; the page says it was shortened and links to `CHANGELOG.md`, which keeps every entry whatever its length. Measured on the 0.20.32 page: 148,498 characters before and 117,831 after, with all thirty `Security` entries, all six `Migration` entries, and thirty of sixty-eight `Fixed` entries.

items.title: The size of a release page is checked before a tag exists, not after
items.body: The publish workflow refused a release page that was suspiciously small and never checked it against the ceiling the API enforces, which is the bound that actually fails. `node scripts/generate-changelog-entry.js --check` renders the page and refuses an oversize one now, and smoke already runs that check, so the failure surfaces while the release is still a working tree. The workflow carries the upper bound beside the lower one as a second reading.

items.title: The fuzzing base image advances, and the two Dockerfiles that pin it are held to the same digest
items.body: `gcr.io/oss-fuzz-base/base-builder-javascript` moves to `sha256:ea9b7826`. Against the digest it replaces: the same 39 layers, 782.7 MiB to 737.4 MiB, the same `compile` command with no entrypoint and no user, and all 39 environment variables identical. The digest is pinned in `.clusterfuzzlite/Dockerfile` and in `oss-fuzz/projects/blamejs/Dockerfile`, and an automated bump proposes one directory at a time, so accepting one leaves the other on the older base and the two fuzzing builds stop sharing a foundation. A `codebase-patterns` check compares the two pins and fails when they differ.

items.title: An operator looking for 0.20.32 on npm
items.body: 0.20.32 is tagged in the repository and its entry is in `CHANGELOG.md`, but it is not on npm: the release failed at creation and the package was never published. 0.20.33 carries the same code plus the fix above. Upgrade to 0.20.33 directly; there is nothing in 0.20.32 that 0.20.33 does not carry.

releases.headline: The mail stack answers what its RFCs define, and a per-actor bucket holds one principal
releases.summary: `b.fileUpload` recorded the owner of an upload as `actor.id || actor.userId`, so a deployment whose tokens name a user any other way put every authenticated user on one key: each could read, resume, finalize and cancel the others' uploads, and `list()` returned every upload in the staging directory. Identity is now derived once, by `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey`, which reads `id`, `userId`, `username`, `sub`, `principalId` and `email`, tags each key with the field it came from, scopes it by `tenantId`, takes an `actorKey` hook for a shape it cannot read, and refuses an actor it cannot name rather than folding it onto a shared literal. `b.mail.server.jmap` keys its `maxConcurrentRequests` and `maxConcurrentUpload` slots the same way, and enforces them for the first time: both were published in the session and consulted by nothing. An IMAP LIST pattern is matched against each mailbox for a cost that no longer grows with how long the pattern is, so a four-kilobyte pattern inside the line cap cannot hold the event loop. RFC 2046 §5.1.4 orders the parts of a `multipart/alternative` simplest to richest, so the last representation is the displayed one; `b.safeMime` had a second answer for this and a stored body could describe a different representation from its own attachment facts. A JMAP refusal now carries one of the four request-level problem types RFC 8620 §3.6.1 defines, `unknownCapability`, `notJSON`, `notRequest` or `limit` with a member naming the cap, sent as `application/problem+json` with `status` and `detail`; the listener had been sending its own codes, and the HTTP and WebSocket transports answered the same input differently. A method error is the bare name §3.6.2 prints rather than a URI, so a client matching `unknownMethod` or any RFC 8621 set error matches. `maxObjectsInGet` and `maxObjectsInSet` were defined in every profile and read by nothing: an `Email/get` handler received 250,000 ids under a profile whose limit is 500, and a `/get` or `/set` over the cap is now `requestTooLarge` before the handler runs, counted after result references resolve. A request body is parsed with the profile's `maxSizeRequest` rather than a 1 MiB default, so a valid 1.17 MB request is no longer reported as invalid JSON. The session's `urn:ietf:params:jmap:core` capability was an empty object and now carries the eight properties RFC 8620 §2 requires, built from the limits the listener applies. `b.mailStore` threaded messages across every folder in the store, so an account holder who appended a message naming a Message-ID could tell whether any other account on the server held it, and a message delivered to two accounts split the second account's thread; a folder now carries an owner and a thread stays inside it. A result reference path with `*` applies the rest of the pointer to every item and flattens the results, an account-scoped method without an `accountId` is refused before its handler runs, and `EmailSubmission/set` compares the envelope sender against the identity by address rather than by exact string. It also reads the `From` header the way a receiving parser does: every field of it, every mailbox in each one, and the whole of each element rather than the first address it recognizes. An author the reader cannot account for is refused instead of skipped, which closes a set of headers that were authorized against one address while naming another, including `ceo@bank.example <ops@example.com>` and its aligned same-domain spelling, where the envelope and the signature still pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC at the receiver.

items.title: A JMAP request slot is held until the work it admitted actually finishes
items.body: `maxHandlerMs` rejects the wrapper around a handler, not the handler: the underlying promise keeps running, because nothing in the handler contract can cancel an operator's database or upstream call. The listener released the account's `maxConcurrentRequests` slot when that wrapper rejected, so the same authenticated client could start another handler at once, and another after that one timed out, accumulating live backend operations without limit while the session reported one request in flight. The slot is the accounting for real work, so it is now held until the real work settles: a handler that outlives its budget hands the listener a handle to what is still running, and the slot returns when that settles rather than when the client is answered. A timeout therefore costs the account its concurrency only for as long as the work actually runs, and `mail.server.jmap.slot_held_for_outstanding_work` records it.
items.migration: An account whose handlers regularly exceed `maxHandlerMs` will see requests refused with `maxConcurrentRequests` where they were previously admitted. That refusal is the bound doing its job; raise `maxConcurrentRequests`, lower `maxHandlerMs`, or make the handler return sooner.

items.title: `LIST (SUBSCRIBED)` returns a mailbox a backend records only in its subscription list
items.body: `b.mail.server.imap` decided whether a mailbox was subscribed from a `subscribed` field on the folder row, filtered on it, and only then read `mailStore.listSubscriptions`. That later pass skips every name that exists, since its job is to report subscriptions whose mailbox is gone, so a backend that keeps subscriptions in `listSubscriptions` alone and returns ordinary folder rows lost every existing subscribed mailbox: `LIST (SUBSCRIBED) "" "*"` answered with nothing while the client was subscribed. The store interface permits that shape, and a missing `subscribed` on a row is not the same as a mailbox that is not subscribed. The subscription list is read before anything filters on it now, and a row named by it is marked `\Subscribed`. A subscription whose mailbox is gone is still reported `\NonExistent \Subscribed`, and a mailbox that is not subscribed is still left out.

items.title: A chain of JMAP result references cannot describe more than the request cap allows
items.body: RFC 8620 §3.7 lets a method call name a value from an earlier call's result instead of repeating it. `b.mail.server.jmap` resolved such a reference by sharing the referenced value, so two references to the same prior call, repeated down a chain, described a structure whose serialized form doubled at every step while the request grew by one short call. Measured on an authenticated connection: sixteen `Core/echo` calls turned a 2,041-byte request into a 5,636,161-byte response, four times larger for each further call, and the default profile permits thirty-two. None of the per-reference checks could see it, because every descriptor was well formed and every one was inside `maxBackRefDepth`: the cost is not in any single reference but in how many times the result each one names is reached. The listener now measures what a call's arguments expand to once resolved, counting each distinct value once however many references reach it, and refuses the call that takes the request past `maxSizeRequest` with `invalidResultReference`. Calls before it keep their results. Measuring by identity is what keeps the check itself cheap: walking the shared structure naively is the same explosion the check exists to stop. A `*` in a reference is charged as each element is taken rather than measured once the array exists, so the expansion is never built and then refused: measured before, a 120 KiB request naming one 60,000-element array from thirty-one references grew the heap by 66 MiB and was answered in full, and at 4.5 MiB of wire it reached 444 MiB. Each element carries a floor of 16 bytes against that budget, because an array of bare numbers costs two bytes each on the wire and far more than that in memory, so the byte count alone let hundreds of thousands of them through. Every reference in one call draws on one budget rather than each getting the whole of what is left: measured at 0.77 MiB of wire, twenty references to one 400,000-element array grew the heap 139 MiB and sixty grew it 318 MiB, each one passing its own check while their sum did not. The growth no longer follows how many references a call carries.
items.migration: A request whose result references expand past the profile's `maxSizeRequest` now fails that method call instead of being served. Split it across requests, or narrow the `path` of each reference so it names the part the next call needs rather than the whole result.

items.title: An option that names a requirement is checked, where a value that was not a boolean used to switch the requirement off
items.body: A primitive that read `opts.requireX === true` turned every value that is not the boolean `true` into `false`, and said nothing about it. For an option that GRANTS something that fails closed and costs a feature; for an option that REQUIRES something it fails open, and the protection the configuration asked for is simply absent. The values that reach these options are often not booleans in the first place: a setting read from an environment variable is the string `"true"`, and one read from a config file is whatever that file's parser produced. Each of these now refuses a value it cannot read, naming the option: `requireSignature` on `b.restore.create` and `b.restoreBundle.extract`, which restored and extracted an UNSIGNED bundle; `requireTLS`, `requireCSPNonce`, `requireCSRF` and `requireRateLimit` on `b.security.assertProduction`, where a typo made the assertion an operator added to catch a misconfiguration pass instead; `requireAttestation` and `requireAttestationAnchor` on `b.auth.passkey.verifyRegistration`; `requireExp`, `requireKeyAttestation` and `requireKeyBinding` on `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify`; `requireOrigin` and `requireJsonContentType` on `b.middleware.csrfProtect`; `requireFingerprintMatch` on `b.middleware.attachUser`; `requireNonce` on `b.middleware.dpop`; `requireIdempotencyKey` on `b.middleware.idempotencyKey`; `requireFlush` on `b.backup.create`; `requireDeterministic` on `b.cbor.decode`; `enforceUnconditional` on the OCSP must-staple gate; `strict` on `b.safeMountInfo.parse` and `b.time.monotonicClock`; `requiresLogin` on `b.darkPatterns`; and the two declarations `b.compliance.aiAct.risk.isHighRisk` reads, where a string classified a system as not high-risk. An option does not have to arrive under a parameter named `opts` to be operator-supplied, and the same reading sat on a role entry, a route's middleware options, a policy spec, an environment schema, a WebAuthn selection and a delivery envelope. Each of these refuses a value it cannot read now: `requireMfa` on a `b.permissions` role and on the `require()` route gate, where a role or route that declares MFA was served without it; `requireFingerprintMatch` on `b.session.verify`, which accepted a session whose client fingerprint had changed; `requireIssParam` on `b.auth.oauth`, which stopped requiring the RFC 9207 `iss` parameter that tells one issuer's response from another's; `requireKeyAttestation` on `b.auth.oid4vp`; `requireResidentKey` in a passkey `authenticatorSelection`, which asked for a resident key as a preference where the caller made it a requirement; `required` on a `b.safeEnv` schema, which started the process without a variable the schema calls required; `requireTls` on a `b.mail` delivery envelope, which relayed without the RFC 8689 REQUIRETLS the message asked for; the two AI Act declarations `b.compliance.aiAct.classify` reads; and on `b.sql.createPolicy`, `allowLiterals` plus `permissive` — where a value that was not a boolean emitted `AS PERMISSIVE` for a caller who asked for `RESTRICTIVE`, and a permissive row-level-security policy OR-combines with its peers, so it widens access where the caller meant to narrow it. The same reading in the other direction leaves a PERMISSION on: `opts.allowX !== false` stays `true` for every value that is not the boolean `false`, so an operator tightening a policy with a string kept the loose setting. `b.middleware.fetchMetadata` reads six options that way, and its `allowSameSite`, `allowMissing` and `allowedNavigate` decide whether a request carrying no `Sec-Fetch-*` header is served; `b.middleware.requestId` went on trusting a caller-supplied id under `trustUpstream: "false"`; `b.sql` kept string literals allowed in a `createIndex` WHERE fragment; `b.network.dns.discoverEncrypted`, `b.safeBuffer` and `b.structuredFields` read theirs the same way. All of them now refuse a value that is not a boolean. A third spelling reads the option for its truthiness rather than comparing it, and that one turns the string `"false"` into `true`: measured on `b.safeJson.parse`, `allowProto: "false"` and `allowProto: "no"` each kept `__proto__` as an own key, exactly as `allowProto: true` does, so the off switch read as on. `allowProto` is checked at all three entry points that take it now, and so are `allowDoctype` and `allowProcessing` on `b.parsers.xml.parse`, where the same reading would have parsed a DOCTYPE or a processing instruction for a caller that refused them; `allowHttp` on `b.auth.oauth.create`, which admitted plain-http endpoint URLs; `trustProxy` on `b.middleware.headers`, which went on trusting forwarding headers a client can set; `allowUnregisteredEnqueue` on `b.jobs.create`; and `allowMultipartAlternative` on `b.guardMailCompose`. What makes `=== true` fail open is not the word `require`: it is that the option tightens something, and six more are spelled with other verbs. `rejectUnknown` on `b.safeEnv.load`, which loaded a file carrying keys the schema does not name instead of refusing it; `forbidProxy` on `b.security.assertProduction`, which sits in the same function as four `require*` options that were fixed while it was not; `forbidSelfApprove` on `b.dualControl.create`, where the requester could approve their own request; `refuseStopSequences` on the MCP sampling guard; `redactBcc` on `b.mail.transports.console`, which printed every blind-copied recipient to the stream; and `seal` on `b.cache.set` and `b.cache.update`, where the value reached the backend unsealed for a caller that asked for it sealed. The verb can also sit in the middle of the name or at its end, which another six carried: `tolerateMissingPeerCert` on `b.middleware.requireBoundKey`, which served a request carrying no client certificate for a key pinned to one; `acceptGrant` on `b.middleware.requireStepUp`, which went on accepting the grant header for an operator who turned it off; `dpopBoundAccessTokensRequired` and `mtlsBoundAccessTokensRequired` on `b.middleware.protectedResourceMetadata`, where the published RFC 9728 document told clients a binding is not required that the operator had declared; and `ignoreSystem` and `replicaFallbackToPrimary` on `b.externalDb`. Every one of these declares `boolean` in its own documentation. There is a fourth reading, and it is the plainest: `if (opts.allowX)`, with no comparison at all, which turns the string `"false"` into a granted permission exactly as `!!opts.allowX` does. Twenty-two options were read that way, each one its own module documents as a boolean. `allowUnsigned` on `b.auditChain.verifyPurgeAnchor` accepted a purge anchor carrying no signature; `allowLegacy` on `b.crypto.decrypt` read the pre-2024 envelope without the caller opting in; `allowCrossBorder` on `b.backup.create` permitted a cross-border transfer without the override; `allowProduction` on `b.dev.create` loaded spawn-on-watch under `NODE_ENV=production`; `allowReserved` and `allowSqliteInternal` on `b.safeSql.validateIdentifier`, `allowAbsoluteRel` on `b.safePath.resolve`, `allowShortRead` on `b.atomicFile.fdSafeReadSync`, `allowHttp` and `allowInternal` on `b.notify.transports.httpJson`, `skipIfUnchanged` on `b.audit.checkpoint`, and `allowPlainMigration` on `b.cryptoField.registerTable`.
