Nine of them belong to the content guards, which do not check their own options: `b.gateContract` refuses a non-boolean for every guard option whose default is a boolean, so `b.guardHtml`, `b.guardSvg`, `b.guardSql`, `b.guardYaml` and `b.guardJson` are covered at once, and so is every guard added later. `b.codepointClass.isForbiddenControlChar` reads its `allowLf` and `allowCr` strictly instead of refusing, because it runs once per codepoint; its `forbidTab` keeps the truthy reading, since that option imposes a restriction and a value that is not a boolean has to leave the tab forbidden. Seven more tighten something and were read the same way: `sandbox` on `b.template.create`, where `sandbox: "true"` skipped the sandbox and left its helpers unchecked; `aad` on `b.cryptoField.registerTable`, which sealed a table's cells without the AAD binding the registration asked for; `validate` on a `b.network.dns.resolver` query, which answered without DNSSEC validation; `assertFormat` on `b.jsonSchema.compile`, where a value that does not match its `format` validated; `designatedSystemicRisk` on `b.compliance.aiAct.gpai.classify`, which classified a model the operator had declared designated as not systemic-risk and did not raise its Article 55 obligations; `auditOnMissing` on `b.middleware.tracePropagate`; and `requireNextField` on `b.structuredFields.recordVersionMatches`, where a record ending right after its version matched anyway, which is the case MTA-STS and TLS-RPT use the option to refuse. A `codebase-patterns` check fails on any of the four readings, in the direction that fails open, when the option is not checked beside it, so the next one is caught before it ships.
items.migration: A configuration that spelled one of these as a string or a number was not getting the behavior it named. It now fails at startup rather than silently, and the message names the option; write `true` or `false`.

items.title: A mail listener refuses a non-boolean where it reads a boolean, instead of reading it as false
items.body: `b.mail.server.imap`, `b.mail.server.pop3`, `b.mail.server.managesieve` and `b.mail.server.submission` each read their boolean options with `=== true`, so any other value became `false` and nothing said so. For `implicitTls` that is a downgrade: a configuration carrying the string `"true"`, which is what a value read from an environment variable or a config file looks like, left the listener answering plaintext with STARTTLS on 143, 110, 4190 or 587 while the operator believed TLS began at the SYN. `requireDkim: "true"` on submission accepted unsigned mail for the same reason. Each of these is now refused at `create` with the option named: `implicitTls` on all four, `allowPlaintext` on ManageSieve, `requireDkim` and `allowSmtpUtf8` on submission. A `greeting` that is not a non-empty string is refused too, where a number reached the wire as the first line of every connection. `b.mail.server.jmap` gains the same treatment for the three options it was not checking: `webSocketMaxMessageBytes`, which bounds the frame the transport buffers before the profile's `maxSizeRequest` applies and which accepted `Infinity`; `webSocketUrl`, which the session advertises; and `collationAlgorithms`, which RFC 8620 §2 defines as an array of names and which accepted a bare string, an empty array, and names this listener does not implement.
items.migration: A configuration that spelled one of these options with a string or a number was not getting the behavior it named, and now fails at startup rather than silently. Write `true` or `false`, and a non-empty string for `greeting` and `webSocketUrl`.

items.title: Every CRL `b.mtlsCa` publishes carries a number, and the number does not repeat
items.body: RFC 5280 §5.2.3 requires the cRLNumber extension on every CRL and requires it to increase for a given issuer, because that number is how a relying party tells which of two CRLs is newer. A `b.mtlsCa` CRL carried no number at all, so a client holding a cached one had nothing to compare and could keep serving a revocation list that predated the revocation it needed to see. The CA now allocates a number from `ca.crl-number` in its data directory before it signs, under the same lock the rest of its state uses, so the sequence survives a restart and a CA reopened on the same directory cannot hand two different CRLs the same number. An unpublished CRL takes its own number too. A number is allocated before signing and signing is not instant, so two CRLs generated at once can finish in the other order; the CA records the number it is publishing before it replaces the file and refuses to replace a published CRL with a lower-numbered one, and the call that lost the race returns `persisted: false`. The number is recorded first, so a write that fails partway leaves the published file older than the number claims rather than leaving the number behind a newer file, which is the direction that could let a later CRL overwrite a newer one. A CRL with no `nextUpdate` was also non-conforming under §5.1.2.5; `b.mtlsEngine.generateCrl` now defaults it to seven days after `thisUpdate` when the caller does not give one, which is the window `b.mtlsCa` was already passing.

items.title: An mTLS leaf no longer asserts keyEncipherment
items.body: Leaves issued by the bundled engine carried `keyUsage` of `digitalSignature` and `keyEncipherment`. The engine signs with ML-DSA-87, ML-DSA-65 or ECDSA P-384, and none of them can perform key transport, so the bit described a capability the key does not have; RFC 9881 §5 forbids it outright on an ML-DSA certificate, which is the default. Leaves now assert `digitalSignature` alone. Nothing that verified before stops verifying: TLS 1.3 client and server authentication reads `digitalSignature`, and the removed bit only ever applied to RSA key exchange.
items.migration: A relying party that required `keyEncipherment` on a leaf from this engine was gating on a bit no key here could use; gate on `digitalSignature` instead. Certificates already issued are unchanged until they are reissued.

items.title: A mail handler past its time budget no longer writes into the connection after the server answered for it
items.body: `b.mail.server.imap` and `b.mail.server.managesieve` give every handler a `maxHandlerMs`, and on a handler that runs past it the dispatcher answers the command: `NO ... exceeded maxHandlerMs` on IMAP, `NO "Internal error"` on ManageSieve. The handler was left running and kept the socket, so the client received whatever it wrote when it finished, with no command in flight. Measured on IMAP with a `mailStore.selectFolder` resolving 1.5 s past a 30 s budget: the refusal arrived at 30 s, then `* 2 EXISTS`, `* 0 RECENT`, `* FLAGS (...)`, `* OK [UIDVALIDITY 1]` and `* OK [HIGHESTMODSEQ 42]` arrived at 32 s, and the session held the mailbox open while RFC 9051 §6.3.2 puts the client in the authenticated state after a failed SELECT; selected-state commands were then served to a client that had been told its SELECT failed. On the same race against EXPUNGE the leaked lines are `* n EXPUNGE`, which renumbers the client's message map. A ManageSieve response carries no tag at all (RFC 5804 §1.2), so a late line there is read as the answer to whatever the client sent next. Both listeners now write an untagged `BYE` after the refusal and close the connection. IMAP also writes at most one tagged reply per command, and it holds that whatever the client sends: the record is per command rather than a memory of recent tags, which a client could overrun by issuing 64 cheap commands while a slow backend call was still open, and a tag the client uses again for a later command is answered again. An `opts.overrides` handler answers through `parsed.answer(text)`, which writes the tagged response for the command it was dispatched for, so an answer a handler has already given is one the listener counts: a handler that answered and then failed had drawn a second tagged line for a tag the client already retired. It is bound to that command rather than to the tag, so a handler that keeps its `parsed` and answers after its command is over does not answer whichever command holds the tag by then, nor suppress that command's own reply. Text that is not a non-empty string is refused the same way, where it had put a bare tag, or `undefined`, on the wire in place of a response. Both refusals return `false` and emit `mail.server.imap.answer_refused`, rather than throwing: a handler may call `parsed.answer` from a timer or another detached callback, and an exception there is caught by nothing. What it returns is what it wrote, so a second call inside one command, which the one-answer rule discards, returns `false` as well. Text carrying CR or LF is refused: a tagged response is one line, and a handler interpolating bytes it read into its answer would otherwise write a further response, for a tag the client never issued, while the listener recorded one answer. A handler may still write to the socket instead, and the listener then has only its own writes to count. It does not read the handler's bytes to decide: the bytes a handler writes for a `FETCH` are message content, a literal holds whatever the sender wrote, and a body line beginning with the client's tag would otherwise suppress the answer to the command that reads that message. `b.mail.server.managesieve` gives its own `opts.overrides` handlers the same `parsed.answer(text)`, with the same refusals including the one for a call made after its command is over, and adds no response of its own once one has been given. A ManageSieve reply is zero or more data lines and then one `OK`, `NO` or `BYE` (RFC 5804 §2.7), so what the handler has written is not the same question as whether it has answered: counting bytes made a `LISTSCRIPTS` that failed after its first script look answered, and the client lost the connection where a `NO` would have kept it in step. That holds whether the handler failed by rejecting its promise or by throwing where it stands, which are two paths to the same place. It holds in the other order too: where the listener answers `NO` for a handler that failed before answering, that answer is recorded, so a callback the handler had already scheduled cannot add a second response on top of it and leave the client reading every later reply against the wrong command.

items.title: A declared body-size cap holds whether the body arrives as bytes or already parsed
items.body: `b.guardJmap.validate`, `b.mcp.parseRequest`, `b.mail.dmarc.parseAggregateReport` and `b.safeJson.parseStringOrObject` each accept a request as a JSON string or as a value a parser has already decoded, and each advertises a byte cap: `maxSizeRequest` (10 MiB at the strict profile), 1 MiB, 8 MiB, and `maxBytes`. The cap was measured on the string alone. `b.mail.server.jmap`'s `apiHandler` reads `req.body`, which is what `b.middleware.bodyParser` leaves behind, so the wiring the doc block prescribes took the branch with no cap on it, and `b.openapi.parse` and `b.asyncapi.parse` did the same with their 16 MiB document bound. A pre-parsed body is now put through the same cap before anything reads it, and the caller is handed its JSON form rather than the object they passed: a cycle and a value nested past `maxDepth` are refused, and a member that would answer a later read differently cannot, because there is no later read of it. `b.guardJmap.validate` reports the refusal as `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:limit` carrying `limit: "maxSizeRequest"`, the shape a string body over the cap already produced. Measuring one value and handing on another bounds nothing, because the two are different objects: a getter, a proxy or a `toJSON` hook answers the measurement and answers the caller separately, and so does a member the walk skips for not being enumerable, for being inherited, or for sitting outside an array's elements. A hook returning `{}` reported two bytes for a body still holding 11 MiB and the handlers received all of it. `b.safeJson.jsonCopyUnderCap` serializes the value and reads it back, so every member is read once and the caller is handed what that one reading produced. `b.safeJson.measureBytes` reports the size a value would occupy as JSON without building the string, for a caller that wants the number rather than the value. It takes `limit` and `maxDepth`, and refuses any other option by name rather than accepting it and ignoring it. `b.guardJmap.validate` carries the proto-poisoning key names through rather than dropping them, in both input forms: `b.mail.server.jmap` refuses an argument named `__proto__` and admits `constructor` and `prototype` as the ordinary names RFC 8620 §1.2 and RFC 8621 §4.1.1 make them, and it can do neither if the key has already been deleted. A body that arrived as text had them deleted before the listener looked, so the same request was refused pre-parsed and served as text with a member missing. `b.safeJson` takes `allowProto: true` with `refuseProtoMover: true` for that, on `parse`, `stringify`, `jsonCopyUnderCap` and `parseStringOrObject`: the names that become ordinary own properties are kept, and `__proto__`, the one that replaces an object's prototype, throws `json/proto-key` wherever it appears, at any depth and inside arrays. `b.pick.movesThePrototype` is the predicate, one answer read by everything that asks. The refusal fires whether or not `allowProto` is set, where `parse` had stripped the key in its reviver before the check could see it and so answered a value `stringify` refused. It cannot be combined with `onCircular: "replace"`, whose cycle-free copy is built before any of these rules is read; that copy now defines each member rather than assigning it, so a `__proto__` member cannot replace the copy's own prototype on the way through. `b.guardJmap.validate` refuses such a request as `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:notRequest` before any handler runs, so no method argument, and no `createdIds` map, is handed on carrying it; RFC 8620 §5.3 tells an operator to merge `createdIds` into their own map, and a merge is an assignment. `b.openapi.parse` and `b.asyncapi.parse` apply the same policy, because `components.schemas` and a JSON Schema `properties` map are free-form name maps: a schema named `constructor` was dropped from the document while `parse` answered `valid: true`, and a `$ref` pointing at it then resolved to nothing. `b.mail.server.jmap` reads a WebSocket frame under that policy too, so a client-chosen name is honored, or refused, the same way on both of its transports. A `/set` method's result maps hold their members rather than assigning them: an id in the `destroy` ARRAY is a client-supplied value that becomes a key only there, so no key-level rule ever saw it, and `__proto__` replaced the prototype of `notDestroyed` instead of being reported in it, where RFC 8620 §5.3 requires every id to come back in exactly one of `destroyed` or `notDestroyed`. `b.openapi.parse` and `b.asyncapi.parse` ask whether a security scheme is declared by looking for it on the document rather than reading through to `Object.prototype`: a requirement naming `toString`, `valueOf` or `constructor` found a function there and was reported as satisfied, so a document whose endpoint is protected only by a scheme nobody declared came back `valid: true`. `b.mail.dmarc.parseAggregateReport` reads each `date_range` bound however it is spelled, because a `Date` an operator built a report with reaches it as the ISO timestamp its JSON form is: epoch seconds, with or without a leading sign or a fractional part, and a timestamp carrying a zone all give the same second, and a value that is no time at all is `null` rather than its leading digits. A timestamp with no zone is `null` as well: ECMAScript reads that form in the host's own local time, so two collectors in different regions would have recorded different windows for one report file, and there is no second for this reader to claim.

items.title: One principal's uploads are no longer reachable by another
items.body: `b.fileUpload` recorded the owner of an upload as `actor.id || actor.userId`, falling back to the literal `_anonymous`. What an actor is called is the deployment's choice, not the framework's, so a token carrying an OIDC `sub` (or a SAML `nameID`, or a nested principal object) put every authenticated user on that one literal. Measured on a default configuration: a second user read the first's upload metadata, wrote chunks into it, finalized it through `onFinalize`, and canceled it; they shared one `maxActiveUploadsPerActor` budget; and `list()` dropped its scoping filter entirely, so such a caller enumerated uploads belonging to users who did carry an id. Identity is now derived once, by `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey`, which reads `id`, `userId`, `username`, `sub`, `principalId` and `email`, tags each key with the field it came from so `{id:"x"}` and `{userId:"x"}` remain two principals, and scopes the whole key by `tenantId`. An actor that carries none of them is refused as `file-upload/unidentified-actor` rather than folded onto a shared key; pass `actorKey` to name the field yourself. An omitted actor still resolves to the shared anonymous owner, which is what an unauthenticated deployment means.

items.title: JMAP concurrency limits count each principal separately
items.body: The `maxConcurrentRequests` and `maxConcurrentUpload` slots were keyed on `id` then `username` alone, so every actor carrying neither shared one bucket and a single client in flight answered 429 to all the others. The listener now derives the key with `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` and refuses an actor it cannot name instead of merging it, naming the `actorKey` option in the refusal. The session resource's `username` reads the same field set through `b.requestHelpers.actorDisplayName`, so what a client is told it is called and what separates its work no longer come from two lists.

items.title: A message sent with the null reverse path gets no DSN, in either spelling
items.body: The guard that stops a DSN being generated for the null reverse path compared `envelope.from` with `""` exactly. On the wire the null reverse path is written `<>`, and that is the spelling it arrives in, so a caller passing it through got a DSN for a message RFC 5321 §4.5.5 says must not receive one: a DSN's `To:` is the original `from`, so bouncing a bounce addresses it to nobody and, to a less careful peer, to itself. The question is now a predicate that recognizes both spellings, so a second site added later cannot repeat the omission. The MX listener already normalized the wire form, which is why this was latent rather than live.

items.title: A forged Authentication-Results is stripped in every spelling the readers accept
items.body: `b.mail.server.mx` removed a peer's forged `Authentication-Results` by matching the field name as a literal line prefix and reading the authserv-id off that same line, while every reader downstream is an RFC 5322 parser. Three spellings the parser accepts as the same header went straight through: folded before the authserv-id (RFC 5322 §2.2.3), a quoted authserv-id (RFC 8601 §2.2), and whitespace before the colon (RFC 5322 §4.5.8 obs-optional). Measured on a real session: a peer failing SPF and DMARC delivered a folded forged header claiming `dmarc=pass`, and the stored message carried two verdicts under the receiving server's own name. The strip now unfolds the header block and reads the field name and authserv-id under the same grammar the parsers use, including a quoted id and leading comments. `b.mail.server.mx.stripForgedAuthResults(message, authservId)` is exported.

items.title: SPF reads its version tag the way its ABNF writes it
items.body: SPF record selection compared the version case-sensitively, so `V=spf1 -all` was not seen as an SPF record at all and a domain publishing a strict policy evaluated as if it published nothing. RFC 7208 §12 writes the version as the quoted ABNF literal `"v=spf1"`, and RFC 5234 §2.3 makes quoted literals case-insensitive, so both halves fold. The other record types do not fold the same way and a uniform rule would be wrong in the other direction: DMARC, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT spell their version value in hex, which is exact, and TLS-RPT spells even the tag name in hex. `b.structuredFields.recordVersionMatches` takes `valueIgnoresCase` for the one grammar that needs it, and MTA-STS no longer shares a constant with TLS-RPT, whose name case differs from its own.

items.title: Authentication-Results reports the dmarc header.from as a domain
items.body: The header this framework writes carried `header.from=someone@example.com`, where the IANA Email Authentication Methods registry defines that property as the domain of the `From` field, which is also the only part DMARC evaluates (RFC 7489 §3.1). A consumer reading the property as specified and calling `parseDomain` on it got a refusal, correctly, and every aggregate report that arrived was recorded with an unreadable carrier domain and left out of the reading a policy decision rested on. Nothing failed loudly. The domain is emitted, and `b.mail.authResults.emit` refuses an address under a domain-valued property rather than publishing the author's local part in a header every intermediary reads. `smtp.mailfrom` is unchanged: RFC 8601 §2.7.1 defines it as the envelope address.

items.title: A message's shape can be read without decoding its content
items.body: `b.safeMime.parse` decoded every body on every call, so a consumer that wanted only the shape of a message, whether it carries a file and how many, had to decode all of its content to find out. Measured against a real store at a page size of 50: the listing alone 153 ms, reading the octets 1385 ms, and reading plus parsing 7526 ms for 2 MB messages, of which about 6100 ms is the decoding. `parse(bytes, { structureOnly: true })` walks the tree and leaves each leaf's `body` null with its `encodedSize` reported, under every cap and allowlist the ordinary mode applies. Reading the octets alone still costs about 5.5 ms per message whatever its size, so that mode does not by itself make per-render derivation viable, which is why the answer is now stored: `b.mailStore` records `has_attachment` and `attachment_count` from the parse it already does at append and carries them in the fetch and listing projections as `hasAttachment` and `attachmentCount`.

items.title: b.mailStore threads inside one account, so a Message-ID in another account is not observable
items.body: `appendMessage` looked each `In-Reply-To` and `References` message id up in `message_id_hash` across the whole messages table, with no folder condition and no ordering, and took the first matching row's thread root; `threadFor` then returned every row with that root, in every folder. One `b.mail.server.jmap` listener takes one store for every account `accountsFor` returns. An account holder who appended a message naming some Message-ID, by IMAP APPEND or by mailing themself, got their own objectid as the thread root only when no message anywhere in the store carried that id, and another account's objectid otherwise, which a JMAP `Email/get` reporting `threadId` shows them: any account holder could test whether another account held any Message-ID they chose. Separately, a message delivered to two accounts put a later reply in the first account's thread and left the second account's own copy in a thread alone. `createFolder(name, { owner })` records the account that holds a folder, `appendMessage(folder, bytes, { threadScope })` names the scope directly, and every message carries the resulting scope. The Message-ID lookup and `threadFor` match only rows in that scope, and the lookup orders by `received_at` then `objectid` so the root does not depend on row order. Folders that declare no owner share the scope `""`, so a single-account store is unchanged.

items.title: A refused IMAP or ManageSieve literal no longer leaves its payload to be parsed as commands
items.body: `b.mail.server.imap` read a command line, handed it to `b.guardImapCommand`, and on a refusal wrote `BAD` and returned without arming the literal reader, so the octets the client had announced arrived as ordinary lines and were executed as commands. RFC 7888 makes this reachable with no cooperation from the server: a non-synchronizing `{N+}` literal needs no continuation, so the payload is already in flight when the refusal is written. Measured: `a1 LOGIN {7+}` followed by `z9 NOOP` answered the refusal and then `z9 OK NOOP completed`. Bytes the sender presented as data became protocol. A non-synchronizing literal cannot be resynchronized after a refusal, because a command carries one literal per line and continues across lines, so consuming the literal the refused line named leaves the rest of that command to be read as a command line: measured, `a1 LOGIN {5+}` refused pre-authentication in one frame with `alice {13+}` and `z9 CAPABILITY` behind it ran the CAPABILITY. Knowing where such a command ends means parsing what was just refused, so the connection is closed with an untagged `BYE` instead. A synchronizing literal needs none of this: the client waits for a continuation that never comes. The same shape was live in `b.mail.server.managesieve`, where an unauthenticated `PUTSCRIPT "x" {11+}` was refused with `NO "AUTHENTICATE first"` and its announced script then ran as a command. Both listeners now consume and discard exactly the announced octets before the next line is parsed, bounded by the profile's literal cap, the body-rate window and the literal deadline; anything beyond the announced count is charged as ordinary pipelined data. An IMAP literal larger than the cap closes the connection instead, since a byte stream that cannot be located again is not recoverable. A synchronizing `{N}` is untouched: its client waits for a continuation the refusal never sends, so nothing is in flight and consuming would eat the client's next command. `b.guardImapCommand.announcedLiteral(line)` reads the announced size and form.

items.title: An account-scoped JMAP method is refused when no account is named
items.body: The account check compared every `*accountId` argument against the accounts `accountsFor` returns and skipped an argument that was absent or null, so `Email/get` and every other method RFC 8620 §1.6.2 gives a mandatory `accountId` ran its handler with no account named. Such a call is now `invalidArguments` before the handler runs. `b.mail.serverRegistry.jmapMethodTakesAccount(name)` answers which methods take one; `Core/echo` is the one that does not. The authorization check that follows reads every argument whose name ends in `accountId`, which is right for a method that takes accounts and wrong for the one that does not: RFC 8620 §4 returns `Core/echo`'s arguments unchanged, so `{ "accountId": "arbitrary-data" }` is data being echoed, and it came back `accountNotFound` instead. `b.mail.serverRegistry.jmapMethodIsAccountFree(name)` names the methods that skip the check, and it is not the negation of the other predicate: a name the registry has never heard of, such as an operator's own method, is not known to be account-free and keeps every check.

items.title: EmailSubmission/set compares the envelope sender with the identity by address
items.body: `envelope.mailFrom` was compared with the identity's address as an exact string, so a sender whose domain differed only in case, or gave an internationalized domain in its A-label form, was refused, while an identity carrying no address accepted any sender. The comparison now folds the domain's case and its A-label form, per RFC 5321 §2.4, folds a subaddress when a delimiter is configured, reads `*@domain` as RFC 8621 §6 defines it, and refuses an identity with no address. The wildcard is the unquoted spelling only: RFC 5322 §3.4.1 lets a local part be a quoted string, so an identity for `"*"@example.com` is the mailbox named `*` and covers itself rather than the domain. The local part keeps its case, which RFC 5321 §2.4 leaves to the receiving host. A bracketed address literal, which RFC 5321 §4.1.3 and RFC 5322 §3.4.1 make a legal domain, is its own canonical form rather than being put through the A-label conversion that declines it, so an identity for `ops@[192.0.2.1]` covers that address and no other. The `From` header is checked against the identity as well, and a message whose `From` it does not cover is `forbiddenFrom`. RFC 6854 §2.1 lets `From` carry an address-list, and RFC 5322 §3.4 makes an address a mailbox or a group, so a group's members are the authors it names: `From: Authors: ops@example.com;` is authorized as the mailbox inside it, every member of a group's mailbox-list is checked in its own right, and a group carrying no member, or one the sender never closes with `;`, names no author the reader can account for and is refused. A colon written where the grammar allows one, inside a comment, inside a quoted display name, or in the IPv6 form of a bracketed domain literal, does not open a group. The field name is read as the bytes carried it, which `b.safeMime.isHeaderFieldName` now answers for both readers: RFC 5322 §2.2 makes it one or more ftext followed immediately by the colon, so `From : ops@example.com` is not a `From` field and a receiving parser sees none. Trimming the text before the colon authorized a message on a header no conformant reader would find. A group's display-name is a phrase, so the text before the colon has to read as one: `From: <ceo@bank.example> Authors: ops@example.com;` names a mailbox where a phrase belongs, and is refused rather than authorized on the group's member alone. An address is matched against an identity only once it reads as a mailbox: the domain was taken by splitting at the last `@` with nothing checking what sat in front of it, so a wildcard identity for `*@example.com` covered `ceo@bank.example;ops@example.com`, which a receiving parser reads as an author at `bank.example`. RFC 5322 §3.2.3 makes an unquoted local part a dot-atom, atoms of `atext` joined by single dots, and `@`, `;` and a doubled or edge dot are none of those, so such a value now matches no identity in either the envelope or the `From` header. RFC 6531 §3.3 adds every non-ASCII character to `atext`, so an SMTPUTF8 deployment's `üser@example.com` still covers itself while `üser@evil.example;x@example.com` does not. A configured `subaddressDelimiter` is applied after the address has been read rather than before: folding first made the second `@` of `ops+foo@evil.example@example.com` disappear ahead of every check on it.

items.title: Folding whitespace and a comment inside an address are read where the grammar puts them
items.body: The address reader deleted every space and tab it met and skipped every comment, so `ops@example.co m` and `ops@example.co(x)m` were both compared as `ops@example.com` and passed the identity check while a conformant reader takes the domain as `example.co`, a lookalike the identity does not own, sent under an identity that keeps SPF, DKIM and DMARC aligned. RFC 5322 §3.2.2 writes `CFWS = (1*([FWS] comment) [FWS]) / FWS`, so a comment and folding whitespace are one construct, and §3.2.3 writes `dot-atom = [CFWS] dot-atom-text [CFWS]`, which puts either at an atom boundary and never between two atext characters. Both spellings now run through the same reader: CFWS at a boundary is still ignored, so `< ops @ example.com >`, `Ops <ops(work)@example.com>` and `Ops <ops@(mail host)example.com>` all name `ops@example.com`; CFWS between two atext characters names no mailbox, and the submission carrying it is `forbiddenFrom`. A comment the sender never closes names no mailbox either. The folded spelling is the same address: unfolding removes the CRLF and leaves the space, per RFC 5322 §2.2.3, so `From: ops@example.co` continued by ` m` is refused on the same rule.

items.title: The From gate holds a header line to the length RFC 5322 gives it
items.body: RFC 5322 §2.1.1 caps a line at 998 characters excluding the CRLF, and `b.safeMime.parse` enforces that as `maxHeaderLineBytes`, so a message carrying a longer line is one this framework will not parse and `b.mailStore` will not store. The `EmailSubmission/set` author check read the header section with no such bound while its address reader walks a field value one character at a time, so a single unfolded field carried the whole cost of its length: 16 MiB on one line took 772 ms and 326 MiB against 71 ms for the same bytes folded onto conformant lines. A header line over the cap is now `forbiddenFrom` rather than read, which costs 3 ms at the same size. The bound is on the line, not on the header section, so a second `From` behind a long conformant header block is still found and still checked.

items.title: A Content-Type that ends inside a quoted string is refused
items.body: `b.safeMime.parse` refuses a charset it does not hold in its allowlist. The splitter that reads the parameters stops at an unterminated quoted string and drops everything after it, so the same header one character apart produced no `charset` parameter at all, and a leaf with no charset takes the RFC 2045 §5.2 default of `us-ascii`. `charset=nonsense-1` was refused and `charset="utf-8` was accepted and decoded as us-ascii: a sender walked a part past the allowlist by leaving a quote open, and the sender is the one who writes that header. A Content-Type whose parameter section ends inside a quoted string is now `safe-mime/malformed-content-type`. `b.structuredFields.endsInsideQuotedString` answers the same question for the other callers of the quote-aware splitter, which is the distinction none of them could make: a parameter that is absent and one an open quote swallowed arrive as the same shorter list. The quote balance is read from the header AS TRANSMITTED, because the parser decodes RFC 2047 encoded words into a header before it reads the header's structure, and a quote or a semicolon that decoding produced is data: `name="=?utf-8?Q?13=22_monitor=2Epdf?="` is a correctly written header whose decoded form carries three quotes. Structure now comes from the wire and each parameter value is decoded after it, so an encoded word can neither have a message rejected nor move a parameter boundary.

items.title: A JMAP result reference cannot name a prototype key
items.body: The back-reference resolver wrote each resolved value with `obj[key.slice(1)]`, and the client chooses that key. `"#__proto__"` therefore reached the prototype setter of the arguments object rather than an own property: the handler read `accountId`, `ids` and every other argument off a prototype the caller supplied, while `hasOwnProperty` reported the object carried none of them, and `accountId` is what the account gate checks. A back-reference naming `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype` is now `invalidResultReference`. The check composes `b.pick`'s poisoned-key list, which the framework already used for this class everywhere else.

items.title: A Sieve script cannot nest its tests past the depth its profile caps
items.body: `b.safeSieve` caps how deep a script nests, and checked it only where a BLOCK opens. A test nests through `not`, `anyof` and `allof` without ever reaching a block, so a 12,019-byte script, well inside the strict profile's 65,536-byte cap, validated clean, was accepted by ManageSieve PUTSCRIPT and stored, and then threw a bare `RangeError` out of `b.mail.sieve.run` at every delivery, with no `code` on it and not a `MailSieveError` for a caller to branch on. The cap now covers the test grammar. `b.mail.sieve.run` takes an AST rather than a script, so it bounds its own recursion as well, through both the test grammar and the command blocks a script nests: the parser's cap is not the interpreter's when a caller can hand it a tree.

items.title: A Sieve redirect address cannot end the SMTP command that carries it
items.body: `redirect` names the address a message is forwarded to, and a delivery agent writes that address into an SMTP `RCPT TO:` line, so a CR or LF inside it ends the command and everything after it is read as another one. `b.mail.sieve.run` now refuses a redirect whose address carries a control character, whether the script wrote the byte out or produced it with an encoded-character run, and names the offset. The check asks only whether the address can break the command, so a host name with no dot, an IP literal and a quoted local part all still redirect.

items.title: An encoded-character run cannot carry a byte the script was not allowed to write
items.body: `b.safeSieve`'s tokenizer refuses a NUL written literally inside a string, and the encoded-character decoder runs after tokenization with nothing re-applying that rule, so `${hex:00}` put a byte into a `fileinto` folder name that the script itself could not have written. A run is now held to what a literal may carry, which is every character except NUL: a Sieve string may hold a raw CR or LF, and the `text:` form builds a value full of them, so refusing those in a run would reject scripts RFC 5228 section 2.4.2.4 requires an implementation to accept while leaving the same bytes reachable by writing them out.

items.title: The SMTP guard and the listeners read one address
items.body: `b.guardSmtpCommand` ends a MAIL or RCPT path at the first `>` outside a quoted string, because RFC 5321 §4.1.2 lets a quoted local part hold one. Both SMTP listeners went on ending it at the first `>` of any kind, so the guard shape-checked one mailbox and the envelope carried a shorter one that no check had seen: `MAIL FROM:<"x@evil.example> y"@example.com>` was validated as `example.com` and delivered with the envelope sender `"x@evil.example`, whose domain check was skipped for want of an `@`. Both listeners now slice the path with the same reader the guard uses, so the line the guard accepted and the address the handler acts on are the same bytes. Text butted against the closing bracket with no space is a malformed command, per RFC 5321 §4.1.1.2, rather than a parameter.

items.title: An IMAP SELECT that fails leaves no mailbox selected
items.body: RFC 9051 §6.3.2 requires a failed SELECT to deselect whatever was open and return the session to the authenticated state. The listener wrote `NO` and left the selection in place, so a client whose SELECT was refused went on issuing EXPUNGE, STORE and FETCH against the mailbox it believed it had left. The failure path now clears the selection and reports `[CLOSED]` when one was open.

items.title: `UID STORE *:*` names one message
items.body: Both ends of `*:*` are the same message, the one holding the largest UID, so the set names one message however large the mailbox is. `b.mail.server.imap` counted any UID range written against `*` as the whole mailbox, which is the right upper bound for `1:*` and the wrong one here, and refused `UID STORE *:*` on a mailbox past `maxSequenceSetItems`. It counts as one. Which messages a set names is the mailbox's answer, so a set reaches `fetchRange` and `storeFlags` as the client wrote it, `*` included, and `storeFlags` is now called with `maxMessages`, the profile's `maxSequenceSetItems`. A backend refuses a set that resolves to more than that many messages. What the listener refuses before the call is what it can count without the mailbox: an enumerated set, and a message-number range against the count it last announced to the connection.

items.title: A `b.safeEnv` schema is checked wherever it is read, not only where a key turns out to be missing
items.body: `b.safeEnv.load` read the type of a key's `required` flag on the branch a MISSING key takes, and nowhere else. A schema written `required: "yes"` was therefore refused on a machine where the variable was absent and accepted in silence on a machine where it was set, though the schema is the same artifact on both. Every key the schema names is now checked before its value is read.

items.title: An option `b.parsers.xml.parse` refuses carries `xml/bad-opt` in `code` and the explanation in `message`
items.body: `SafeXmlError` takes the message first and the code second, and both option refusals were built the other way round. A caller matching `err.code === "xml/bad-opt"` never matched, because `code` held the whole sentence; a log that prints only the message printed `xml/bad-opt` and nothing about which option was wrong or what was passed. Both now carry the code in `code` and the explanation in `message`, which is what every other refusal in the parser already did. A `codebase-patterns` check fails on any error class that is registered message-first and constructed code-first.

items.title: A message over the scanner's stream limit is refused, not reported as a scanner outage
items.body: `b.mail.scan` queued the whole message into the socket in one pass. clamd stops reading once a stream passes `StreamMaxLength` and answers `INSTREAM size limit exceeded`, so the reply and the write error raced, and the writer never got a turn in which to notice the refusal. Measured against clamd with `StreamMaxLength 1M`, sending 4 MiB: 48 concurrent scans returned 47 size refusals and one `mail-scan/transport`. The two are not interchangeable. A size refusal is permanent and a transport failure is worth retrying, so the losing scan sent a caller back to retry a message that will never fit. The body is now written with backpressure, so a daemon that stops reading is noticed rather than fed, and a reply that arrives after the write error is still read: the transport waits for the socket to close before deciding, and reports `mail-scan/transport` only when nothing came back. 96 concurrent scans now return 96 size refusals. The same write discipline applies to the ICAP transport, which had queued the message the same way. An ICAP reply is not self-delimiting the way a NUL-terminated clamd reply is, so it keeps its own rule: a reset with a partial response there remains a transport failure rather than a verdict.

items.title: A parsed leaf says what its Content-Type header carried
items.body: `b.safeMime.parse` wrote `charset` onto every leaf, defaulting to `us-ascii` per RFC 2045 §5.2, and exposed nothing else the header said. A caller could not tell a sender who wrote `charset=us-ascii` from one who wrote no charset at all, which is the distinction RFC 8621 §4.1.4 asks for, and could not read `format=flowed` or `delsp` (RFC 3676) when rendering a body. Each leaf now carries `contentTypeParams`, the frozen parameter map as written, beside the defaulted `charset`. Only `name` and `filename` are decoded out of RFC 2047 encoded-word form, because mail agents write display names that way; `boundary`, `charset` and the rest are the bytes the header carried, since RFC 2047 section 5 gives no encoded-word form for a parameter value and decoding `boundary` would compare a delimiter the body never used. `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties` reads that map rather than parsing the header a second time. It also holds RFC 8621 §4.1.4's rule that `partId` and `blobId` are null if and only if a part is `multipart/*`: a multipart whose own boundary never appears in its body parses to no children, and deciding by child count handed that part a fetchable `blobId` while reporting a multipart type, with no list naming it. `subParts` follows the same rule, an array for a multipart and null for every other part, where it had been an empty array throughout. `language` reports the tags a part's `Content-Language` header carries, `["en-GB", "fr"]` for `en-GB, fr`, and null for a part that carries none; it had been null either way. A tree from `b.safeMime.parse(bytes, { structureOnly: true })` keeps no bodies, so `size`, which §4.1.4 defines as the octets after content-transfer decoding, cannot be answered for it: every attachment had been advertised at `size: 0` beside a blobId a client could fetch. Such a tree is now refused with `safe-mime/structure-only`, which is what `b.safeMime.extractText` already answered for it.

items.title: maxHeaderLineBytes counts bytes
items.body: `b.safeMime.parse` compared a header line against `maxHeaderLineBytes` using the string's length in UTF-16 code units, so a line of multibyte characters passed a cap it exceeded: 700 two-byte characters measure 700 against the 998 default and occupy 1400 octets. RFC 5322 §2.1.1 counts characters of US-ASCII and RFC 6532 §3.4, which widens a field body to UTF-8, keeps the limit in octets. The comparison now runs through `b.safeBuffer.byteLengthOf`, and the refusal reports the byte count.

items.title: A multipart/related is rooted at the part its start parameter names
items.body: RFC 2387 §3.2 gives a `multipart/related` a `start` parameter naming the `Content-ID` of its root body part, and makes the first part the root only when `start` is absent. The classification took the first part either way, so a message whose sender declared a later root, the ordinary shape when an inline image precedes the HTML, had its body classified as a file: `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties` answered with an empty `textBody` and `htmlBody` and offered the body for download, while `b.safeMime.extractText` still answered with it, so the two readers described one message differently. The root is now the part `start` names, compared without the angle brackets either side may write, and the first part when `start` is absent or names a `Content-ID` no part carries. Both values are read from the header as transmitted, because decoding an RFC 2047 encoded word can produce a quote or a semicolon that is data rather than syntax. A non-root child is a resource whether it is a leaf or a multipart of its own, so a `multipart/alternative` sitting beside the root is offered as files rather than having its representations read as the body. A `Content-Disposition: attachment` on a container carries the same way: the disposition was read when the walk reached a leaf and not when it descended, so an attached `multipart/alternative` had its representations read as the message's body while `attachments` and `hasAttachment` reported no file at all. The sender writes that disposition, and it now applies to the whole subtree it heads.

items.title: extractText answers prefer: "any" with the richest representation, whatever its text type
items.body: RFC 2046 §5.1.4 orders the parts of a `multipart/alternative` simplest to richest, and `b.safeMime.extractText(tree, { prefer: "any" })` answers with the richest. It ranked them by the body classification RFC 8621 §4.1.4 defines, which names `text/plain` and `text/html` and nothing else, so an alternative whose last representation was `text/enriched` (RFC 1896) or `text/markdown` (RFC 7763) was answered with the plain representation the sender wrote first. The ranking is now over text types: the answer is the last representation that the sender did not mark `Content-Disposition: attachment`, and one wrapped in another multipart counts as that choice. Which list a leaf belongs to is unchanged, so a `text/enriched` is still a file to `b.safeMime.selectBodyParts`, `b.safeMime.extractAttachments` and the stored attachment count. An alternative carrying no HTML answers `prefer: "html"` with the text representation a reader displays, which is the last one.

items.title: A part of a multipart/digest that carries no Content-Type is an enclosed message
items.body: RFC 2046 §5.1.5 changes the default `Content-Type` of a body part inside a `multipart/digest` from `text/plain` to `message/rfc822`, and RFC 8621 §4.1.4 says the same for the `type` property it defines. `b.safeMime.parse` applied the `text/plain` default everywhere, so the parts of a digest were read as plain-text bodies: the first enclosed message became the digest's body and the rest became files, and `b.mailStore` recorded an attachment count taken from that reading. The default now follows the enclosing multipart, and a part with no `Content-Type` anywhere else is still `text/plain`.

items.title: Only the name parameter is read as a part's name
items.body: The `Content-Type` fallback in `b.safeMime.filenameFromHeaders` searched the raw header for the text `name=`, which is the tail of any parameter ending in those letters and occurs inside quoted values. `x-username=bob` was read as a file named `bob`, and a `name=` written inside another parameter's quoted value supplied the filename. The parameter is now looked up in the parsed header. `Content-Disposition` still takes precedence over it.

items.title: A quoted local part names the mailbox its bare spelling names
items.body: RFC 5321 §4.1.2 lets a local part be written as a quoted string, and `"ops"@example.com` is the mailbox `ops@example.com`. Both the submission listener's strict identity binding and `b.mail.server.jmap` compared the two spellings as text, so an account whose client quoted its own address was refused with `forbiddenFrom` or a 553. The quoted form is now decoded, quoted pairs included, before the comparison. Case is still significant in the local part, a quoted local part is still not subaddress-folded because its delimiter is literal mailbox data, and an unterminated quoted string names no mailbox.

items.title: A named inline file is counted as an attachment
items.body: `b.safeMime.extractAttachments` skipped every part marked `Content-Disposition: inline`, so a PDF sent as `inline; filename="a.pdf"` was not counted. The classification is now one primitive, `b.safeMime.selectBodyParts`, which sorts a parsed tree's leaves into the text a reader displays, the HTML it displays and the files it offers; `extractAttachments` and `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties` both read it, so a mailbox listing and `Email/get` cannot disagree. A superseded representation takes nothing with it. Which alternative a reader displays decides what the BODY is; it does not decide which leaves exist, and RFC 8621 section 4.1.4, the classification this implements, puts a payload leaf of a losing branch in `attachments`, as its own worked example does with an image inside a `multipart/related` inside an alternative. Every input a narrower rule could read is one the sender writes, the disposition, the media type, the `Content-ID` and the order of the branches, so each such rule left a shape whose bytes were downloadable through `bodyStructure` while no list named them and `b.mailStore` recorded no attachment. `b.mailStore`'s `appendMessage` records `hasAttachment` and `attachmentCount` from that list while `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties` follows RFC 8621 §4.1.4 and counts a named inline part, so a mailbox listing said a message carried no file while Email/get offered it for download. Both readers now classify a part the same way, and a name is evidence of an attachment wherever another part can be the body instead: a named first part beside an unnamed sibling is a file, in a `multipart/mixed` and in a `multipart/alternative` alike, and the first part's exemption applies only when nothing unnamed is there to show. RFC 8621 section 4.1.4's algorithm exempts the first part outright (`i === 0 ||`), which taken literally offers a file as the message text whenever the sender puts it first. Reading the exemption as a fallback keeps the shape it exists for, a lone `text/plain` a gateway wrote as `inline; filename="message.txt"`, which is the body because the message has nothing else to show, and an alternative whose representations are all named keeps its body for the same reason. Inside a `multipart/related` the first part is the root and the rest are files, which is that section's own rule. A part is otherwise an attachment when its disposition is `attachment` or when it is a leaf that is not displayed body text, so a payload sitting in an alternative representation nobody displays is offered rather than dropped while `bodyStructure` goes on advertising its blobId. The parameter reader also accepts the linear whitespace RFC 2045 §5.1 permits around a parameter's `=`, so `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename = "notes.txt"` names a file; requiring the `=` to sit against the attribute found no parameter at all, and the part read as body text and left the attachment list.

items.title: textBody and htmlBody carry one alternative representation
items.body: The parts of a `multipart/alternative` are one body written several ways. `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties` collected every descendant, so a message carrying two `text/plain` representations put both in `textBody` and a client rendering the list in order showed the message twice. Each alternative is now considered by what it contributes: RFC 2046 §5.1.4 orders them simplest to richest, so the LAST representation offering plain text and the last offering HTML are the displayed ones, and a representation wrapped in a `multipart/related` or `multipart/mixed` counts as that one choice, keeping all of its sections and its inline files. A part the sender marked `Content-Disposition: attachment` is not a spelling of the body, so it is offered whichever branch it sits in. A displayed section that is NOT one of several representations of one body is named in both lists, which is what RFC 8621 §4.1.4 defines: a plain-text introduction in front of an alternative reaches `htmlBody` as well, so an HTML client renders the whole message rather than the alternative alone, and a `text/plain`-only or `text/html`-only body reaches both lists for the same reason. The one-list-each rule applies to the alternatives themselves, and to an alternative offering only one representation that one representation serves as both. Every representation remains in `bodyStructure`.

items.title: maxConcurrentRequests and maxConcurrentUpload bound what they advertise
items.body: The JMAP session published both values from `b.mail.server.jmap.create` options, and neither was consulted when admitting work: an account could hold any number of dispatches and uploads open at once. Each is now an admission limit per account. A request beyond it is refused with the RFC 8620 §3.6.1 `limit` problem naming `maxConcurrentRequests`, answered 429 so a client that retries on 429 recovers rather than reading it as a bad request; an upload beyond it answers 429 with `limit: "maxConcurrentUpload"`. Every other `limit` problem keeps the status it had. An upload holds its slot until the backend has finished with the bytes, not merely until the request body has been read, and a connection that drops mid-body releases it. Actors are counted apart by tenant and by identity, whether that identity is written as a string or a number.

items.title: A From address is read past the comments and quoted text inside it
items.body: A comment (RFC 5322 §3.2.2) may appear anywhere folding whitespace may, inside the angle brackets and between the atoms of the address included, and `Ops <ops@example.com (work)>` names the mailbox `ops@example.com`. The JMAP From reader removed only the comments outside the brackets, so an authorized submission was refused as `forbiddenFrom`. Comments and the whitespace around them are now removed from the address before the identity is compared, and a quoted local part keeps its own spaces. RFC 5321 §4.1.2 writes a local part as a quoted string when it holds characters a dot-atom cannot, the angle bracket among them. `b.guardSmtpCommand` ended a MAIL or RCPT path at the first `>`, and the JMAP From-header reader ended the address there too, so `<"a>b"@example.com>` was cut inside the quotes: a valid sender was refused and the tail was read back as extension parameters. Both now find the first delimiter outside a quoted string, through the new `b.safeBuffer.unquotedIndexOf`. A path with no closing bracket outside the quotes is still refused.

items.title: A download filename is decoded once
items.body: The JMAP download handler percent-decoded the filename segment even when `b.router` had already decoded the pathname, so a file named `report%20final.txt` was served as `report final.txt`. It now decodes only the segment it reads from the raw path and uses a router-supplied `req.params.name` as it stands.

items.title: A JMAP extension error keeps the name its handler gave
items.body: RFC 8620 §3.6.2 lets an extension define its own method error under the `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:` prefix. The dispatcher matched a returned `type` against the standard names alone, so a handler refusing with `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:customFailure` produced a successful method response carrying the error object as its data. A prefixed name is now sent as an error under its bare spelling, with the members alongside it: RFC 8620 §3.6.2 gives the standard errors members of their own and leaves an extension error to define its own, so an error is not held to `type`, `description` and `properties`. An unprefixed name outside the standard set is still data, and an unprefixed standard name is an error only when it carries nothing else, because a result may legitimately carry a `type` member. `Core/echo` answers with the client's own arguments, so its result is never read as an error.

items.title: An encoded-character run that is not UTF-8 is refused
items.body: A Sieve string is UTF-8 text (RFC 5228 §2.4.2), and `${hex:...}` writes octets. A run whose octets are not a UTF-8 sequence was decoded with replacement characters, so `${hex:ff}` and `${hex:fe}` became the same string: an `i;octet` comparison matched a byte sequence the script never wrote, and an action named a folder it never named. Such a run is now refused at parse as `safe-sieve/bad-encoded-character`. A complete character is still accepted however it is spelled, including octets split across two substitutions. Deciding that a `${` opens no encoded character reads the `hex:` or `unicode:` keyword where it would begin, rather than searching ahead for the closing brace and copying everything between: a string of openers cost the square of how many it held, 606 ms for 32,000 of them against 3 ms now, and a mebibyte script holds many such strings. The two encodings have different grammars and the decoder applies each one: §2.4.2.4 writes `hex-pair-seq = *blank hex-pair *(1*blank hex-pair) *blank` with `hex-pair = 1*2HEXDIG`, so octets are separated by whitespace and `${hex:41 42}` is `AB` while `${hex:4142}` is a four-digit run no pair matches and stays literal, which is what the section's own `${hex:400}` example shows; `unicode-hex` is `1*HEXDIG` with no upper bound, so `${unicode:0000041}` is `A`.

items.title: A Sieve equality test is charged for the characters it reads
items.body: Gas for a match was charged as the product of the value length and the key length, which is the cost of `:contains` and `:matches` but not of `:is`, an equality comparison. A valid `header :is` against a 3,500-character header exhausted the default 10,000-unit budget and aborted the filter. `:is` is now charged for the characters it reads; the searching forms keep the product charge.

items.title: A refused JMAP request carries an RFC 8620 §3.6.1 problem type
items.body: The listener answered a malformed request with its own codes, `guard-jmap/bad-json`, `guard-jmap/bad-input`, `invalidArguments`, `requestTooLarge` and `limit/<name>`, and put an empty `methodResponses` array and a `sessionState` in the body. A conforming client could not tell a body that would not parse from one that was not a Request, or either from an over-limit request, and the HTTP path sent a different type than the WebSocket path for the same input. A refusal is now `unknownCapability`, `notJSON`, `notRequest`, or `limit` with a `limit` member naming the cap reached (`maxSizeRequest`, `maxCallsInRequest`, `maxUsingCapabilities`, `maxBackRefDepth`), sent as `application/problem+json` with `status` and `detail` and no method-response envelope. Both transports send the same type for the same input. An account backend that fails answers 500 rather than 400.

items.title: A JMAP method error is the bare name RFC 8620 §3.6.2 defines
items.body: A method error was written as the request-level URI, `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:unknownMethod`, where §3.6.2 writes `[ "error", { "type": "unknownMethod" }, "c0" ]`. A client matching the names the RFC prints, and the names RFC 8621 defines for the Email and Mailbox set errors, matched none of them. Method errors are now bare names, and a handler that returns or throws one has that name sent to the client rather than `serverFail`. A returned result counts as an error only when it carries an error name and nothing besides `description` and `properties`, so a result whose own data happens to include a `type` is still a result.

items.title: maxObjectsInGet and maxObjectsInSet are applied
items.body: Both were defined in every `b.guardJmap` profile and documented as enforced, and no code read either: under the strict profile, whose limit is 500, an `Email/get` handler received 250,000 ids and an `Email/set` handler 250,000 destroy ids in one request. A `/get` call's identifier arguments, and the combined `create`, `update` and `destroy` of a `/set` or `/copy` call, are now counted after result references resolve, and an over-cap call is `requestTooLarge` before the handler runs, per RFC 8620 §5.1 and §5.3. `ids` is not the only argument that names objects: RFC 8621 §5.1 gives `SearchSnippet/get` an `emailIds` argument, so the count covers `ids` and any `…Ids` argument rather than one name, and a list of something other than objects, such as `properties`, is not counted. `b.guardJmap.limitsFor(opts)` resolves the caps a profile and posture select.

items.title: A request body is parsed against the declared maxSizeRequest
items.body: A string or Buffer body was measured against the profile's `maxSizeRequest`, 10 MiB under the strict profile, and then parsed with the 1 MiB default of `b.safeJson.parse`, so a valid 1.17 MB request came back as "body is not valid JSON". The parse now uses the profile's limit, and a body over it is the `limit` problem naming `maxSizeRequest`.

items.title: The session publishes the core capability RFC 8620 §2 requires
items.body: `urn:ietf:params:jmap:core` was an empty object, so a client could read none of the limits it has to obey. It now carries `maxSizeUpload`, `maxConcurrentUpload`, `maxSizeRequest`, `maxConcurrentRequests`, `maxCallsInRequest`, `maxObjectsInGet`, `maxObjectsInSet` and `collationAlgorithms`, built from the profile the listener enforces and from `maxBlobBytes`. `create` refuses a `serverCapabilities` core value that differs from what the listener applies. RFC 8620 §5.1 makes a `/get`'s `ids` nullable, and a request that omits it asks for every record of the type, which counting the request's arguments cannot see: `maxObjectsInGet` is now read off what the handler returned as well, so an account holding more records than the cap gets `requestTooLarge` rather than the whole collection.

items.title: A download's Content-Disposition filename survives the round trip
items.body: `b.staticServe` built the `filename*` ext-value with `encodeURIComponent`, whose escaping set is not RFC 8187 §3.2.1 `attr-char`: it emits `'`, `(`, `)` and `*` raw, and the apostrophe is the delimiter the ext-value is parsed on. A file named `reçu café's.pdf` went out as `filename*=UTF-8''re%C3%A7u%20caf%C3%A9's.pdf`, and this framework's own `b.safeMime` reader split on the third delimiter and returned `reçu café`. The encoder now percent-escapes everything outside `attr-char`. Two defects on the reading side went with it: `b.safeMime` took whichever of `filename` and `filename*` appeared first, and RFC 6266 §4.3 writes the plain one first, so the extended name was discarded for every sender that follows the RFC; and an unescaped apostrophe in the value truncated the name rather than being kept. The builder is exported as `b.staticServe.attachmentDisposition(filename)`, because a consumer serving a stranger-named file had to write the header itself, and the obvious way to write it is the way this module wrote it.

items.title: A JMAP Email/get can answer the body-part properties RFC 8621 defines
items.body: `b.mail.server.jmap` carried no `bodyStructure`, `attachments` or `hasAttachment` anywhere, so a JMAP client could not see that a message held a file, list its parts, or fetch one. Nothing was refused and nothing was logged: the response was well formed, the client read the properties it knew, and a message with three files looked the same as one with none. `Email/get` is an operator-supplied handler, so the new piece is the builder it composes: `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties(tree, { blobIdPrefix })` turns the tree `b.safeMime.parse` returns into `{ bodyStructure, textBody, htmlBody, attachments, hasAttachment }`, with the `partId` and `blobId` RFC 8621 §4.1.4 puts on each `EmailBodyPart`. A `blobId` is the prefix's length, the prefix and the part's path, and the prefix must satisfy the RFC 8620 §1.2 Id grammar, because the download handler in the same module refuses anything else. That grammar admits `-` and `_`, so a separator also occurs inside a prefix and joining the two plainly let two different messages name one blob: a message `m` with a first part and a message `m-0` with none both read `m-0`, and a download handler keyed on `blobId` inside an account could answer one with the other's bytes. The length in front lets a reader take exactly the prefix and leave the path, whatever either contains.

items.title: An extracted attachment says which part it came from
items.body: `b.safeMime.extractAttachments` returned `filename`, `contentType`, `body` and `headers` with nothing identifying the part, so a consumer serving one part at a URL had no stable key and paired a second `walk` to this list by index, which is correct only while both traversals visit leaves in the same order. `walk` already computes the position and hands it to its visitor; each entry now carries it as `path`, the index array from the root. `b.safeMime.filenameFromHeaders(headers)` is exported so a caller walking the tree reads filenames the way this module does instead of writing another `Content-Disposition` reader.

items.title: b.mail.dkim.create refuses a private key whose type its algorithm does not name
items.body: `create` parsed `opts.privateKey` and never compared its type with `opts.algorithm`, and nothing downstream compared them either. An RSA key in the `ed25519-sha256` slot produced a `DKIM-Signature` whose `a=` tag said `ed25519-sha256` over an RSA signature: every conforming verifier refuses that message, and the sender saw nothing wrong because the signer returned a header and the send succeeded. An Ed25519 key in the `rsa-sha256` slot failed later and uncoded, throwing Node's `ERR_CRYPTO_UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION` from inside `sign()`. `create` now refuses the mismatch with `dkim/key-algorithm-mismatch`, pairing `rsa-sha256` with an RSA key and `ed25519-sha256` with an Ed25519 key per RFC 6376 §3.3.3 and RFC 8463 §3. `verify` already made this comparison on the receiving side.

items.title: mtaSts.fetch takes an httpClient, as its sibling already did
items.body: `b.network.smtp.policy.mtaSts.fetch` built its HTTPS client inline, so nothing depending on a fetched MTA-STS policy document could be exercised without a live network. `tlsRpt.submit`, in the same module, already declared `httpClient` and read `opts.httpClient || httpClient()`: one question answered two ways. The fetch takes the same option, and its option list is declared, so a misspelled one is refused by name rather than ignored. The policy document decides whether mail to a domain goes out under an enforced TLS policy, which is exactly the path a consumer needs to be able to cover.

items.title: The MTA-STS lookup goes through the resolver the sender pinned
items.body: `b.mail.send.deliver` used `opts.resolver` for the MX and DANE TLSA lookups and called `mtaSts.fetch(domain)` with the domain alone, so `_mta-sts.<domain>` was answered by whatever the host resolves with. That record is the whole decision: RFC 8461 §3.1 gives a receiver one TXT record to declare a policy and a sender that sees none enforces nothing, so a suppressed answer and an honest absence are the same answer. The lookup deciding whether a message goes out under an enforced TLS policy was the one lookup a pinned resolver did not reach. `mtaSts.fetch` and `tlsRpt.fetchPolicy` now take a `resolver` handle alongside the existing `dnsLookup` function, and the composer passes its own through.

items.title: b.guardImapCommand applies the mailbox, sequence-set and SEARCH-depth caps it declares
items.body: Every profile declared `maxMailboxBytes`, `maxSequenceSetItems` and `maxSearchDepth`, the documentation said they were enforced, and no code read any of them: a consumer selecting the strict profile for its sequence-set bound got the line bound instead, so the effective limit moved with the length of the line rather than with the element count the cap names, and nothing bounded SEARCH nesting at all. `validate` now bounds the mailbox-name argument in bytes (`guard-imap-command/mailbox-too-long`), the elements a sequence set expands to, counting a message-number range by its span and a UID range as one element, since UIDs are sparse and `UID FETCH 100000:120000` can name two messages (`guard-imap-command/sequence-set-too-large`), and the nesting of a SEARCH key outside quoted strings (`guard-imap-command/search-too-deep`). A `UID` prefix is unwrapped so the caps apply to the command it qualifies. A seventh value, `allowLegacyMUtf7`, was declared `true` for the balanced profile while `b.mail.server.imap` derived its own answer from `profile === "permissive"` and refused it: the table now states what the listener has always applied, and the listener reads it through the new `b.mail.server.imap.legacyMUtf7Allowed(profile)` rather than deriving a second answer. `b.guardImapCommand.limitsFor(opts)` resolves the caps a profile and posture select. The mailbox cap is on every operand rather than the first: `RENAME` names two mailboxes, and its destination went unmeasured, so a name over the cap reached the backend and was then refused on the next command that mentioned it. The listener holds each operand to the cap in bytes, where it had compared a JavaScript string length, which counts a character outside ASCII as one however many bytes it occupies. The cap it holds them to is the profile's own `maxMailboxBytes`, 1024 at strict, 2048 at balanced and 4096 at permissive, rather than a kilobyte the listener kept to itself: a 1500-byte name passed the guard under balanced and was then refused by the handler, so the published number and the served one disagreed. The strict default is unchanged. A refusal from the command guard is also addressed to the tag the command was sent under, which RFC 9051 §7.1.3 requires ("When the server detects a protocol error ... it MUST send a tagged BAD response"); these were written untagged, so a client waiting for its tag waited out the whole command. A line whose tag cannot be read, an empty one or one whose first atom is outside the tag grammar, is still answered untagged, since there is nothing to address it to. `b.guardImapCommand.tagOf(line)` is the reader, returning the tag or null. `maxSequenceSetItems` counted a range written against `*` as a single message, so `FETCH 1:20000` was refused at strict while `FETCH 1:*` over the same mailbox was admitted. RFC 9051 §9 makes `*` the largest number in use, a count only the selected mailbox knows, so such a range is no longer counted here at all and the cap states what it bounds: the messages a set names on the wire. `FETCH 1:*` keeps working, which is how a client reads a mailbox, and is bounded by the per-handler response-byte and wall-clock budgets. `STORE` is not: it writes, a `.SILENT` one writes while answering almost nothing, and a handler timeout does not undo what the backend already wrote. `b.mail.server.imap` calls `storeFlags` with `maxMessages`, the profile's `maxSequenceSetItems`, and a backend refuses a set that resolves to more than that many messages. The cap travels rather than being applied in the listener, because the listener holds a count taken at `SELECT` and another connection moves the mailbox under it in both directions: appending makes the count too low and the cap passes a command that mutates the larger mailbox, expunging makes it too high and the cap refuses one that now names a single message. Which messages a set names is the mailbox's answer, so the set reaches the store as the client wrote it, `*` included. An `opts.overrides` handler is handed the same numbers as `parsed.limits`: `COPY` and `MOVE` are the operator's to implement and they mutate, and a handler had no way to learn the cap its own command was subject to. The `UID` form is handed them too. It re-enters the registry by its own path, so it had been reaching a handler with nothing, and it is the form that needs them most, since a UID range's width is not a message count and the command guard leaves it uncounted. `SEARCH`, `COPY`, `MOVE`, `EXPUNGE`, `FETCH`, `STORE`, `CLOSE`, `UNSELECT` and `CHECK` are held to the selected state before the registry is reached, in both forms. RFC 9051 §6 rejects a command issued in a state that does not permit it with `BAD`. Each of these answered that question from inside a handler an override replaces, or, for `SEARCH`, `COPY` and `MOVE`, did not answer it at all, so an operator handler that reads, copies, moves or deletes could be reached by a client that had not selected a mailbox, or authenticated. `EXPUNGE` answered `NO No mailbox selected`; the answer is now `BAD`, given once, in front of all six. `MOVE`, `EXPUNGE` and `STORE` are refused on a mailbox opened by `EXAMINE`, which RFC 9051 §6.3.2 makes read-only: `STORE` refused there from inside its own handler and the other two did not, so a client that opened a mailbox read-only could still empty it. `COPY` is served, since it writes to the other mailbox. `UID FETCH` and `UID STORE` reach the registry like the other four, so a handler supplied for one serves its `UID` form, which is what the surrounding documentation already said of every override. `CLOSE` removes the messages flagged `\Deleted` through `mailStore.expungeFolder` before returning to the authenticated state, which RFC 9051 §6.4.2 requires and which is the difference between it and `UNSELECT`: the two ran the same code, so a client that flagged mail and closed the mailbox was told the deletion had happened and it had not. A mailbox opened by `EXAMINE` keeps its messages through `CLOSE`, as that section also says. `CLOSE` removes through `mailStore.expungeFolder`, and not through an `opts.overrides` EXPUNGE handler. That handler is written to serve the `EXPUNGE` command: it holds the connection, writes untagged responses and answers a tag, and §6.4.2 allows `CLOSE` none of those. Driving it from `CLOSE` would mean containing what it writes, which cannot be done, because the handler is also handed `state` and `state.socket` is the client's own socket. A deployment whose removal lives in an override supplies `expungeFolder` as well, and where there is none `CLOSE` still completes, since it is how most clients leave a mailbox, and says in the same response that nothing was removed. A removal that lands after another connection has deleted or renamed the mailbox is recorded and reported, by `CLOSE` and by `EXPUNGE` alike: the `mail.server.imap.expunge` event is emitted for it, where it had been skipped so the audit trail showed no deletion at all, and `CLOSE` answers `OK`, since both things it promises, the removal and the return to the authenticated state, have happened. `EXPUNGE` against a store with no `expungeFolder` answers `NO EXPUNGE backend not configured` rather than `OK` with nothing removed, which is what `FETCH` and `STORE` already answered for their own backends. `fetchRange` is told whether the selection is read-only, so a backend can honor RFC 9051 §6.4.5's rule that a `BODY[]` fetch does not set `\Seen` there. A command is answered once: a handler awaiting a backend can be answered by the dispatcher first, when it outruns `maxHandlerMs` or its selection goes, and would then answer its own tag a second time, which puts a client's replies out of step with its requests for the rest of the connection. A tag the client uses again for a later command is answered again, since that is a new command. A handler that outran `maxHandlerMs` went on running and went on holding the socket, so the connection is now closed with an untagged `BYE` after that refusal. `STARTTLS` is refused outside the not-authenticated state, which is the only one RFC 9051 §6.2.1 permits it in: it was served afterwards, renegotiating underneath a session that kept its actor and its selected mailbox. Every verb that needs an authenticated session is held to one in front of the registry rather than inside a handler an override replaces, which RFC 9051 §6.3 requires and which thirteen of them were served without: `CREATE`, `DELETE`, `RENAME`, `SELECT` and the rest reached an operator handler with no actor at all. The gate names the verbs §6.1 and §6.2 admit before login, `CAPABILITY`, `NOOP`, `LOGOUT`, `STARTTLS`, `AUTHENTICATE`, `LOGIN` and `ID`, and refuses the rest, so a verb added later is refused by omission rather than admitted by it. A verb the server does not implement is still answered as unimplemented rather than as a state error. The refusal is `BAD <verb> only valid in Authenticated state`, where the shipped handlers had answered `NO Login first`. `ENABLE` is held to the part of the authenticated state before any mailbox is selected, which §6.3.1 requires: a client could otherwise turn `CONDSTORE` on under a selection it had already established, and `FETCH` began carrying `MODSEQ` for a mailbox opened without it. A refusal that is about the command comes before one that is about the server: `UID EXPUNGE` on a mailbox opened read-only says the mailbox is read-only rather than naming which handlers are configured.

items.title: A compliance posture the guard does not know is refused by name
items.body: `b.gateContract.makeProfileResolver` and `b.gateContract.resolveProfileName` dropped a `posture` value their table did not hold and fell through to `profile` or the default, and the 24 guards built on them inherited that. An operator who wrote `{ profile: "permissive", posture: "hippa" }`, or `"HIPAA"` in the wrong case, ran permissive with no signal that the posture had been ignored. Both resolvers now throw `<guard>/bad-posture` naming the value and the postures the guard accepts. `b.guardJmap`, `b.guardImapCommand`, `b.guardPop3Command` and `b.guardManageSieveCommand` each resolved the profile and posture with their own copy of the same code and kept dropping it; all four now use the shared resolver. A posture that is absent, null or empty is not a value and is not refused.

items.title: A guard profile cannot be edited from outside the guard
items.body: `b.guardJmap.limitsFor` returned the profile object itself, so `limitsFor({}).maxCallsInRequest = 9999` raised the cap the guard enforces for every listener in the process. The profiles are frozen. The walk that freezes them carries a depth bound so a cyclic policy cannot run it out of stack, and past that bound it returned the rest of the policy untouched, which handed back a writable cap under a policy reported as frozen. A policy nested deeper than eight levels, a cyclic one among them, is refused with `gate-contract/policy-too-deep` instead; the deepest policy any shipped guard carries is three.

items.title: The JMAP WebSocket transport applies the request size the session declares
