items.body: The WebSocket path carried its own 10 MiB limit in the upgrade cap, the frame-length check and the parse, while the session publishes the profile's `maxSizeRequest`. Under the balanced profile a client was told 50 MiB and refused at 10 MiB. All three read the profile's limit, and `webSocketMaxMessageBytes` overrides it.

items.title: A mail-store move between accounts is refused
items.body: A move kept the message's thread scope, so a message moved from one account's folder into another's sat in the second account's mailbox carrying the first account's thread, and `threadFor` on it listed the first account's messages. A move between folders with different owners throws `mail-store/cross-account-move`; RFC 8621 §5.4 gives `Email/copy` as the cross-account move, and it makes a new Email id.

items.title: A result reference path applies the whole pointer
items.body: `*` returned the array itself and dropped the tokens after it, so the chain RFC 8620 §3.7 uses as its example, `Email/query` to `Email/get` to `Thread/get` to `Email/get` through `/list/*/threadId` and `/list/*/emailIds`, passed the previous method's objects instead of thread ids and message ids. `*` now applies the rest of the pointer to every item and flattens array results into one array. A path no item satisfies fails the call with `invalidResultReference` rather than resolving to the array, an array index follows the RFC 6901 grammar, and an arguments object carrying both `ids` and `#ids` is `invalidArguments`. RFC 6901 §5 separates the empty pointer from `/`: the first selects the whole result and the second selects the member whose name is the empty string. Both had selected the whole result, so a reference to `/` handed the entire response to an argument that asked for one member.

items.title: A JMAP blob download names the file, whatever the name is
items.body: The download handler built `Content-Disposition` from the URL's last segment, testing it against an ASCII-only pattern and serving a bare `attachment` when it did not match, so a name in any language other than English lost its filename and no `filename*` was ever written. It now builds the header with `b.staticServe.attachmentDisposition`, which pairs a quoted ASCII form with an RFC 8187 ext-value, escaped against `attr-char` so an apostrophe cannot truncate it. The segment is percent-decoded first and reduced to its basename, and a name carrying CR, LF or NUL is served as `download`.

items.title: A Sieve test is charged for the work it does
items.body: `mail.sieve` charged one gas unit per test and then compared every header value against every key, each comparison walking a pattern against a value, so the charge was one unit for work whose cost is the product of the operand lengths. A single `header :matches` with a long pattern against a large header spent 15 seconds of the delivery path for 2 of its 10,000 units, and a 63 KiB script spent 57 seconds for 28. Gas is now charged inside the comparison loop in proportion to the characters compared, so a filter that is expensive because it is genuinely large still runs and one that is expensive because of a product exhausts the budget it was always meant to be charged against.

items.title: safeSieve resolves command and test names at validate
items.body: The grammar reads any identifier followed by arguments as a command, so a script naming an action the interpreter does not implement validated clean and was stored, and the name was resolved at delivery where the throw costs the whole script rather than the one line. `vacation`, `reject` and ordinary typos like `fileinfo` were accepted with `ok: true` while every later message was filtered by nothing. `b.safeSieve.parse` now resolves both command and test names against `b.mail.sieve.implementedNames()`, refusing with `safe-sieve/unimplemented-action` or `safe-sieve/unimplemented-test` at the point the author is still looking. The interpreter keeps its own refusal for an AST that did not come from the parser.

items.title: A MIME header name is held to the grammar its value already was
items.body: `b.safeMime.parse` checked the header value for control characters and applied no rule at all to the name, so a field name carrying a C1 control, an ANSI escape or a bidi override was stored and came back through `names()` and `raw`. A name is now checked against RFC 5322 §3.6.8 `ftext` (`%d33-57 / %d59-126`) and refused with `safe-mime/bad-header-name`, reported as a hex code and an offset rather than by echoing the bytes.

items.title: A refusal that quotes its input renders it
items.body: `b.safeMime`, `b.safeIcal` and `b.safeVcard` each capped the text they quoted in a refusal at 64 characters and interpolated it unchanged, so an escape opening an erase-in-line sequence reached whatever printed the message and erased the line beside it, and a right-to-left override reversed the rest of the sentence. The three now compose `b.safeBuffer.previewText`, which passes printable US-ASCII through, renders every other code point as an escape, and keeps the cap.

items.title: extractText and selectBodyParts describe one message the same way
items.body: `b.safeMime.extractText` walked every leaf of the type it was asked for, so a message carrying an attached `.txt` and an inline HTML body answered with the attachment's contents as the body, which is the same part `b.safeMime.selectBodyParts` reports as a file. `b.mailStore`'s `appendMessage` seals `body_text` from the first and derives `hasAttachment` from the second, so one message was stored with an attachment's text as its body and a flag saying it carried one. A part the sender dispositioned `attachment` is now passed over when the body is chosen, and reached only when a message has no other text at all, which keeps a single-part message that spells its one file that way readable.

items.title: A quoted filename keeps the semicolon inside it
items.body: The `Content-Disposition` filename reader ended the parameter at the first `;` anywhere in the header, found with a plain search that did not know it was inside a quoted string. A semicolon is an ordinary filename character, so `filename="one;two.txt"` read back as `"one`: cut at the semicolon and still carrying the opening quote, and with no extension for `b.guardAll.byExtension` to dispatch on. The parameter now ends at the first `;` outside the quotes, and the quoted form is unescaped, so `filename="one\"two.txt"` reads as `one"two.txt`.

items.title: extractText on a structure-only tree refuses rather than crashing
items.body: `parse(bytes, { structureOnly: true })` keeps the shape and drops the bodies, and `b.safeMime.extractText` read `leaf.body` anyway: asking a shape-only tree for its text came back as `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`, which carries no code and reads as a programming mistake rather than as this tree being the wrong one to ask. It is now `safe-mime/structure-only`.

items.title: A folded header continuation is not read as the From header
items.body: The JMAP From reader ran its field parser over every line of the header block, so a continuation of some other header, which RFC 5322 §2.2.3 marks by leading whitespace and nothing else, parsed as a field of its own. A sender folding `From:` into the continuation of a header nobody checks chose the address the submission gate reads. A line beginning with whitespace now continues the previous field, as the grammar says, and the real From header still folds.

items.title: Every mailbox of a From list is checked against the identity
items.body: RFC 5322 §3.6.2 makes `From` a mailbox-list, and every mailbox in it is an author the message claims. `EmailSubmission/set` read the first and stopped at the comma, so an authorized address in front covered any address behind it and the message went out claiming both. Every mailbox is now checked, and neither a comma inside a quoted display name nor one inside an RFC 5322 comment starts a new one. Comments matter in both directions: ctext (§3.2.2) admits a DQUOTE, so `ops@example.com ("), ceo@bank.example` read as one unterminated quoted string and hid the second author from the check entirely, while `Ops <ops@example.com> (a, b)` was refused as though the comment's comma had begun another author. Comments nest, and the reader now walks them.

items.title: An unterminated Sieve string is refused rather than dropped
items.body: The tokenizer walked a quoted string with a step that only moves while there is input left, so the refusal that followed the loop could never fire. A string with no closing quote ran off the end, pushed no token, and the tokenizer went straight to end-of-input: everything from the opening quote onward vanished and the parser saw a well-formed prefix. `b.safeSieve.validate` reported `ok: true` for a script a conformant RFC 5228 implementation rejects, and the framework ran the prefix.

items.title: A Sieve extension needs the require that declares it
items.body: RFC 5228 §2.10.5 forbids using an extension unless `require` declared it, and this module's own description says `envelope` is available when the capability is declared. Both `envelope` and `fileinto` ran without one, so a script this parser accepted was refused by any conformant implementation it was moved to. Using either without its `require` is now `safe-sieve/undeclared-extension`, naming the capability and the line.

items.title: An IMAP mailbox name sent as a literal takes the same cap
items.body: `b.guardImapCommand` applies the profile's `maxMailboxBytes` to the command LINE, and a literal arrives after it. `CREATE {N}` decoded up to `maxLiteralBytes`, which is 64 MiB under the strict profile, quoted the result and built it into the argument string, and only then did operand parsing turn it away: the name never reached the store, but the listener did all of that work for every such command and answered with a message about operand count rather than about the cap that was exceeded. The six mailbox verbs now refuse a literal past `maxMailboxBytes` before decoding it, and say so.

items.title: b.mail.server.imap.create reads its allowLegacyMUtf7 option
items.body: `create` accepted `allowLegacyMUtf7` by name and never read it: the listener took its answer from the profile table alone, in both directions, so an operator turning the legacy modified-UTF-7 mailbox encoding off under a profile that allows it still had it accepted. The option now decides when it is given, and the profile is the default when it is not.

items.title: Thirty-four @example blocks state the answer the code gives
items.body: Every `@example` in `lib/` was already executed on each run, which proves the API it names still exists. Nothing compared its `// →` with what the call returned, so an example could name a real primitive, run clean, and state an answer the code has never given. 769 such claims are now checked. Among the ones corrected: `b.ssrfGuard.canonicalizeHost` documented an IPv4-mapped address canonicalizing to `::ffff:7f00:1` when it folds to `127.0.0.1`, which is the string an allowlist compares against, and the prose said it too; `b.problemDetails.fromError` takes its `type` suffix from the error's `code` while the example passed the code as the message, so an operator following it ships every error as `internal-error`; `b.guardAll.allGuards` listed 25 guards where there are 29; `b.guardImapCommand.validate` showed `args` as a list of arguments where it is the unparsed remainder of the line; and `b.requestHelpers.ipPrefix` showed an IPv6 prefix with four groups where it writes eight. An arrow whose answer depends on something the example does not set says so in the documentation rather than in a list inside the gate.

items.title: A Sieve action refuses an empty name in both spellings
items.body: `fileinto ["x"]` and `fileinto "x"` name the same folder, and the argument reader turned an empty list entry into a refusal while letting an empty STRING through: `fileinto ""` filed the message into a folder with no name and canceled the implicit keep, and `redirect ""` did the same with an address. Both spellings of an empty value are now `mail-sieve/bad-fileinto` and `mail-sieve/bad-redirect`.

items.title: A folder cannot be parked on INBOX's name in another case
items.body: `b.mailStore.createFolder` inserted the name as written and the folders table's unique index is binary, so `inbox` was a folder distinct from `INBOX`. `deleteFolder` and `renameFolder` decide by folding case, so they refused every case variant: the folder that had just been created could never be removed or renamed, and renaming an ordinary folder TO `Inbox` reached the same dead end from the other side, taking its messages with it. Creating or renaming onto a spelling of INBOX is now `mail-store/reserved-folder-name`.

items.title: The JMAP listener writes to the audit sink it documents
items.body: `b.mail.server.jmap.create` documents an `audit` option, and the listener bound the process-global emitter directly, so an operator wiring a per-tenant store, a compliance sink or a test double got silence with nothing refused and nothing logged. It now composes the same dual emitter its sibling listeners use, so events reach both the process audit chain and the operator's sink.

items.title: Every From field of a message is read, and every mailbox in each one
items.body: RFC 5322 section 3.6 lets `From` appear exactly once, and the author check read the first field and stopped. A message carrying two was authorized against whichever the submitter put first while `b.mail.send.deliver` sent both verbatim, so the same pair of authors was accepted or refused on an order the submitter chooses. Every `From` field is read now and every mailbox in all of them is checked against the identity. The element reader now accounts for the WHOLE element rather than stopping at the first `<`, because every part of it that went unread was a place to put a second author. Refused with it: an element yielding no mailbox (`ops@example.com, <ceo@bank.example`), content after the angle-addr (`Ops <ops@example.com> ceo@bank.example`), an address written where the display name goes (`ceo@bank.example <ops@example.com>`, whose same-domain spelling keeps SPF, DKIM and DMARC aligned so nothing downstream catches it), and a comment the sender never closes, which is not whitespace because the reader cannot say what follows it. A `>` written inside a comment no longer ends the address early, since RFC 5322 section 3.2.2 ctext admits one. An empty or comment-only element is still not an author, which section 3.6.2 obs-mbox-list allows, so a trailing comma is not a refusal. The header section is read to its end, which is the blank line RFC 5322 section 2.1 puts before a body or the end of the message when it carries no body; the reader took a fixed 64 KiB window before, so a sender who filled it chose which `From` field the check saw while `b.mail.send.deliver` sent every field verbatim. A message with no body is no longer read as a header block that was cut short.

items.title: extractText answers with a body, not with an attachment
items.body: `b.safeMime.extractText` falls back to searching the whole tree when the representation it was asked for is not among the displayed parts. It guarded that search on `Content-Disposition: attachment` alone while the selection also treats `inline` with a filename as a file, so the two readers disagreed and a `text/plain` part spelled `inline; filename="notes.txt"` was returned as the body of a message that had an HTML body: `b.mailStore` sealed the attachment's bytes into `body_text` while its own attachment count named the same leaf. The search now runs only when the selection found no body of either type, which is the message a naming gateway produces, and not when the message has a body of the other type to answer with.

items.title: A compliance regime passed under the other spelling is refused, not ignored
items.body: The framework takes a guard's compliance regime under two names: `b.guardSmtpCommand` and the other command guards read `posture`, and the twenty-eight content guards read `compliancePosture`. Each resolver ignored the other's spelling without a word, so `b.guardCsv.gate({ posture: "hipaa" })` ran at the default profile while the call said HIPAA, and `b.guardSmtpCommand.gate({ compliancePosture: "hipaa" })` did the same. Neither name is wrong and neither is renamed, so a guard now refuses the one it does not read with `<guard>/bad-opt` naming the one it does. `b.guardAll` validates the shared regime itself rather than through those resolvers and dropped `posture` on the way out, so it refuses it too. Measured across every guard the aggregator dispatches to: twenty-nine ignored the other spelling before, none do now.

items.title: b.mailStore names the backends it accepts
items.body: `b.mailStore`'s description offered `b.externalDb` (Postgres) as a backend. `create()` requires `prepare(sql)` returning `{ run, get, all }`, and `b.externalDb` is asynchronous and carries no `prepare`, so the call the description named was refused with `opts.backend must be sqlite-shaped`. The schema `create()` installs is SQLite dialect, which PostgreSQL rejects at the first statement, so the deployment the sentence described could not be reached by supplying an adapter either. The description now names what composes: `b.db`, or any object exposing that synchronous shape over a SQLite-compatible database.

items.title: A refused ManageSieve command does not leave its literal to be read as commands
items.body: RFC 5804 §4 gives ManageSieve the non-synchronizing literal RFC 7888 gives IMAP: `{N+}` needs no continuation, so a client sends the octets without waiting. Where `b.guardManageSieveCommand.validate` refused the opening line, `b.mail.server.managesieve` answered `NO` and read no further, so the payload that was already on the wire arrived as ordinary lines and was executed. A refused `PUTSCRIPT` whose script began `DELETESCRIPT "victim"` deleted that script. The announced size comes from a line that did not parse, so the connection is told `BYE` and closed rather than resynchronized on it, which is the answer the IMAP listener gives for the same shape. `b.guardManageSieveCommand.announcedLiteral(line)` reads the opener for a caller that has refused the line, as `b.guardImapCommand.announcedLiteral` does. A run of digits is an announcement at any length, because leading zeroes spell a small size in as many digits as a sender likes, and a reader that stopped recognizing one past some number of digits was a way back into the same smuggle.

items.title: A filename split across RFC 2231 continuations is read whole
items.body: RFC 2231 §3 lets a sender split a long parameter across numbered segments, and §4.1 puts the `charset'language'` prefix on the first while flagging each percent-encoded segment with a trailing `*`. The reader consumed the `*` and then required an `=`, so `filename*0*=utf-8''long%20; filename*1*=notes.txt` was not a filename at all and the part came back named `null`. A part whose only mark of being a file is that name then reads as displayed text, so it is missing from `b.safeMime.extractAttachments`, from `b.safeMime.selectBodyParts` and from a JMAP `Email/get`'s attachment list. The segments are assembled in index order now, whatever order they arrive in. §3 may split a character between segments, so they are joined as bytes and decoded once with the charset the first segment names, rather than one at a time: decoding `r%C3` and `%A9el.pdf` separately leaves both undecodable and the escapes in the name. An unflagged segment is not percent-decoded, and it joins the same run of octets as the flagged segments around it, because §3 concatenates the sections into one value and §4 gives that value one charset: a percent sign in one is a percent sign, an empty one ends nothing, and a character split across the boundary between the two forms still reads whole. A header carries ASCII in an unflagged section, and ASCII text is its own octets. A non-ASCII character there is outside that grammar, and it is taken as the text it already is rather than read a second time as bytes. Both halves of the `charset'language'` prefix are optional under §4, so a first segment written `''notes.txt` carries neither and is still a prefix, with the charset falling back to UTF-8. That prefix belongs to the `*`-flagged form alone: a plain `filename=` holds a literal string, and a file the sender named `''report.txt` keeps both apostrophes. A run missing a segment names nothing, so it reads as `null` rather than as the pieces that did arrive.

items.title: A renamed mailbox keeps its selection instead of being reported closed
items.body: Renaming a selected mailbox cleared the session's selection and sent `* OK [CLOSED]`, so a client had to SELECT again before it could FETCH. RFC 9051 §3 ends the selected state on CLOSE, UNSELECT, an unsolicited CLOSED, a failed SELECT or EXAMINE, or LOGOUT, and a rename is none of those; §7.1 defines `CLOSED` for a mailbox closed implicitly by SELECT or EXAMINE on another mailbox, as a boundary between two selections, so sending it for a rename reported something that had not happened. A `b.mailStore` rename updates the folder row's name and nothing else, so UIDVALIDITY is unchanged and the messages are the same messages. The selection now follows the name, for a descendant of a renamed parent as well, and every session holding it is sent the unsolicited `* LIST` with the `OLDNAME` extended data item that RFC 9051 §6.3.9.7 defines for exactly this. A DELETE still clears the selection and says so: that mailbox is gone. Renaming INBOX is unchanged, because §6.3.6 leaves INBOX in place. A selection is identified by the SELECT that opened it rather than by the mailbox's name, so a `FETCH`, `STORE` or `EXPUNGE` already talking to the store when another connection renames the mailbox completes and its rows reach the client, where comparing names would have answered `NO [CLOSED]` for a selection the server still holds. A delete across the same window still invalidates the command, because that mailbox is gone.

items.title: An unknown compliance posture is refused by the module the operator called
items.body: `b.guardEnvelope.check`, `b.mail.greylist.create`, `b.mail.helo.evaluate`, `b.mail.rbl.create`, `b.mail.scan.create` and `b.mail.spamScore.create` all read their posture through one shared resolver, and it built the refusal from its own error class: an operator who mistyped a posture got a `GateContractError` with `gate-contract/bad-posture` from a module they never called, while each of those primitives documents `<module>/bad-posture` and their own error class is what a caller catches on. The resolver takes the caller's class and code prefix now, so the refusal comes from the primitive the operator called, and all six are walked by one test rather than one being spot-checked.

items.title: A comment in a structured header is skipped, not read as content
items.body: RFC 5322 §3.2.2 places a `(...)` comment between the tokens of a structured field and lets `ctext` hold a double quote and a semicolon, so `Content-Type: text/plain; x-note=token (a " comment)` is a conforming header. `b.structuredFields.splitTopLevel` read the semicolon inside one as a field separator and split the parameter in half, and `b.structuredFields.endsInsideQuotedString` read the quote as opening a string that never closed, which made `b.safeMime.parse` refuse the message as malformed and stopped it being stored. Both take `{ comments: true }` and then skip a comment whole, nesting and backslash escapes included, through one scan rather than two, because a caller asking where a quoted string runs and a caller asking where a field ends cannot be allowed to disagree about it. It is off by default and only the MIME parsers ask for it: RFC 9651 defines no comments, and RFC 6265 §4.1.1 makes `(` an ordinary character in a cookie path, where reading one as a comment would swallow every attribute after it and store `sid=secret; Path=/foo(; Secure; HttpOnly` with no `Secure` at all. Parentheses inside a quoted string are content either way. A value that ends inside an unterminated comment drops its trailing piece, as one ending inside an unterminated quoted string already did, and `endsInsideQuotedString` reports every run the split drops rather than the quoted string alone: otherwise `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-7 (unterminated` parsed as `us-ascii` with no parameters, which is the charset allowlist skipped rather than applied. The two read one scan, so a shape the split drops is a shape the check reports.

items.title: An IMAP FETCH carries the sequence-set cap to the store, as STORE does
items.body: `FETCH 1:*` and `UID FETCH 1:*` name a set only the store can resolve, and the listener forwarded them with no bound at all: the backend read the whole mailbox and the listener awaited and held every row. `STORE` already travelled with `maxMessages`, the profile's `maxSequenceSetItems`, and `FETCH` now does the same, for the plain and UID forms alike. What can be counted from the line, an enumerated set or a message-number range, is still refused by `b.guardImapCommand` before the listener is reached.

items.title: Email/import and Email/parse are bounded by the object caps the session advertises
items.body: The cap a method is subject to was chosen from the word its name ends in, so two standard methods carrying objects under other names reached the operator's handler at any size. RFC 8621 §4.8 gives `Email/import` an `emails` map of creation id to EmailImport, which asks the server to create objects and so takes RFC 8620 §5.3's bound, "the total number of objects to create, update, or destroy"; §4.9 gives `Email/parse` a `blobIds` array, which is ids requested and so takes §5.1's, "the number of ids requested by the client". Both are now counted before the handler runs and refused with `requestTooLarge` over `maxObjectsInSet` and `maxObjectsInGet` respectively, the numbers the session already published.

items.title: A maxBlobBytes the upload reader cannot apply is refused at create, not per upload
items.body: `b.mail.server.jmap.create` took any truthy `maxBlobBytes`, including `-1`, `Infinity` and a string. The upload handler reserves one of the account's `maxConcurrentUpload` slots and then builds the bounded reader, which refuses a cap it cannot apply by throwing, before the listeners that release the slot are installed. Each attempted upload therefore kept a slot for the life of the process, and after `maxConcurrentUpload` attempts every upload for that account was answered 429. `maxBlobBytes` must now be a positive integer and is refused at `create` with `mail-server-jmap/bad-blob-cap`, where an operator sees it. The reader is also built before the slot is taken, so nothing is constructed between reserving a slot and arming its release.

items.title: A refused MCP envelope carries the JSON-RPC code for what was wrong with it
items.body: `b.mcp.serverGuard` answered every envelope refusal with -32700, which JSON-RPC 2.0 defines as "Invalid JSON was received". A body with an empty method, a wrong `jsonrpc` version, an id of the wrong type or non-object params had parsed cleanly, so a client reading the code looked at its own encoding for a refusal about the content. A body that did not parse is still -32700; wrong-typed params are -32602; every other envelope refusal is -32600. The HTTP status is 400 in all three cases, as before.

items.title: An IMAP connection that drops while idling disarms its IDLE timer
items.body: RFC 9051 §6.3.1 IDLE runs until the client sends DONE, and `b.mail.server.imap` arms a 29-minute timer so a connection that idles past that window is ended. DONE was the only thing that disarmed it. A client that goes away while idling never sends DONE, so the timer stayed armed for the rest of its 29 minutes, holding the connection state and the socket, and then wrote `BYE IDLE timed out` to a client that had been gone that whole time. A client that reconnects on a loop accumulated one per cycle, and the listener could not exit while any were outstanding. Closing a connection now disarms it, whichever way the connection ends.

items.title: One request body is bounded the same way whether it arrives as text or already decoded
items.body: `b.mcp.parseRequest` and `b.guardJmap.validate` both accept either a JSON string from the transport or the object an upstream body parser produced, and they read the two through different halves of `b.safeJson`. Only one of those halves carried a per-object member cap by default, so a body wide enough to sit between the two numbers was served on one path and refused on the other: a JMAP request that `b.mail.server.jmap` accepted over HTTP was refused over WebSocket, and the refusal reported the JSON as malformed when it was valid and far inside the declared `maxSizeRequest`. The two halves now take the same default, and each consumer names the cap its own documentation promises. `b.guardJmap.MAX_KEYS_PER_OBJECT` is that number for JMAP, and the WebSocket transport, which reads the frame itself to find its `@type` and `id`, reads it under the same one. Past it the body is refused as `notRequest` with a message naming the bound, and a body nested deeper than the parser reads the same way: RFC 8620 §3.6.1 keeps `notJSON` for a body that did not parse. A frame the transport cannot read is classified by the request validator rather than by the transport, so the two answer one body the same way rather than each deciding what it was. A `/copy` method refused for naming no destination says which arguments RFC 8620 §5.4 defines: it copies into the account `accountId` names and reads from the one `fromAccountId` names, and there is no `toAccountId`.

items.title: `b.pick.movesThePrototype` separates the name that replaces a prototype from the names that only look like it
items.body: `b.pick.isPoisonedKey` answers for `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` together, which is the right set for a sanitizer and the wrong one for a protocol that has to admit names by their own rules. Assigned to a fresh object, only `__proto__` replaces that object's prototype; `constructor` and `prototype` become ordinary own properties, and RFC 8620 §1.2 admits both as JMAP creation ids while RFC 8621 §4.1.1 admits them as keywords. `b.pick.movesThePrototype(key)` answers the narrower question, and `b.safeJson` and `b.mail.server.jmap` both read it rather than each keeping their own copy. It is a fact about the language, so `b.pick.registerPoisonedKeys` does not widen it.

items.title: `b.codepointClass.isDotAtomText` and `b.codepointClass.isAtext` read the RFC 5322 atom grammar
items.body: `b.codepointClass.isAtext(cc)` reports whether a code unit is RFC 5322 §3.2.3 `atext`, and `b.codepointClass.isDotAtomText(text)` whether a string is `dot-atom-text`, one or more atoms joined by single dots. Three places had their own answer to that question and two of them were wrong: `b.guardEmail.validate` folded the dot into the atom's own character set, so `a..b@example.com`, `.ab@example.com` and `ab.@example.com` all read as valid addresses, and `b.mail.server` did not check the local part at all before matching a wildcard identity by domain. Both now read the shared grammar, and `b.guardMessageId` reads it in place of its own copy. `b.guardListId` keeps its narrower rule, because RFC 2919 §2 wants a hostname-shaped label rather than any atom. `b.codepointClass.isUtf8DotAtomText` is the RFC 6531 §3.3 reading of the same shape, `atext` extended with every non-ASCII character and the dot rule unchanged, for the internationalized addresses an SMTPUTF8 deployment carries.

items.title: `b.safeJson.measureBytes` sizes a value as JSON without building the string
items.body: `b.safeJson.measureBytes(value, { limit, maxDepth })` returns `{ bytes, exceeded }`, the UTF-8 byte count `JSON.stringify` would produce, counted by walking the value. The walk stops once the running total passes `limit`, so `exceeded: true` reports `bytes` as a lower bound and a hostile value costs at most `limit` bytes of counting rather than a serialized copy of itself. It refuses what `JSON.stringify` refuses: `json/circular` on a cycle, `json/wrong-input-type` on a BigInt, plus `json/too-deep` past `maxDepth` (default 100). It counts what `JSON.stringify` would write: `toJSON` is called once per value with the key it sits under, a boxed `Number`, `String`, `Boolean` or `BigInt` is unboxed first, and a member whose value is `undefined`, a function or a symbol is skipped in an object and counted as `null` in an array. What it returns is a number about a value the caller still holds, so it answers what something would cost to write, not what a caller is about to be handed. Measuring a value and then handing on the original bounds nothing, because the two are different objects: a `methodCalls` reporting one call to the cap produced ten thousand to the dispatcher. `b.safeJson.jsonCopyUnderCap(value, { maxBytes })` is what these sites use instead. It writes the JSON form once, refusing at `maxBytes` while it writes rather than after, and reads it back, so the caller is handed the value the cap was taken against and there is no second reading to differ from the first. `allowProto: true` keeps `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` in the copy, for a caller whose own layer refuses or admits those names itself, and `refuseProtoMover: true` alongside it throws `json/proto-key` on `__proto__` while keeping the other two, which is what the callers here pass. That covers a getter at an object key or an array index, a proxy, an inherited `toJSON`, a boxed primitive, a member that is not enumerable and a property named so that it sits outside an array's elements, without naming any of them: none of them is in what `JSON.stringify` wrote. A cap that is not a non-negative finite number is a `TypeError` at the call rather than the default silently taking its place, so a `maxBytes` read from configuration or computed is a failure where it is written, and an option NAME it does not know is refused with `json/bad-opts`, since a one-character typo in the cap of a primitive whose whole job is that cap would otherwise be the 1 MiB default in silence. A caller that names no `maxKeys` gets `parse`'s per-object default from the copy as well, so one body is bounded the same way whether it arrives as text or already decoded, and a consumer whose own cap is larger names it and gets it on both halves. `b.safeJson.stringifyForScript` measures a `maxBytes` against the escaped form it returns rather than the JSON it wrapped, where each `<`, `>`, `&`, U+2028 and U+2029 becomes six bytes after the count and handed a caller up to six times what it asked for. It takes `indent` together with that cap, which `stringify` refuses for itself, because the string it measures already carries the newlines and padding; a `maxBytes` that is not a non-negative finite number is refused there too, so an indented call cannot pass a `NaN` or a string past the check and run uncapped; and a value with no JSON form at all still returns `undefined` under a cap, where the byte count had thrown a `TypeError` naming its own argument. A value whose JSON form is not an object, an array among them, which a `toJSON` returning a string or null produces, is refused as input rather than handed on for a consumer to read members off, and the text form is held to that too: `b.openapi.parse("null")` had returned `null` to a caller that then read `.openapi` off it, so a truncated or empty specification came back as a raw `TypeError` instead of the parser's own refusal. `b.safeJson.stringify` takes the same `maxBytes` and refuses with `json/too-large` as it writes, counting the bytes the form occupies: a key and a string by their escaped UTF-8 size, a number by its written form, `false` by five and `true` by four, a member `JSON.stringify` drops by nothing inside an object and by the four `null` takes inside an array, a container by its two brackets, the root by no key, and one byte for each separator after the first member. Separators and the `null` an array writes for a dropped member were not counted at all, so a value made of them returned a string five times the cap: `jsonCopyUnderCap` caught that on the finished string, but only after it had been built, which is the peak the cap is there to bound. A `JSON.rawJSON` member is charged the bytes its text occupies rather than its UTF-16 code units, which is what `measureBytes` already charged for the same thing, and which had let a document of non-ASCII raw JSON run three times past the cap. A member whose form is decided by code the value carries, a `toJSON` hook, an accessor, or a boxed wrapper with its own `valueOf`, is charged the least its kind can occupy and never invoked by the count, since the count and the write would read it separately; `jsonCopyUnderCap` measures the finished string for that case. `maxDepth` now covers a member an array writes as `null`, which `parse` already refused at that depth and `stringify` wrote. The finished string is measured exactly as well, so a document whose form is exactly `maxBytes` is served and one byte more is not. A string is counted by the bytes its escaped form occupies rather than by its characters, and a non-finite number by the four `null` takes, so neither refuses a document the string would have fitted nor lets one run six times past the cap before the refusal. A `maxBytes` or `maxDepth` that is not a non-negative finite number is a `TypeError`, and so is `maxBytes` together with `onCircular: "replace"`, whose cycle-free copy is built before the count begins, or together with `indent`, whose newline and padding per member grow with a nesting depth the count cannot see: at ten spaces and eight hundred levels the refusal landed after half a gigabyte had been written for a one-megabyte cap. `maxDepth` is applied on the same pass, so a value nested past it is refused where it is met rather than exhausting the stack on the way down: a twenty-thousand-deep value reported `json/stringify: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. A member `JSON.stringify` drops is not a level of nesting, so a document whose deepest member is left unset is read the same way whether it arrives decoded or as text. `b.openapi.parse`, `b.asyncapi.parse`, `b.mcp.parseRequest`, `b.guardJmap.validate` and `b.mail.dmarc.parseAggregateReport` each name their own key cap, since the parser's default is sized for a request body and a description with ten thousand schemas in one object is ordinary; the two ways of handing a document over now admit the same documents.

items.title: IMAP LIST answers what the client asked for
items.body: `LIST` read neither its reference nor its pattern and returned every folder for every request, so `LIST "" "INBOX"`, `LIST "" "%"` and `LIST "Archive/" "%"` all produced the same full list, `LIST (SUBSCRIBED)` was unanswerable, and a client listing mailboxes had to issue one `STATUS` per mailbox. The handler now applies the RFC 9051 §6.3.9 grammar: a reference prepended to the pattern, `%` matching within one hierarchy level and `*` across the delimiter, the `SUBSCRIBED` selection option, and `RETURN (SUBSCRIBED CHILDREN STATUS (...))`, so a mailbox list and its counts arrive in one round trip. A pattern carrying more wildcards than a hierarchy needs is refused rather than walked, and the two scans over the mailbox set answer from maps built once for the request rather than walking the whole list per mailbox: `RETURN (CHILDREN)` cost 58 ms at 8000 mailboxes and 292 ms at 16000, and enumerating the hierarchy levels between matches cost 62 ms and 190 ms, both held synchronously ahead of the reply and the second paid even when the pattern matched nothing. A `LIST` that needs more than 50,000,000 character comparisons is refused rather than walked: the matcher costs the pattern's length times each name's, so the product is the client's to drive, and collapsing wildcard runs does not reduce an alternating pattern. Measured before the bound, `"*a"` repeated 500 times took 2088 ms against 2000 names of a kilobyte. The budget is charged as each name is matched rather than estimated from the folder list, because `LIST` matches three sets of names: the folders, the hierarchy levels it synthesizes between them, and the subscriptions whose folders are gone. Fifty names 980 segments deep synthesize 24,550 ancestors, so an estimate over the folders alone admitted a request that then matched billions of comparisons against names no folder list held. A plain wildcard over 2000 kilobyte names needs 2,000,000 comparisons and an ordinary prefix pattern 18,000,000, so both are served. The reference is a mailbox name and is matched literally: a `%` or `*` written inside it is one of the characters a mailbox name may carry, not a wildcard, so `LIST "100%/" "*"` answers with what sits under `100%/` and not with the siblings a wildcard reading would have reached. The work bound charges each pattern a base cost as well as its length, because matching allocates arrays the size of the name whatever the pattern's length: a pattern of length zero charged nothing while still running a full match per folder, so `LIST "" ("" "" ...)` bought unbounded matching for free. Measured on a thousand empty patterns over a thousand mailboxes: served in full, 487 ms of synchronous work, nothing charged.

items.title: The IMAP mailbox-management verbs, behind an operator-supplied administrator
items.body: `CREATE`, `DELETE`, `RENAME`, `SUBSCRIBE` and `UNSUBSCRIBE` answered `NO ... not configured` whatever the store could do, so a client implementing `DELETE` left an empty folder row behind for every mailbox it deleted. They now work when `create()` is given `mailboxAdmin`, an object whose methods are called as `method(actor, ...mailboxNames)`. They mutate a namespace the client names by string, and on a listener serving several accounts which actor may rename or delete which mailbox is the operator's question, so the listener does not answer it: without `mailboxAdmin` the verbs refuse exactly as before. The listener validates the operands as mailbox names, refuses `DELETE INBOX` per RFC 9051 §6.3.5, and follows the session's selected mailbox across a rename.

items.title: b.mailStore removes, renames and subscribes to folders
items.body: `b.mailStore` could create and list folders and not remove one. `deleteFolder(name)` removes the folder with its messages, flags, search-index and quota rows in one transaction, and refuses INBOX, a folder that is not there, one holding a message under legal hold, and one that is the parent of another. `renameFolder(from, to)` refuses a name already taken, and refuses INBOX, whose RFC 9051 §6.3.6 rename moves the messages and leaves INBOX in place rather than moving the delivery target. `subscribeFolder` / `unsubscribeFolder` record the subscription `LIST (SUBSCRIBED)` reads, and `listFolders` reports it as `subscribed`. An existing store gains the column at `create()`. Every operation that takes a folder NAME resolves INBOX in whatever case the client wrote it, which RFC 9051 §5.1 requires: appending to `inbox` and subscribing to it reach the same mailbox as `INBOX`, and unsubscribing by another spelling removes the subscription rather than reporting success and leaving it. The case is ASCII case, since a folder name is `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+` and a Unicode mapping can only over-match: `ınbox`, whose uppercase is `INBOX`, is a name the store does not hold. A name that is already a row is that row: an earlier version did not refuse `createFolder("inbox")`, so a store may already hold one, and resolving every spelling to INBOX would put its messages out of reach behind a rename and a delete that both refuse INBOX. The reserved name answers only when no row carries the spelling asked for. Resolving the folder and writing its modification sequence read the name the same way, so a mutation under any spelling advances `modseq_max` and no sequence is handed out twice. Every other mailbox is matched by its own case. `renameFolder` keeps the mailbox's `uidvalidity`: RFC 9051 §2.3.1.1 makes that number the one a client checks before reusing anything it has cached, and a rename moves no messages and renumbers nothing, so issuing a fresh one told every client its cache was worthless and discarded the QRESYNC state it would have resumed from. A mailbox created afterwards at the freed name is a different mailbox and gets its own number. Each of the six default folders is seeded with its own `uidvalidity` rather than one shared timestamp: a client keys its cache on the mailbox name together with that number, so two mailboxes holding one number is safe only while both names exist, and deleting `Trash` then renaming `Archive` onto its name handed a reconnecting client a name it knew, a number it knew, and another mailbox's messages. Seeding runs on an empty database, so a store written by an earlier version keeps the shared value it was given: opening one now gives each folder after the first a number of its own, once, leaving the first with what it had. A `DELETE` the store refuses because the mailbox holds children is answered `NO [HASCHILDREN]`, the response code RFC 9051 §6.3.5 asks for when a server takes that option, so a client knows to delete the children rather than read the mailbox as undeletable.

items.title: b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey and b.requestHelpers.actorDisplayName
items.body: One derivation of the key that separates one principal from another for a per-actor bucket: an ownership record, a quota, a concurrency slot. It reads `id`, `userId`, `username`, `sub`, `principalId` and `email`, tags each key with the field it came from, scopes it by `tenantId`, and takes an `actorKey` hook for a deployment whose actors carry none of them. It answers `null` for an actor it cannot name, so a caller refuses rather than folding it onto a shared literal, and `ANONYMOUS_ACTOR_KEY` only for the absence of a principal. `actorDisplayName` answers the name to show, reading the same fields in reader order. `ACTOR_IDENTITY_FIELDS` and `ACTOR_DISPLAY_FIELDS` are exported so a consumer can see which fields name a principal.

items.title: b.safeMime.selectBodyParts
items.body: Sorts a parsed tree's leaves into the text a reader displays, the HTML it displays and the files it offers, applying the RFC 2046 §5.1.4 rule that the last alternative is the preferred one. `b.safeMime.extractText`, `b.safeMime.extractAttachments` and `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties` all read it, so a stored body, a mailbox listing's attachment facts and what `Email/get` returns describe one representation.

items.title: b.safeBuffer.readQuotedString and b.safeBuffer.previewText
items.body: `readQuotedString(input, at?)` reads one operand of the quoted-string grammar `quoteString` writes, returning `{ value, next }` so a caller walks a line of operands, and refusing an unterminated quote rather than guessing where it ends. `previewText(value, opts?)` renders untrusted input for a refusal message: printable US-ASCII through, every other code point as an escape, capped. The reader lives beside the writer so the two cannot drift apart.

items.title: b.mail.sieve.implementedNames
items.body: Returns the action and test names the interpreter resolves, so `b.safeSieve.parse` refuses an unimplemented name at upload and a consumer needing the same answer reads it here instead of keeping a copy that rots at the next extension.

items.title: b.structuredFields.endsInsideQuotedString
items.body: Reports whether a field value ends with a quoted string still open, counting RFC 9651 §3.3.3 backslash escapes. `splitTopLevel` drops the piece it cannot terminate, so a caller reading that array cannot tell a parameter that is absent from one an unterminated quote swallowed. Ask this before treating a missing piece as unwritten: a grammar whose default for an absent value is weaker than the value being smuggled past has to refuse the field instead.

items.title: A store write is atomic inside a transaction the caller opened
items.body: `b.mailStore`'s multi-statement writes are atomic when the store owns the transaction. Composing them inside a transaction the CALLER opened is a supported shape, and on that path the helper ran the body directly and opened no savepoint: a `deleteFolder` that failed partway left the flag, index, message and quota deletes sitting in the caller's transaction, so a caller batching several mailbox deletions committed a folder that still existed with its messages already gone. The nested path now takes a savepoint and rolls back to it, so the same failure leaves the same state whoever owns the transaction. Whether a transaction is already open cannot be read off the documented contract, which is `prepare(sql)` and `transaction(fn)` and offers no way to ask, so the store asks by opening a savepoint: a backend that accepts one is inside a transaction and joins it, and a backend that refuses one is not, so the store opens its own. The earlier answer read the text of the error a refused `BEGIN` carried, which is a property of one driver rather than of the contract. A backend that answers a second `BEGIN` without raising, as a wrapper that normalizes errors or a pooled handle can, left the store committing the caller's transaction and reporting success, and the caller's own rollback then had nothing to undo. A backend offering only `prepare` reaches the same answer as one offering both. Releasing that savepoint IS the commit when the store opened the transaction, and a commit can fail: SQLite answers `SQLITE_BUSY` while another connection holds a read transaction in rollback-journal mode. The release ran outside the guard that unwinds the body, so a refused commit left the transaction open with its rows pending on the writer connection, the database locked against every other connection, and the next write reporting success inside a transaction nobody would commit. It now runs inside that guard: rolling back to the savepoint undoes everything the store did, and the store returns there, so a refusal inside a transaction the CALLER opened leaves the caller's work and the caller's transaction as they were. The transaction is ended outright only when that rollback itself fails, which is the one state that says the store owns it: only the outermost savepoint's release commits, so a release that fails the way a commit fails was the outermost one. Reading ownership off the handle instead would have left the documented `prepare`-only backend, which reports no state, holding a transaction it could never close: the connection keeps the write lock, every other connection is refused, and the store's later calls open savepoints inside it that commit nothing.

items.title: Vendored bundles refreshed
items.body: `@blamejs/pki` 0.7.45 to 0.8.31 and the public suffix list to its 2026-09-24 revision, both rebundled and re-signed through `scripts/vendor-update.sh` with `lib/vendor/MANIFEST.json` and `NOTICE` updated to match. The framework's runtime dependency set is unchanged: these ship as reviewable source inside the tarball. 0.8.28 checks a certificate or CRL against the RFC 5280 profile while it is being built and refuses one that violates it, which caught three artifacts the bundled mTLS engine was emitting; those are described under Security and Migration.

items.title: The permissive JMAP profile declares 64 MiB, the largest request it can accept
items.body: `b.guardJmap.PROFILES.permissive.maxSizeRequest` was 100 MiB, and `b.mail.server.jmap` publishes it to clients in the session's `urn:ietf:params:jmap:core` capability as the size a request may reach. No branch honored it: a string body goes through `b.safeJson.parse`, which refuses anything over its own 64 MiB ceiling whatever the caller asks. Measured at the declared limit, a 66 MiB request came back as `notJSON`, "body is not valid JSON", rather than as a size refusal. The profile now declares 64 MiB, which both branches accept, and a test holds every profile's `maxSizeRequest` at or under that ceiling so a later bump cannot publish a number the parser will not honor. The strict (10 MiB) and balanced (50 MiB) profiles are unchanged. A deployment relying on requests between 64 and 100 MiB was already being refused them.

items.title: New options
items.body: `b.mail.server.jmap.create` takes `maxConcurrentUpload`, `maxConcurrentRequests` and `collationAlgorithms`, all published in the session. `b.mailStore.createFolder` takes `owner`, and `b.mailStore.appendMessage` takes `threadScope`. `b.guardJmap.limitsFor(opts)` is new.

items.title: A deployment whose actors carry no id, userId, username, sub, principalId or email
items.body: `b.fileUpload` and `b.mail.server.jmap` refuse such an actor instead of putting it on a shared key with every other one. Pass `actorKey: function (actor) { return …; }` to `b.fileUpload.create` or `b.mail.server.jmap.create` to name the field your tokens carry. Ownership keys are tagged by the field they came from now. An upload staged by a previous version is still reachable by the principal that started it, because a record holding the old untagged value is matched against the old derivation as well, so a resumable upload is not stranded by the upgrade. A record left under the old shared `_anonymous` owner is not handed to an actor that merely cannot be named: those are the uploads the collapse exposed, and they expire on their own TTL.

items.title: A client that matched the old JMAP error strings
items.body: A client matching `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:unknownMethod` and the other method-level URIs should match the bare names instead. A client matching `guard-jmap/bad-json`, `guard-jmap/bad-input` or `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:requestTooLarge` on a refused request should match `notJSON`, `notRequest` and `limit`. A refused request no longer carries `methodResponses` or `sessionState`.

items.title: A misspelled compliance posture now throws at config time
items.body: A guard call naming a compliance regime outside the guard's table throws `<guard>/bad-posture` where it used to run the default profile silently, and the message names the value and the regimes that guard accepts: `hipaa`, `pci-dss`, `gdpr`, `soc2`. A call that names the regime under the option the guard does not read throws `<guard>/bad-opt` and names the option it does read: the command guards take `posture`, the content guards take `compliancePosture`, and each used to ignore the other's spelling silently. Passing no regime is unchanged.

items.title: A mail store that holds more than one account
items.body: Give each folder an `owner` at `createFolder`, or pass `appendOpts.threadScope` on append. Messages written before this carry the scope `""` and keep their existing thread roots; RFC 8621 §3 makes `threadId` immutable, so moving them into per-account scopes means reinserting them with new objectids.

items.title: A caller reading an upload list entry's actorId
items.body: `list()` entries report `ownerKey` rather than `actorId`. The value is the opaque, field-tagged key `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` derives, not the bare id a caller passed in, and the old name said otherwise. Match against it by deriving the key the same way: `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey({ id: "alice" })`.

items.title: A Sieve script that uses fileinto or envelope without require
items.body: Such a script is now refused at parse with `safe-sieve/undeclared-extension` rather than accepted, per RFC 5228 §2.10.5. Add `require ["fileinto"];` or `require ["envelope"];` at the top. A stored script that omits it fails at its next upload or validation rather than at delivery.

releases.headline: A signed backup restores only under a known signing key, and backup retention deletes nothing until the new bundle reads back intact
releases.summary: `b.restore` and `b.backup.verifyManifestSignature` verified a backup manifest's signature with the public key the manifest itself carries, so a writer of backup storage could edit a signed bundle, re-sign it with a key of its own, including an Ed25519 key, and restore it with `requireSignature: true`. A signature is now trusted only when its key matches `expectedFingerprint` or is the active or a rotated `b.auditSign` key, and its type matches `signature.algorithm`. New bundles derive every file key from one bundle key, so a blob copied in from another bundle no longer decrypts, and a backup of many files runs one Argon2id derivation instead of one per file. `b.restoreRollback.rollback` did not check that its target was a rollback point and could leave the live data directory where `purge` deletes it; it now accepts only a rollback point under the rollback root and undoes a half-finished swap. Backup retention counted a partial or planted directory as the newest bundle and deleted complete bundles before reading the new one back; `diskStorage` now renames a finished copy into place, listings require `manifest.json`, and `run()` compares the stored bundle with what it wrote before deleting anything. `b.restore` staged decrypted files under `os.tmpdir()`, so a restore into a mounted volume failed and left them there; it now stages beside `dataDir` and refuses a layout its rename swap cannot complete before decrypting anything. Manifest readers refused a manifest above 4 MiB that the writer produced; every reader and the writer now apply one 64 MiB limit.

items.title: A backup manifest signature is trusted only under a known key
items.body: `b.backupManifest.verifySignature`, `verifyBytes`, `b.backup.verifyManifestSignature`, the `scheduleTest` drill, `b.restoreBundle.extract` and `b.restore` checked a signature against the `publicKey` in the signature block itself, so any key that produced a valid signature was accepted, and `requireSignature: true` only required a signature to be present. A bundle edited in storage (a blob rolled back to an older copy, a file entry removed) and re-signed with a fresh ML-DSA-65, Ed25519 or Ed448 key restored. The key must now match `expectedFingerprint`, or, without one, be the active or a rotated `b.auditSign` key; a process that has not run `b.auditSign.init()` gets `ok: false` unless it pins a fingerprint. `signature.algorithm` must be one of `b.auditSign.SUPPORTED_SIGNING_ALGS` and must name the type of the key, and `signature.value` must be canonical base64. The `fingerprint` in the result is computed from the key. `requireSignature: true` with `verifySignature: false` now throws `restore/bad-opts` or `restore-bundle/bad-opts`. `blamejs restore apply`, `blamejs backup verify` and `blamejs backup extract` gain `--expected-fingerprint`, `--require-signature` and `--no-verify-signature`; the CLI holds no audit-sign key, so a signed bundle needs the pinned fingerprint or the explicit skip.

items.title: A blob copied from another backup bundle does not decrypt
items.body: Each file in a bundle was encrypted under a key derived from the passphrase and the file's own salt, with the file's path as associated data, so an older bundle's blob for the same path, copied in with its manifest entry, decrypted in an unsigned bundle. A new bundle records `keyScheme: "argon2id-hkdf-sha3-512-path-digest"` and a random `bundleSalt`: one Argon2id derivation produces the bundle key, and each file key and the vault-key wrapping key are derived from it with HKDF-SHA3-512 over the entry's salt and a label carrying a digest of the file's path. A blob from another bundle fails with `restore/decrypt-failed`. One derivation replaces one per file: a backup of 40 small files took 1.8 s and its restore 2.1 s, and both now take about 0.3 s. Bundles without `keyScheme` are still read with one Argon2id key per file.

items.title: b.restoreRollback.rollback accepts only a rollback point
items.body: `rollback` moved the live `dataDir` aside and renamed whatever `rollbackPath` named into its place without checking that it was a rollback point. When that second rename failed, the live data stayed in a `discarded-*` directory that `purge` deletes. `rollback` now refuses with `restore-rollback/bad-rollback-path` a path that is not a timestamp-named directory directly under the rollback root (after resolving symlinks), or that is, contains or sits inside `dataDir`, and it moves the live data back when the second rename fails.

items.title: Backup retention deletes only bundles older than a bundle that reads back intact
items.body: `b.backup.diskStorage` copied a bundle directly to its final directory, and `listBundles` returned every directory with a bundle-id name, so a copy interrupted by a killed run, or an empty directory with a later timestamp, counted as the newest bundle. With `retention: { keep: 1 }`, `run()` could delete the bundle it had just written, and a storage backend that kept part of a new bundle caused complete older bundles to be deleted. `diskStorage` now copies into `.partial-<bundleId>` and renames it into place, removes partial copies and backup staging directories more than 24 hours old, and reports a bundle from `listBundles`, `hasBundle` and `readBundle` only when it holds `manifest.json`. `bundleAdapterStorage` in the `directory` format writes `manifest.json` last and lists only bundles that have it. `run()` reads each new bundle back through `storage.readBundle` and compares it byte for byte with what it wrote; a difference deletes the new bundle, skips retention and rejects with `backup/verify-after-write-failed`. Retention and `purgeOlder` give no keep slot to, and do not delete, a bundle whose id sorts after the current run or the current time.

items.title: b.restore stages beside dataDir and refuses a layout its swap cannot complete
items.body: `b.restore` pulled and decrypted the bundle under `os.tmpdir()` and then renamed `dataDir` into the rollback root and the staging directory onto `dataDir`. A rename cannot move a mount point or cross filesystems, so a restore into a volume failed with `restore/swap-failed` and left the decrypted files in the temp directory. `run()` now pulls and decrypts under `stagingRoot` (default: the parent directory of the rollback root), refuses before pulling anything a `dataDir` that is a mount point (`restore/datadir-is-mount-point`) and a `stagingRoot` or rollback root on another filesystem (`restore/cross-device`), removes the decrypted staging directory when the swap fails, and removes a rollback root it created that is still empty. `blamejs restore apply` gains `--staging-root`.

items.title: A backup manifest larger than 4 MiB restores
items.body: The backup writer produced a manifest of any size, while `b.restoreBundle.extract`, `inspect`, `b.backup.verifyManifestSignature` and the `scheduleTest` drill refused one above 4 MiB, so a backup of several thousand files could not be restored. Every reader now uses `b.backupManifest.readFile` with `b.backupManifest.MAX_MANIFEST_BYTES` (64 MiB), and `b.backupManifest.serialize` refuses a larger manifest with `backup-manifest/too-large`, so `run()` rejects before anything reaches storage.

items.title: b.backupManifest verification returns a verdict when the fingerprint cannot be computed
items.body: A `b.auditSign.fingerprintOf` that throws or is missing now yields `ok: false` with the reason, instead of an exception from `verifySignature` or `verifyBytes`.

items.title: A value nested deeper than a validator can walk is refused by name
items.body: `b.safeSchema.parse` and `safeParse` threw a raw `RangeError` for a value about 500 levels deep, `b.jtd.validate` did the same past about 3,000 levels because its cap of 10,000 sat above the JavaScript stack, and `b.cbor.encode` did the same past about 6,000. `b.jsonSchema.validate` counted every descent into the value against its `$ref` cap, so a 300-level value under an ordinary recursive schema was reported as `json-schema/ref-loop` ("cyclic $ref?") though nothing was cyclic. `b.safeJson.parse` reported a well-formed 2,000-level document as `json/syntax`, because the prototype-stripping reviver it passes to `JSON.parse` is what ran out of stack, and every throw from the parse was reported as a syntax error. Each now refuses by name: `safe-schema/value-too-deep`, `jtd/too-deep`, `cbor/too-deep`, `json-schema/value-too-deep`, and `json/too-deep`, the last decided by counting nesting on the text before the parse runs. `b.jsonSchema` keeps `json-schema/ref-loop` for a schema that resolves 256 `$ref`s on one value without reaching into it, which is what a cycle does.

items.title: A shared validator builds the caller's error class with the code in .code
items.body: `b.validateOpts.requireNonEmptyString` and the `b.numericBounds` requirement helpers build the error class the caller passes. Sixteen framework error classes take `(message, code)` while the generated ones take `(code, message)`, so a refusal from one of the sixteen arrived with the message in `.code` and the code in `.message`, and an operator matching on `err.code` matched nothing. Every class now carries a factory that both conventions answer.

items.title: A backup to a recipient this host cannot decrypt still completes
items.body: `b.backup.run()` reads each bundle back from storage before retention runs. A `b.backup.bundleAdapterStorage` configured with `cryptoStrategy: "recipient"` and only the recipient's public keys cannot read its own bundles, so that read failed and the bundle it had just stored was deleted. Such a backend now reports `canReadBundle: false` and offers `verifyStoredContent(bundleId)`, which compares the stored bytes against what was written without decrypting them, so a truncated or corrupted payload is still caught. The result's `verifiedBy` says which check ran: `"readback"`, `"stored-content"`, or `"presence"`. Retention does not run after a presence-only check, because a stored key says nothing about the bytes under it and deleting an older bundle on that basis could leave only a corrupt one; the result then carries `retentionSkipped`.

items.title: maxBundleBytes bounds the archive, framing included
items.body: `b.backup.bundleAdapterStorage`'s `maxBundleBytes` was applied to the sum of the file sizes while the archive it writes also carries a 512-byte header and padding per entry. `b.backup.run()` reads each bundle back before retention deletes anything, and that read applied the archive reader's 128 MiB per-entry default, so a bundle holding a larger database file, or a bundle whose framing pushed it past the cap, read back as `backup/verify-after-write-failed` and the bundle just stored was deleted, leaving the deployment with no new backup. `writeBundle` now measures the archive it built, so `backup/bundle-too-large` names the framing cost before anything is stored, and the read path carries the same limit. A bundle of many small files spends more on framing than on payload: 100 empty files cost 100 headers.

items.title: restoreRollback.list reports the points rollback accepts
items.body: `b.restoreRollback.list` returned any directory in the rollback root, so an ordinary directory an operator had put there sorted to the front by its newer timestamp, became the default target of `rollback()`, and was then refused while a real rollback point sat behind it. The listing now reports only direct children whose name is the timestamp `swap` gives a rollback point.

items.title: A staging or rollback root inside dataDir is refused by either spelling
items.body: The preflight compared paths lexically, so a `stagingRoot` or `rollbackRoot` symlinked into `dataDir` was accepted and the decrypted staging landed inside the directory the restore renames aside, failing the swap after the bundle had been decrypted. Both spellings are refused now: the path as written, and the path with its symlinks resolved. A bind-mounted `dataDir` that shares its parent's device number is also refused, read from the mount table rather than inferred from device numbers.

items.title: A symlinked dataDir is refused before a bundle is decrypted
items.body: `b.restoreRollback.swap` moved a symlinked `dataDir` into the rollback root, which stores the link rather than the data and leaves a rollback point `rollback` refuses, so there was no way back. Both the restore preflight and `swap` refuse it now, the preflight before anything is pulled or decrypted: `restore/datadir-is-symlink` and `restore-rollback/datadir-is-symlink`.

items.title: A path that cannot serve as a restore directory is refused before pulling
items.body: The restore preflight asked about filesystems and mount points but not about what each path is, so a `dataDir` that was a regular file swapped without complaint and left a rollback `b.restoreRollback.rollback` refuses, while a `stagingRoot` or `rollbackRoot` that was a file, or a symbolic link resolving to nothing, failed only after the bundle had been pulled and decrypted. Each of the three roles is now checked before anything is pulled: `restore/datadir-not-a-directory`, `restore/bad-staging-root`, `restore/bad-rollback-root`.

items.title: A working directory is swept only when the work in it has stopped
items.body: `b.atomicFile.removeStaleDirs` read the start time out of a directory's name, so a backup or restore running for longer than the window had its staging directory deleted under it by the next run. A directory is removed now only when nothing inside it has been written within the same window, and a phase that reads without writing (uploading what was staged, pulling a bundle from storage) holds the new `b.atomicFile.heartbeat(dir)` so the sweep sees it as active. A scan that cannot be finished keeps the directory rather than treating the part it did not read as idle.

items.title: A bundle missing the blobs its manifest names is not a bundle
items.body: `b.backup.diskStorage` counted any directory holding a `manifest.json` as a bundle, so a copy interrupted after the manifest and before its files was listed, reported by `hasBundle`, and took a retention slot from a bundle that restores. A directory is reported now only when every encrypted file its manifest names is present at the size the manifest records. A manifest this release cannot parse is reported as before, since it says nothing about which files to expect.

items.title: The disaster-recovery runbook prints calls that exist
items.body: `b.drRunbook.emit` wrote a restore procedure naming `b.backupBundle.verifyManifestSignature`, which the framework does not export, `b.auditChain.verify`, whose name is `verifyChain`, and an `extract` call with `outDir` and `vaultKeyJsonOnly` arguments it does not take. An operator following the generated runbook hit a TypeError at step 2. The runbook now names `b.backup.verifyManifestSignature(bundleDir, { expectedFingerprint })`, `b.restoreBundle.extract({ bundleDir, stagingDir, passphrase, requireSignature, expectedFingerprint })` and `b.auditChain.verifyChain`, and a test resolves every framework call the runbook prints. The same name was corrected in the NIST CP-9 crosswalk, the CIS crosswalk documents and README.

items.title: b.restore has a reference page
items.body: `b.restore` carried no documentation, so it had no page in the generated reference. `b.restore.create` now documents its options, the four steps of a restore, the layouts it refuses and the codes it reports.

items.title: Restore reports each extract failure under its own code
items.body: `b.restore.run` reports every `restore-bundle/<name>` failure as `restore/<name>`. `restore/bad-manifest` and `restore/vault-key-recovery-failed` were reported as `restore/extract-failed`.

items.title: backup.create validates retention
items.body: `b.backup.create` throws `backup/bad-retention` unless `retention` is `{ keep: <positive integer> }`. A `keep` of 0 skipped retention without an error, and a `keep` between 0 and 1 deleted every bundle, including the one `run()` had just written.

items.title: b.atomicFile.removeStaleDirs
items.body: `b.atomicFile.removeStaleDirs(parentDir, { prefix, olderThanMs, keep })` removes directories named with a prefix and a `pathTimestamp` stamp older than the given age.

items.title: b.safeJson.parseTyped
items.body: `b.safeJson.parseTyped(input, opts)` parses under the same caps as `parse` and reports a failure as the caller's own error class and code, so a document read at a protocol boundary refuses with the code that boundary documents. The backup manifest reader, the TLS-RPT report reader, the CIBA notification reader and the OAuth response reader use it.

items.title: Tests report an unavailable host precondition instead of a passing check
items.body: A test that could not reach openssl(1), a resolver, or a platform API recorded a passing check and returned, so the suite counted coverage that never ran. Those rows now print `UNAVAILABLE` and count nothing, and the preconditions a test can create for itself (a TLS context, a temp directory, a local server) are created, so failing to build one fails the test.

items.title: The disaster-recovery runbook prints the arguments verifyChain takes
items.body: The generated restore procedure printed `b.auditChain.verifyChain({ db: restoredDb })` while the function takes a query callback and a table name, so an operator following the runbook hit an argument error before any audit row was checked.

items.title: Pin the signing key when restoring a signed bundle
items.body: A process that restores or verifies a signed bundle without the signing key initialized in `b.auditSign` passes `expectedFingerprint` (the value of `b.auditSign.getPublicKeyFingerprint()` in the backing-up process), or `--expected-fingerprint` to `blamejs restore apply`. A bundle signed under a key that `b.auditSign` no longer holds as active or rotated needs the pin as well.

items.title: Bundles written by this release need this release to restore
items.body: A bundle written by 0.20.31 records `keyScheme`, which earlier releases do not read; they report `restore/decrypt-failed` for it. Upgrade every process that restores before the first backup runs on 0.20.31. A bundle written by an earlier release restores under this one unchanged: its manifest records no `keyScheme` and each file is read with the per-file key that release derived.

items.title: Custom storage backends report complete bundles only
items.body: A custom backend's `listBundles` and `hasBundle` must not report a bundle until all of its files, `manifest.json` included, are stored, and its `readBundle` must return what `writeBundle` stored: `run()` now reads every new bundle back before retention.

items.title: Restore error handling
items.body: `restore/swap-failed` no longer carries `stagingDir`, because the staging directory is removed. Code matching `restore/extract-failed` for an invalid manifest or an unrecoverable vault key matches `restore/bad-manifest` and `restore/vault-key-recovery-failed`. A restore whose `dataDir` parent directory is not writable passes `stagingRoot` on the same filesystem as `dataDir`; a `dataDir` that is itself a mount point is replaced by a directory inside the volume.

items.title: Raise maxBundleBytes for a bundle of many small files
items.body: `b.backup.bundleAdapterStorage({ maxBundleBytes })` now bounds the archive rather than the sum of the file sizes, so a bundle whose entries cost more in tar framing than in payload is refused with `backup/bundle-too-large` at write. Each entry costs a 512-byte header plus padding to the next 512-byte boundary: raise the cap or split the source tree. A deployment at the 8 GiB default is unaffected.

releases.headline: Schema validation costs the size of the schema and the value, not the number of paths through them
releases.summary: Four validators and one schema converter walked every path through a schema or a value, so an input of linear size could cost exponential time. The most exposed was `b.safeSchema`, which `b.router` runs on every request body: an expression-tree schema built from a `union` of operator objects that recurse through `lazy` took 2.5 seconds and 1.7 GB of heap on a 339-byte JSON body twelve levels deep, and wrote a 531 MB 400 response; one more level exhausts the heap. `b.jsonSchema.validate` was exponential in the same way for a schema whose definitions reach the next one twice per level and for an ordinary recursive `anyOf`/`oneOf` schema against a deeply nested value, and `uniqueItems` compared every pair of items, so a 785 KB array of 128,000 numbers took 3.2 seconds. Each validator now runs a subschema at most once per value where one can be reached by several paths, and each refuses with its own error the shapes that cannot be collapsed that way. Separately, the framework writers that set their own `Cache-Control` (`b.render`, `b.middleware.sse`, the API-document and well-known middlewares, `b.staticServe`) replaced the `no-store` that `b.middleware.noCache` had set, so an authenticated page reached the browser with a header that lets the browser store it; they now keep an earlier `no-store`. Options that keep an operator RegExp and run it on later calls now refuse the `g` and `y` flags, which made each match start where the previous request's match ended: `b.middleware.csrfProtect({ skipPaths: [/\/health/y] })` skipped the CSRF check for a POST to `/api/v1/health` sent right after a POST to `/health`. `b.middleware.sse` no longer throws on every node:http response. `b.mail.arc.evaluate` reported a message sealed with an attacker's own key as sealed by a domain in `trustedSealers` when the ARC-Seal named that domain in an earlier `d=`; it now trusts only the domain whose key verified the seal. `b.mail.dmarc.evaluate` returned `none` for mail spoofing a domain that publishes `v = DMARC1; p=reject` or `V=DMARC1; p=reject`, or a valid record beside one starting `v=DMARC10`, so that mail was not rejected; the DMARC, SPF, MTA-STS, TLS-RPT and DKIM key-record lookups now select records by the version grammar their RFCs define. `b.network.smtp.mtaSts.fetch` returned no policy as soon as the `_mta-sts` TXT answer was missing or the policy host was unreachable, so an attacker who can block those responses could turn off an `enforce` policy the sender had already cached; it now applies the cached policy until its `max_age` elapses (RFC 8461 §3.3). The control-character checks now refuse the C1 controls U+0080 to U+009F, which include U+009B, the one-character form of `ESC [`.

items.title: b.mail.arc.evaluate reports a trusted sealer only for the domain whose key verified the seal
items.body: `arc.evaluate` read each hop's sealer domain with its own pattern, the first `d=` after a delimiter in the ARC-Seal header, while `arc.verify` verified the seal with the key named by the parsed `d=` tag. A sealer holding only the key for its own domain could therefore be reported as any domain in `trustedSealers`. A message sealed and signed with `attacker.example`'s key returned `chainStatus: "pass"`, `trusted: true` and `trustedDomain: "trusted.example"` when the ARC-Seal carried `d=trusted.example` earlier in the header than its real `d=attacker.example` tag, in any of three forms: as a repeated `d=` tag, as text after the signature inside the `b=` value, or inside the value of an unknown tag. An operator that relaxes DMARC for mail sealed by a trusted intermediary accepted such a message. `arc.verify` now returns the domain it verified each seal with as `hops[].sealDomain`, and `arc.evaluate` trusts only that domain.
