The ARC-Seal `cv=` value is read from the same parsed tags: a seal with `cv=nonesuch` was read as `cv=none` and now fails the chain with reason `invalid-cv-at-i=<n>`.

items.title: DKIM and ARC refuse a tag-list that repeats a tag name, and a b= value that is not base64
items.body: RFC 6376 §3.2 makes a tag-list that repeats a tag name invalid as a whole. `b.mail.dkim.verify` kept the last value of a repeated tag, so a DKIM-Signature carrying `s=` or `h=` twice verified as `pass`, and a key record carrying `p=` or `k=` twice was used. Such a signature is now `permerror`, and such a key record is skipped like any other invalid record. `b.mail.arc.verify` fails a chain whose ARC-Seal or ARC-Message-Signature repeats a tag with reason `invalid-tag-list`. The signature value was decoded with a base64 reader that ignores text after the padding, so a `b=` of the signature followed by other text verified; a `b=` that is not canonical base64 is now `permerror` for DKIM and fails the ARC hop (RFC 6376 §3.5). ARC reads a hop's instance number with one reader in `arc.verify`, `arc.evaluate` and `arc.sign`, following RFC 8617 §3.9 and §4.1: the header opens with `i=` and a number followed by `;`, with folding whitespace and comments allowed around each token (`i = 1 (forwarded);`), in the ARC-Seal and ARC-Message-Signature as well as the ARC-Authentication-Results. A header whose `i=` is not first is not read as part of a hop. `arc.evaluate` takes `finalAr` from the ARC-Authentication-Results that `arc.verify` grouped for the last hop, now also returned as `hops[].authenticationResults`, and returns `null` when that instance carries two of them.

items.title: b.safeSchema validates a recursive union in time proportional to the value, and bounds the issues it reports
items.body: `union` tried every option in turn and collected every failed option's issues, and `object` kept validating keys after its first failure. For a schema like `Expr = s.union([bin("+"), bin("-"), bin("*"), s.number()])` with operands that recurse through `s.lazy`, a value that fails at its deepest leaf was validated options^depth times and returned options^depth issues. Through `b.router`'s `{ body: schema }` validation, a 339-byte body twelve levels deep took 2.5 seconds and wrote a 531 MB 400 response. A `union` evaluated inside another union's option now checks each option's literal, enum, string, number and boolean keys first and stops the option at its first failure, for objects, arrays, tuples and records whose schema holds no `refine`, `transform` or `preprocess` callback, no `default` or `catch` factory and no unresolved `lazy`; those are still validated field by field in order. While a `union` or a `lazy` target is being validated, a schema that already failed for a value is not run again for that value: the earlier failure is reported at the new position, and each of its issues counts toward the evaluation limit below. A schema that already accepted a value at the same position returns that result again. A result is reused only when no `refine`, `transform` or `preprocess` callback, `lazy` getter, or `default` or `catch` factory ran while it was computed or has run since. This shape now costs the size of the body, including the first parse with a newly built schema whose `lazy` references are not yet resolved, and a `transform` or a `default` factory still runs for every value it produces. A failed `union` reports its summary issue, the first 100 issues its options reported, and one `union/issues-omitted` issue with the count it left out; a nested union reports only the first failure of each of its options. A value built in code that reuses one object at every level of a recursive schema is refused with `safe-schema/evaluation-limit` (from `safeParse` as the only error, from `parse` as the thrown `SafeSchemaError`) once validation passes 100,000 checks and 1,000 checks per node of the value.

items.title: b.jsonSchema.validate no longer walks every path through reference diamonds and recursive alternatives
items.body: A schema whose `$defs` each reach the next definition twice (through `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `if`/`then`/`else`, `not`, a `$ref` beside another applicator, `dependentSchemas`, `unevaluatedProperties`, or `$dynamicRef`) cost 2^depth evaluations: a 24-level schema of about 2 KB took 6.3 seconds to validate the string `"aaa"`. An ordinary recursive schema whose alternatives descend into the same child, such as an expression tree, cost branches^depth on a value a few hundred bytes long. Validation now remembers the result of a `$ref` target referenced from more than one place, and of every `$dynamicRef` target, for each value and dynamic scope, so these shapes cost the size of the schema and the value. The errors reported are unchanged, including their order and the `maxErrors` cut-off. A shape that still reaches the same subschema and value through more paths than its size accounts for, such as a value built in code that reuses one array at every level, is refused with `json-schema/evaluation-limit` once validation passes 100,000 evaluations and four times the schema's positions multiplied by the value's size.

items.title: Framework responses keep a Cache-Control no-store that is already on the response
items.body: `b.middleware.noCache` sets `Cache-Control: no-store` on authenticated and individualized responses, and the framework writers that ran after it replaced the header with their own default. A page sent through `b.render` behind `noCache` reached the browser with `private, no-cache, must-revalidate`, which lets the browser's own cache store the page (RFC 9111 §5.2.2.4); `no-store` forbids storing it (§5.2.2.5). The same replacement happened in `b.render.json`, `text`, `htmlString`, `redirect`, `stream` and `create().html` (`private, no-cache, must-revalidate`); `b.middleware.sse` and `b.sse.create` (`no-cache, no-transform`); the JMAP EventSource handler (`no-cache`); `b.middleware.openapiServe`, `b.middleware.asyncapiServe` and `b.openapi.create().middleware` (`public, max-age=300` or their `cacheControl` option); `b.middleware.securityTxt`, `assetlinks` and `webAppManifest` (`public, max-age=86400`); `b.middleware.protectedResourceMetadata` (`public, max-age=3600`); `b.a2a.middleware.agentCard` (`public, max-age=300`); and `b.staticServe` and `b.router.serveStatic` (their file cache policy, including on 304 responses). Each now sends the `Cache-Control` already on the response when it carries `no-store`, adding `no-transform` where its own default has that directive. A `Cache-Control` the caller passes in `opts.headers` does not remove it either: keep a route that must stay cacheable out of the middleware's scope with `b.middleware.noCache({ when })`. The rule is available as `b.cdnCacheControl.keepNoStore(res, fallback)` and as `b.requestHelpers.finalizeHeaders(res, headers)`, which applies it after merging caller headers and merges `Vary`.

items.title: Framework responses keep a Vary that is already on the response
items.body: A middleware that makes the response depend on a request header adds that header to `Vary` with `setHeader`: `b.middleware.cors` adds `Origin` and `b.middleware.compression` adds `Accept-Encoding`. node:http lets a header object passed to `res.writeHead` replace a header set that way, so a writer that sent its own `Vary` dropped the earlier tokens, and a shared cache could store one response for every value of the dropped header. `b.render.json`, `text`, `htmlString`, `redirect` and `stream` sent only the `Vary` in `opts.headers`; a response with `Vary: Cookie` already set and `opts.headers: { Vary: "Accept-Language" }` went out as `Vary: Accept-Language`. `b.middleware.sse` sent only a `Vary` in its `headers` option, `b.middleware.openapiServe` and `b.middleware.asyncapiServe` replaced `Vary` with `Origin` when `accessControl.allowOrigin` is set, `b.middleware.noCache` replaced it with its `vary` option, and `b.middleware.compression` appended `Accept-Encoding` to the header object a handler passed to `writeHead` without the `Vary` already on the response. Each now sends the earlier tokens followed by its own, each once. The merge is available as `b.requestHelpers.mergeVary(res, headers)`.

items.title: Options that keep an operator RegExp and run it on later calls refuse the g and y flags
items.body: A RegExp with the `g` or `y` flag starts each `test()` at the `lastIndex` the previous call left, so a pattern stored in configuration gave answers that depended on the request, row or file before. `b.safeSchema.string().regex(/^alice$/g)` accepted `"alice"` on every second parse. `b.guardCsv.schema` with a `/^[a-z]+$/g` column refused the second of three matching rows. `b.middleware.csrfProtect({ skipPaths: [/\/health/y] })` refused a POST to `/api/v1/health` with 403, and skipped the CSRF check for the same POST sent right after a POST to `/health`; `skipPaths` on `b.middleware.fetchMetadata`, `b.middleware.rateLimit` and `b.middleware.botGuard` is matched the same way. These options now throw when they are given a RegExp with either flag: `b.middleware.botGuard` `allowedAgents`, `blockedAgents` (`bot-guard/stateful-pattern`); `skipPaths` on `csrfProtect`, `fetchMetadata`, `rateLimit`, `botGuard` and `b.requestHelpers.makeSkipMatcher`, and `b.middleware.requestLog` `skipPaths` (`regex/stateful-pattern`); `b.middleware.spanHttpServer` `ignorePaths` (`span-http/stateful-pattern`); `b.middleware.requestId` `formatRegex` (`request-id/stateful-pattern`); `b.middleware.cors` `origins` (`cors/stateful-pattern`, as before); `b.staticServe.create` `hashedPathPattern` (`static/stateful-pattern`); `b.safeSql.validateIdentifier` `pattern` (`sql/stateful-pattern`); `b.safeSchema.string().regex` (`safe-schema/stateful-pattern`); `b.guardCsv.schema` column `regex` (`csv.stateful-pattern`); `b.mail.helo.evaluate` `genericRdnsPatterns` (`mail-helo/stateful-pattern`); `b.selfUpdate.poll` `assetPattern` and `signaturePattern` (`selfupdate/stateful-asset-pattern`, `selfupdate/stateful-sig-pattern`); `b.dev.create` `ignore` (`dev/stateful-pattern`); and `b.parsers.env.parse` `keyShape` (`env/stateful-pattern`). The check is available as `b.guardRegex.assertStateless(input, label?, ErrorClass?, code?)`. `skipPaths` and `ignorePaths` are copied when the middleware is created, so an entry added to the caller's array afterwards is not matched.

items.title: Operator patterns run against request data are screened for ReDoS
items.body: Five options ran an operator RegExp without `b.guardRegex.assertSafe`: `b.safeSchema.string().regex` (run on request bodies through `b.router`), `b.guardCsv.schema` column `regex`, `b.middleware.requestId` `formatRegex` (run on the inbound request-id header), `b.parsers.env.parse` `keyShape`, and a RegExp `sep` passed to `b.structuredFields.parseTagList`. Each now screens the pattern and throws `safe-schema/unsafe-pattern`, `csv.unsafe-pattern`, `request-id/unsafe-pattern`, `env/unsafe-pattern` or `regex/unsafe-pattern` for a shape the screen refuses.

items.title: b.mail.dmarc.evaluate reads a DMARC record whose version tag has spaces or an uppercase V
items.body: RFC 9989 defines the DMARC version tag as `"v" *WSP "=" *WSP %s"DMARC1"`: the tag name is case-insensitive and whitespace may surround the `=`. The record lookup kept only TXT records that began with the exact characters `v=DMARC1`. For a domain publishing `v = DMARC1; p=reject` or `V=DMARC1; p=reject`, `evaluate` returned `result: "none"` for mail that failed SPF and DKIM alignment, and a domain publishing `v=DMARC1; p=reject` beside a second record starting `v=DMARC10` also returned `none`. All three now return `fail` with `p=reject`. A record starting `v=DMARC10` or `v=DMARC1x` is not a DMARC record: as the only record it returned `permerror` and now returns `none`. `b.mail.dmarc.parseRecord` refuses a record whose version tag does not match the grammar.

items.title: b.network.smtp.mtaSts.fetch applies a cached policy when no live policy is available
items.body: `fetch` resolved the `_mta-sts` TXT record before it consulted its cache, and returned `null` when the record was missing, malformed or could not be resolved. When the TXT `id` changed and the policy host was unreachable, answered 404, answered another non-2xx status or served a policy that did not parse, `fetch` returned `null` or threw `smtp/mta-sts-fetch-failed`. An attacker able to block DNS or HTTPS responses for a recipient domain could therefore turn off an `enforce` policy that `b.mail.send.deliver` had already cached. RFC 8461 §3.3 requires a sender to apply a valid cached policy in each of those cases, and `fetch` now returns the cached policy; with no cached policy it returns `null` or throws as before. The policy was also cached for 60 minutes whatever its `max_age`. A cached policy is now used until its `max_age` elapses, for at most 52 weeks, or for 60 minutes when the policy has no `max_age`. A TXT `id` equal to the cached policy's `id` returns the cached policy without an HTTPS request, and a fetch that failed for a new `id` is not retried for 60 minutes. The returned policy no longer carries the internal `_cacheTtlMs` field.

items.title: SPF, MTA-STS, TLS-RPT and DKIM key records are selected by their RFC version grammar
items.body: `b.mail.spf.verify` treated a TXT record starting `v=spf10` or `v=spf1x` as an SPF record: `v=spf10 +all` on its own returned `pass`, and `v=spf1 -all` published beside it returned `permerror`. RFC 7208 §4.5 ends the version section at a space or the end of the record, so those records are now ignored (the two examples return `none` and `fail`), and `b.mail.spf.parseRecord` refuses them. `b.network.smtp.mtaSts.fetch` fetched the HTTPS policy for a TXT answer that carried `v=STSv1` anywhere in a record, started `v=STSv10`, had no `id`, had an `id` longer than 32 characters, or held two `v=STSv1` records; RFC 8461 §3.1 treats each as no policy, and `fetch` now returns `null` for them unless it holds a cached policy for the domain. `b.network.smtp.tlsRpt.fetchPolicy` accepted records starting `V=TLSRPTV1`, `v=TLSRPTv1-x` or `v=TLSRPTv1.5` and used the first of two `v=TLSRPTv1` records; each now returns `null` (RFC 8460 §3). `b.mail.dkim.verify` and the key lookup in `b.mail.arc.verify` used the first TXT record at the selector that started `v=DKIM1` or contained `p=`, so a key record starting `v=DKIM2` or `v=DKIM10`, or one whose `v=` tag was not the first tag, verified signatures. RFC 6376 §3.6.1 requires `v=` to be absent or to be the first tag with the value `DKIM1`. Other records are now skipped, the first remaining record that has `p=` is used, and a signature whose selector has no remaining record gets `permerror`. The check is available as `b.structuredFields.recordVersionMatches(record, name, value, grammar)`.

items.title: Control-character checks refuse the C1 controls U+0080 to U+009F
items.body: U+009B is the one-character form of `ESC [` and starts a terminal escape sequence, and U+0085 NEXT LINE is a line break under Unicode line breaking. The shared control-character checks covered only C0 and DEL: `b.guardText` under `balanced` answered `ok: true` for text carrying either character and `sanitize` kept both, and `b.codepointClass.isForbiddenControlChar(0x9b)` returned `false`. `b.codepointClass.CTRL_RANGES`, which the text guards read for `controlPolicy`, and `isForbiddenControlChar` and `firstControlCharOffset` now include the C1 block, which is also exported as `C1_CTRL_RANGES`. The C1 controls are now refused by `b.guardText`, `b.guardFilename` (`filename.control`), `b.guardCsv`, `b.guardSql` quoted identifiers, `b.guardJwt.kidSafe`, `b.guardMessageId`, `b.guardMailCompose` header values, `b.guardMailMove` folder names, `b.guardMailSieve` names and scripts, `b.guardIdempotencyKey`, `b.guardDsn.parse`, `b.guardListId`, `b.guardListUnsubscribe`, the SMTP, IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve command guards and the mail servers that run them, `b.safeIcal`, `b.safeVcard`, `b.safeMime` header values, `b.safeJsonPath.validateKey`, `b.inbox` message ids, `b.storage.chunkScratch` assembly ids, `b.auth.stepUp.buildChallenge`, `b.middleware.bearerAuth` realms, `b.mail.feedbackId`, `b.mail.spamScore` reasons, `b.mail.deploy` domains, JMAP URLs and email addresses, and `b.localHttp` request paths. `b.safeRedirect.resolve` returns its fallback, `b.requestHelpers.extractBearer` returns `null`, `b.ai.input.classify` counts the character in `ctrlCount`, and `b.guardMarkdown` removes it from link targets. `b.structuredFields.refuseControlBytes` and `containsControlBytes` still accept 0x80 to 0x9F, because Node exposes an HTTP field value as a latin1 string in which those codes are UTF-8 continuation bytes, and `b.parsers.toml` still accepts C1 in strings, as TOML 1.0 allows; both pass the new `allowC1` option.

items.title: b.auth.fidoMds3.fetch stops serving a cached BLOB after its nextUpdate
items.body: `fetch` passed the time until the BLOB's `nextUpdate` to the cache as a bare number, which the cache ignored, so every fetched BLOB was cached for 30 days. A call made after `nextUpdate` returned the cached BLOB, with the authenticator status reports it held when it was fetched, instead of downloading the replacement. The BLOB is now cached until its `nextUpdate`, and for at most 30 days, and a cached BLOB whose `nextUpdate` has passed is fetched again.

items.title: b.jsonSchema uniqueItems runs in linear time
items.body: `uniqueItems: true` compared every pair of items, so an array of 128,000 distinct numbers (785 KB) took 3.2 seconds and an array of 32,000 small objects took 9.3 seconds. Each item is now reduced to an identifier that is equal for exactly the pairs `enum` and `const` treat as equal, so the check costs the size of the array. The error still names the first duplicate pair, `(indices i, j)`, with the lowest first index.

items.title: A Vary wildcard stays alone when a token is added
items.body: `b.requestHelpers.appendVary` appended the new token to the list it parsed without looking for `*`, so a `Vary: *` already on the response became `*, Accept` when `b.middleware.sse` added `Accept`, and `*, Cookie, Authorization` under `b.middleware.noCache`. RFC 9110 section 12.5.5 gives the wildcard its never-reuse meaning only when it stands alone, so a cache reading that list could store and reuse the response. `b.middleware.compression` carried its own appender, which collapsed the wildcard only when it was the whole earlier value, so `Cookie, *` grew an `Accept-Encoding`. Both now go through the new `b.requestHelpers.appendVaryValue(existing, value)`, which reports the merged value, `null` when the token is already carried, and `*` alone whenever either side carries the wildcard.

items.title: b.jsonSchema enum and const equality is symmetric
items.body: Object equality compared the enumerable keys of one side with the own keys of the other, so an object with a non-enumerable own property could equal a second object while the second did not equal the first. Both sides now compare enumerable own keys, which is also the equality `uniqueItems` uses.

items.title: b.jtd checks a schema object reused at several positions once
items.body: A schema built in code that reuses one object at several positions was checked once per path before any value was validated, doubling per level. Each object is now checked once. A schema whose root reappears below the root is still refused with `jtd/bad-schema`, and so is a schema object graph that contains a cycle, such as `s.elements = s`, which previously overflowed the stack.

items.title: b.safeSchema catch factories run for null
items.body: `.catch(fn)` called `fn` for a value that failed validation, but for `null` it returned `fn` itself as the parsed value: `s.number().catch(function () { return 7; }).parse(null)` returned the function. It now returns `7` in both cases.

items.title: b.middleware.sse streams over a node:http response
items.body: `b.middleware.sse` added `Vary: Accept` after `writeHead` had sent the response head. node:http refuses that with `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`, so the middleware threw before writing any event. It now adds `Vary: Accept` before the head is written, next to any `Vary` an earlier middleware set.

items.title: b.flag providers apply regex targeting rules and name themselves in result metadata
items.body: `b.flag.providers.memory`, `localFile` and `environmentVariable` validated each flag's rules but evaluated the unvalidated copy, which never carries the compiled pattern, so a rule with `op: "regex"` never matched and the flag fell back to its default. The providers now evaluate the validated rules. Their results also carried `metadata.provider: null` for every evaluation that found the flag; it is now the provider kind (`memory`, `local-file` or `environment`).

items.title: Pattern options reject a value that is not a RegExp
items.body: `b.middleware.requestId` accepted a string `formatRegex` and then threw a `TypeError` on every request that carried the request-id header; it now throws `request-id/bad-format-regex` when it is created. `b.safeSql.validateIdentifier` threw a `TypeError` for a string `pattern` and now throws `sql/bad-pattern`. `b.parsers.env.parse` ignored a `keyShape` that was not a RegExp and applied the default key shape; it now throws `env/bad-opt`. `b.mail.helo.evaluate` ignored `genericRdnsPatterns` entries that were not a RegExp and now throws `mail-helo/bad-pattern`. `b.safeSchema.string().regex` throws `safe-schema/bad-regex`, `b.guardCsv.schema` throws `csv.bad-schema` for a column that is not an object or a `regex` that is not a RegExp, and `b.dev.create` throws `dev/bad-ignore` for an `ignore` entry that is neither a RegExp nor a string.

items.title: b.guardCsv.schema copies and freezes its columns; b.auditDailyReview freezes its exported tables
items.body: `b.guardCsv.schema` kept the caller's column objects and returned them as `columns`, so changing a column's `regex` after the schema was built changed how later rows were validated without screening the new pattern. It now copies each column, and the returned `columns` array and its entries are frozen. `b.auditDailyReview.ALERT_PATTERNS`, `CRITICAL_PATTERNS`, `SEVERITY_ORDER` and `POSTURES_REQUIRING_NOTIFY` were exported as mutable arrays that the default classifier reads for every event; they and the RegExps in them are now frozen.

items.title: b.auth.jwt.verifyExternal applies jwksCacheMs
items.body: `verifyExternal` accepted `jwksCacheMs` and passed it to the cache as a bare number, which the cache ignored, so keys fetched from `jwksUri` were cached for the 10-minute default whatever the option said, and values such as `-1`, `"60000"` and `Infinity` were accepted. The option now sets how long the keys are cached (`0` does not cache them), and a value that is not a non-negative finite integer throws `auth-jwt-external/bad-jwks-cache-ms`.

items.title: b.openapi.toYaml and b.asyncapi.toYaml escape line breaks and non-printable characters
items.body: The YAML writer behind `b.openapi.toYaml`, `b.asyncapi.toYaml`, `b.middleware.openapiServe` and `b.middleware.asyncapiServe` quoted a string only when it held a YAML indicator character or leading or trailing whitespace. A key containing a line feed was written unquoted and changed the document's structure: `{ "x\ny": 1 }` read back as the string `"x"`. A value containing a carriage return made the document unparseable, and C0 controls, DEL, C1 controls, U+2028, U+2029 and U+FEFF were written unescaped, which YAML 1.2 does not allow in a stream. A string holding any of these characters is now written double-quoted, with the character written as `\n`, `\r`, `\t` or a `\u` escape.

items.title: b.openapi.schemaWalk refuses a schema it would expand without bound
items.body: `schemaWalk` copied a subschema into every position that references it, so a schema object reused at every level expanded to 2^depth nodes in the generated document, a cyclic schema overflowed the stack, and a schema nested a few thousand levels deep did the same. It now refuses with `openapi/schema-too-large` past 100,000 nodes, `openapi/schema-cycle` for a subschema that is its own ancestor, and `openapi/schema-too-deep` past 1,000 levels. A subschema used in a few places is still copied into each one.

items.title: b.cache wrap and set refuse options that are not an object
items.body: `cache.wrap(key, fn, 60000)` and `cache.set(key, value, 60000)` ignored the number and stored the entry for the instance's default `ttlMs`. Both now throw `cache/bad-opt` when the options argument is present and is not an object.

items.title: C1 controls are refused
items.body: Input carrying U+0080 to U+009F is now refused by the checks listed under Security. A caller of `b.codepointClass.isForbiddenControlChar` or `firstControlCharOffset` that scans a latin1 view of bytes, where 0x80 to 0x9F are parts of a longer UTF-8 sequence, passes `{ allowC1: true }`.

items.title: Publish one well-formed _mta-sts TXT record
items.body: Publish exactly one `_mta-sts` TXT record that starts `v=STSv1;` and carries `id=` with 1 to 32 letters and digits, the form `b.mail.deploy.mtaStsPublish` returns. A domain whose record lacks `id`, or that publishes two records, is now treated as having no MTA-STS policy by senders that have not cached one.

items.title: Scope noCache off routes that must stay cacheable
items.body: A `Cache-Control` passed in `opts.headers` to a `b.render` writer, to `b.middleware.sse`, or to an API-document middleware no longer replaces a `no-store` that `b.middleware.noCache` set on the response. A route that must remain cacheable behind that middleware is excluded from it with its predicate: `b.middleware.noCache({ when: function (req) { return req.url.indexOf("/public/") !== 0; } })`.

items.title: Pass cache options as an object
items.body: Replace a bare number passed to `cache.wrap` or `cache.set` with `{ ttlMs: <number> }`.

items.title: New refusals and a bounded union issue list
items.body: `b.jsonSchema.validate` and `isValid` can throw `json-schema/evaluation-limit`; a value built in code that reuses one array at every level of a recursive schema is refused this way. `b.safeSchema` union failures carry at most 100 option issues plus a `union/issues-omitted` issue, and `parse`/`safeParse` refuse with `safe-schema/evaluation-limit` a value that reuses one object at every level of a recursive schema. `b.openapi.schemaWalk` throws `openapi/schema-too-large`, `openapi/schema-cycle` or `openapi/schema-too-deep` for the shapes above; define a subschema used in many places once under `components/schemas` and reference it with `$ref`.

items.title: Remove the g and y flags from stored patterns
items.body: A RegExp with the `g` or `y` flag passed to any of the options listed under Security is now refused when the option is accepted. Remove the flag: `test()` matches the same values without it. A pattern that `b.guardRegex.assertSafe` refuses must be rewritten for `s.string().regex`, a `b.guardCsv.schema` column, `b.middleware.requestId` `formatRegex`, `b.parsers.env.parse` `keyShape` and a RegExp `sep` for `b.structuredFields.parseTagList`; the refusal names the shape.

releases.headline: Operator RegExp patterns are matched against the whole value: form validation and CORS origins
releases.summary: Two places matched an operator-supplied RegExp with an unanchored `.test()`, where a whole-string match was expected. `b.forms.validate` tested a field's `pattern` unanchored, so a value that merely contained a match passed server-side even though the browser rejects it: the same pattern is rendered as the HTML5 `pattern=` attribute, which the browser anchors over the entire value, so `pattern: /[0-9]{4}/` accepted `"12345"` (and `/[a-z]{3}/` accepted `"abc; DROP TABLE users"`) on the server while the client refused them. Server-side validation now anchors the pattern to the whole value (`^(?:source)$`, preserving flags), matching the browser and closing the client/server divergence. Separately, `b.middleware.cors` reflected a matched Origin into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so a RegExp origin that admitted more hosts than intended leaked responses to an attacker origin: an unanchored `/example\.com/` matched `https://example.com.attacker.test`, and with `credentials:true` a pattern like `/^https:\/\/.*\.com$/` reflected any registrable `.com` origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Because no finite check can prove an arbitrary RegExp is host-specific, `create()` now refuses a RegExp origin outright when `credentials:true` (use exact string origins for credentialed CORS); for `credentials:false` it requires whole-origin anchoring and rejects catch-all patterns, and matching consumes the entire origin. Separately, `b.network.tls.ocsp.buildRequest` built the RFC 6960 CertID lookup hash with SHA-1; it now defaults to SHA-256, with a `certIdHashAlg` opt to downgrade for a responder that only indexes SHA-1 CertIDs. Separately, `b.mailStore` now records `Cc` and `Reply-To`, so a reply or a reply-all can be addressed from the store alone.

items.title: b.forms.validate anchors a field pattern to the whole submitted value
items.body: A field `pattern` is rendered verbatim as the HTML5 `pattern=` attribute, which the browser compiles anchored over the entire value. Server-side, `b.forms.validate` ran `pattern.test(value)` unanchored, so it accepted a value that only contained a match even though the browser rejects that value. An attacker bypassing the client (or any non-browser client) could submit `"12345"` against `pattern: /[0-9]{4}/`, or trailing payload past a short pattern, and pass server validation. Validation now matches the pattern against the whole value (`^(?:source)$`, preserving the `i`/`s`/`u` flags and dropping `g`/`y`/`m`), so the server and the browser agree. A pattern already written as `^...$` is unaffected.

items.title: b.middleware.cors refuses a RegExp origin with credentials, and matches non-credentialed RegExp origins against the whole origin
items.body: Origin matching runs `pattern.test(origin)` and reflects a matched Origin into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. A credentialed CORS response reflecting a pattern-matched origin leaks authenticated responses to any host the RegExp admits, and an arbitrary RegExp cannot be proven host-specific: `/^https:\/\/.*\.com$/` trusts every registrable `.com`, and a scheme, port, or IP-form wildcard evades any finite probe. `create()` now throws `cors/regex-origin-with-credentials` when a RegExp origin is paired with `credentials:true`; use exact string origins for credentialed CORS. For `credentials:false`, where no credentials are reflected, RegExp origins are still allowed but must match the whole origin: `create()` throws `cors/unanchored-pattern` for a pattern not anchored at both ends (`^...$`) and `cors/overbroad-pattern` for a catch-all, matching consumes the entire origin (so an internally half-anchored alternation cannot substring-match), and the previous ReDoS screening remains. Anchor RegExp origins to the complete origin, for example `/^https:\/\/([a-z0-9-]+\.)?example\.com$/`.

items.title: b.network.tls.ocsp.buildRequest builds the CertID with SHA-256 by default
items.body: The OCSP request CertID (`issuerNameHash` + `issuerKeyHash`, RFC 6960 §4.1.1) was built with SHA-1. RFC 9919 §3.1.1, which obsoletes RFC 5019, requires OCSP clients to use SHA-256 for the CertID. `buildRequest` now defaults the CertID hash to SHA-256, and accepts `certIdHashAlg` (`sha256` | `sha384` | `sha512` | `sha1`, listed in `b.network.tls.ocsp.CERTID_HASH_ALGS`) so an operator whose responder indexes revocation only by a SHA-1 CertID can opt down explicitly. `undefined` or `null` selects the default; any other value, including an empty string, throws `tls/ocsp-bad-certid-hash-alg`. `b.network.tls.ocsp.fetch` forwards the option, and `b.cert.create` accepts it as `ocsp.certIdHashAlg` for stapling refreshes. `b.cert.create` validates the value when the manager is created and throws `cert/bad-ocsp-certid-hash-alg` for an unsupported one; a refresh records its failure only as an audit event, so a misspelled value accepted at create time would leave the server running without fresh staples. The verifier already reads the hashAlgorithm from the response CertID and recomputes with it, so a SHA-256 request round-trips against a conforming responder with no other change. A responder that indexes revocation only by SHA-1 CertIDs cannot answer a SHA-256 request: the `tls/ocsp-not-good` and `tls/ocsp-fetch-bad-status` errors from `ocsp.fetch` now name the CertID hash that was sent and the `certIdHashAlg: "sha1"` option, and `b.cert` logs a warning for every failed staple refresh, where only a `cert.ocsp.refresh-failed` audit event recorded it before.

items.title: b.mailStore records Cc and Reply-To, and fetchByObjectId returns them
items.body: The messages table stored `To` and neither `Cc` nor `Reply-To`, and the store keeps no raw message bytes, so a client composing a reply from the store alone addressed it to `From` even when the author had set `Reply-To` (RFC 5322 §3.6.2), and a reply-all dropped everyone on `Cc`. `appendMessage` now writes sealed `cc_addrs` and `reply_to` columns, sealed the same way as `to_addrs`, and `fetchByObjectId` (and `b.mail.agent` `fetch`) returns `cc` and `replyTo` next to `to`. Each field holds every instance of its header joined with `", "`, the same shape as `to`, and an empty string when the message has none. `Bcc` is not recorded. `create()` adds the two columns to a store created by an earlier version; when several processes open the same store at once, a process whose `ALTER TABLE` finds the column already added by another process continues, and any other `ALTER TABLE` failure is still thrown. Messages appended before the upgrade return `cc: null` and `replyTo: null`, because the store has no copy of their headers to fill the columns from.

items.title: The RSA key-size floor is cited to RFC 8301 §3.2, including in refusal messages
items.body: The RSA floor in `b.mail.dkim`, `b.mail.crypto.pgp` and `b.mail.crypto.smime` was attributed to RFC 8301 §3.1, which covers signing algorithms, and to `draft-ietf-dmarc-rfc8301bis`, which does not resolve. RFC 8301 §3.2 is the key-size section: signers MUST use RSA keys of at least 1024 bits and SHOULD use at least 2048. The refusal messages from `b.mail.dkim.verify`, `b.mail.dkim.bootstrap`, `b.mail.crypto.pgp.sign`, `b.mail.crypto.pgp.verify` and `b.mail.crypto.smime.checkCert` now cite §3.2 and state 2048 as the framework's floor following that recommendation; the error codes and the 2048-bit value are unchanged. `b.mail.crypto.pgp` and `b.mail.crypto.smime` take their floor from `b.mail.dkim.RSA_MIN_BITS` instead of keeping their own copies. Code that matched the old message text needs to match the new text.

items.title: OCSP stapling against a responder that answers only SHA-1 CertIDs
items.body: `b.cert` stapling and `b.network.tls.ocsp.fetch` now send a SHA-256 CertID. If your CA's responder does not answer it, the refresh warning and the `ocsp.fetch` error name the CertID hash; set `ocsp: { certIdHashAlg: "sha1" }` on `b.cert.create`, or pass `certIdHashAlg: "sha1"` to `ocsp.fetch` or `ocsp.buildRequest`.

items.title: Stores opened with init: false need two new columns
items.body: `b.mailStore.create({ init: false })` does not touch the schema, so a store whose schema you manage must have `cc_addrs` and `reply_to` (both `TEXT`) on the messages table before it is opened with this version; the insert statement prepared at `create()` names both columns. With the default `init: true`, `create()` adds them.

releases.headline: `b.auth.passkey.verifyRegistration` can require an attestation, not only anchor one
releases.summary: `requireAttestationAnchor` refuses a certificate chain that does not terminate at a trusted root, but a `none` or self attestation carries no chain, so it was accepted regardless. A relying party that wanted to register only authenticators whose model is attested had to read `registrationInfo.attestationType` after the fact and reject `None`/`Self` itself, which is easy to forget. A new opt-in `requireAttestation: true` refuses a credential whose attestation type is `None` or `Self` at the verification chokepoint, so the check cannot be skipped. It permits `Basic`, `AttCA`, and `AnonCA` attestations and composes with `requireAttestationAnchor` and `attestationRoots` (require an attestation, and require its chain to anchor). It is off by default: platform and synced passkeys legitimately use `none`/self, so requiring attestation is a deployment choice.

items.title: requireAttestation option on b.auth.passkey.verifyRegistration
items.body: Set `requireAttestation: true` to refuse a registration whose attestation type is `None` or `Self` (thrown as `auth-passkey/attestation-required`). These types carry no proof of the authenticator model, so `requireAttestationAnchor` (which validates certificate chains) never applied to them and an unattested credential verified as long as the ceremony bindings held. High-assurance deployments that must register only model-attested authenticators can now enforce that at verification time instead of post-processing `registrationInfo.attestationType`. The option permits `Basic`/`AttCA`/`AnonCA` and composes with `requireAttestationAnchor` + `attestationRoots`. It stays off by default because platform and synced passkeys use `none`/self attestation; enabling it is a per-deployment policy decision.

releases.headline: DANE-TA trust anchors are validated by signature path, not name equality
releases.summary: SMTP DANE verification accepted a TLSA usage 2 (DANE-TA) record when the matched trust-anchor certificate's Subject byte-equaled the presented leaf's Issuer, a name comparison rather than a signature check. An active attacker on the delivery path could present a leaf whose Issuer field copied the pinned anchor's Subject but that the anchor never signed, and the chain was accepted; a certificate whose Issuer or Subject could not be parsed was accepted with a flag set but still reported valid. In trust-anchor mode the TLS stack's own chain validation is turned off and this check is the sole authority, so the leaf was effectively unauthenticated. DANE-TA now requires a cryptographically validated path from the leaf to the matched anchor (each link's signature verified against its issuer's key, the anchor and intermediates confirmed as CAs), reusing the same path resolver as the X.509 chain primitives, and fails closed when a certificate cannot be parsed.

items.title: DANE-TA (TLSA usage 2) requires a validated certificate path to the matched anchor
items.body: `b.network.smtp.dane.verifyChain` accepted a DANE-TA match when the matched anchor's Subject DN byte-equaled the leaf's Issuer DN, and accepted a chain with an unparseable Issuer or Subject as a flagged-but-valid match. Neither verified that the anchor actually signed the presented chain. Because SMTP DANE turns off the TLS library's chain validation in trust-anchor mode (`b.mail` sets it when a DANE-TA or DANE-EE record is in play), that name comparison was the only thing standing between a delivery and a substituted certificate, so an on-path attacker could present a leaf carrying the anchor's name and have it accepted (RFC 7672 §3.1.1). Verification now builds a certification path from the leaf to the matched anchor and accepts the match only when every link's signature verifies against its issuer's public key and each issuer is a CA, using the same resolver as `b.x509Chain.resolveChain`. A certificate that cannot be parsed fails closed rather than being accepted with a flag. DANE-EE (usage 3), which pins the leaf directly, and the opt-in PKIX modes (usage 0 and 1), which defer to an external validator, are unchanged.

releases.headline: DKIM binds every oversigned header instance, closing a signed-header injection bypass
releases.summary: DKIM signing and verification resolved each name in the signature's `h=` tag to the last (bottom-most) matching header field, so a name listed more than once in `h=` (oversigning, the RFC 6376 defense against a prepended duplicate of a signed header) bound the same instance every time. An attacker could prepend a spoofed copy of an oversigned header (Subject, Reply-To, and so on) to a validly signed message and it still verified as DKIM-pass, and the spoofed value flowed through to the DMARC decision. Signing and verification now consume repeated `h=` names bottom-up, one header instance per occurrence, per RFC 6376 §5.4.2: an injected instance is bound and the signature fails. The same change makes blamejs's oversigned signatures interoperate with conforming verifiers.

items.title: Oversigned (repeated h=) DKIM header names bind their instances bottom-up
items.body: `b.mail.dkim.verify` and `b.mail.dkim` signing resolved each `h=` entry with a last-match lookup, so listing a header name more than once in `h=` (oversigning) selected the same bottom-most instance for every occurrence. Oversigning is the RFC 6376 §5.4.2 mechanism that binds a header more times than it appears, so an added copy is covered by the signature; with last-match it bound nothing extra, and an attacker who prepended a spoofed copy of an oversigned header to an otherwise-valid message kept a DKIM-pass result (and, through `b.mail.inbound.verify`, a DMARC-pass and delivery on the spoofed header). Signing and verification now share one resolver that consumes repeated `h=` names from the bottom of the header block upward, one instance per occurrence, treating an occurrence beyond the header's count as the null input. An injected instance is bound to the signature and fails verification. A message that does not oversign is unaffected.

items.title: Oversigned signatures interoperate with conforming verifiers
items.body: Because signing used the same last-match resolution, blamejs-produced oversigned signatures did not verify at an RFC-conforming verifier, and blamejs rejected a conforming oversigned signature. With bottom-up per-occurrence consumption on both sides, oversigned mail now crosses the boundary in both directions. Verification also excludes the DKIM-Signature it is checking from that header's own `h=` selection (RFC 6376 §5.4) while keeping every other signature instance, so a message that oversigns the `dkim-signature` header verifies.

items.title: ARC message signing shares the corrected header selection
items.body: `b.mail.arc.sign` resolved each repeated `headersToSign` name to the last matching header, and ARC-Message-Signature verification runs through the DKIM verifier. Now that the verifier consumes repeated names bottom-up, ARC signing uses the same resolver, so an oversigned ARC seal binds each header instance and an unmodified oversigned message verifies.

releases.headline: Verifiable-credential verification checks revocation status and refuses a revocable credential it cannot check
releases.summary: `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify` and `b.auth.oid4vp.verifier.verifyResponse` verified a credential's signature, key binding, and validity window but never consulted its `status` claim (Token Status List), so a revoked credential verified as valid. Verification now checks status: when a credential carries a `status` claim it is revocable, and the verifier requires a `statusListResolver` to resolve its entry. A resolver that reports any non-valid status (revoked or suspended) rejects the credential; a credential that carries a `status` claim with no resolver configured is refused rather than accepted unchecked.

items.title: statusListResolver on the SD-JWT-VC and OpenID4VP verifiers
items.body: `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify` accepts `opts.statusListResolver`, and `b.auth.oid4vp.verifier.create` accepts it as a create-time option threaded through to the credentials it verifies. The resolver is called as `statusListResolver({ idx, uri })` with the credential's Token Status List reference and returns the integer status for that index (0 = valid). Operators resolve the reference with `b.auth.statusList.fromJwt` (fetch the status-list token from `uri`, verify its signature under their trust configuration, and return `list.get(idx)`).

items.title: A revoked credential no longer verifies, and a revocable credential is refused when its status cannot be checked
items.body: `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify` (and `b.auth.oid4vp.verifier.verifyResponse`, which composes it) checked signature, key binding, and the validity window but ignored the credential's `status` claim, so a credential the issuer had revoked still verified as valid. A credential carrying a `status` claim (Token Status List) is now treated as revocable: the verifier resolves the entry through `opts.statusListResolver` and rejects the credential (`auth-sd-jwt-vc/revoked`) when the resolved status is anything other than valid. A credential that carries a `status` claim while no `statusListResolver` is configured is refused (`auth-sd-jwt-vc/status-check-required`) rather than accepted without a revocation check. A credential with no `status` claim is unaffected.

items.title: Supply a statusListResolver to verify revocable credentials
items.body: If you verify credentials that carry a `status` claim through `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify` or `b.auth.oid4vp.verifier`, supply `statusListResolver({ idx, uri })` returning the integer status for the credential's index (0 = valid). A typical resolver fetches the status-list token from `uri`, verifies it with `b.auth.statusList.fromJwt`, and returns `result.list.get(idx)`. Without a resolver, a credential carrying a `status` claim is refused with `auth-sd-jwt-vc/status-check-required`; a credential with no `status` claim continues to verify unchanged.

releases.headline: SAML Single-Logout messages must be signature-verified by default
releases.summary: The SAML Single-Logout parse methods (`parseLogoutRequest`, `parseLogoutResponse`, `parseLogoutRequestPost`, `parseLogoutResponseSoap`) verified the inbound message against the IdP key only when `idpVerifyKey` was supplied. With no key configured they parsed the message without any signature check, so a forged, unsigned LogoutRequest was accepted and its NameID surfaced — letting any party on the path force-log-out a chosen user. Verification is now mandatory by default: a parse with no `idpVerifyKey` configured is refused with `auth-saml/slo-verification-required`. An operator that intentionally accepts unsigned SLO messages opts in explicitly with `allowUnsigned: true`. The login path (`verifyResponse`) already required a signature and is unchanged.

items.title: Unsigned Single-Logout messages are refused unless verification is configured
items.body: Every SAML SLO parse path — `sp.parseLogoutRequest`, `sp.parseLogoutResponse`, `sp.parseLogoutRequestPost`, `sp.parseLogoutResponseSoap` — gated signature verification on the presence of `idpVerifyKey`. With no key configured the message was parsed and its NameID / InResponseTo returned without any signature check, so a forged unsigned LogoutRequest verified and could terminate a chosen user's session (a forced-logout / denial-of-service). Verification is now on by default: a parse with no `idpVerifyKey` throws `auth-saml/slo-verification-required`. A half-configured pair (key without alg, or alg without key) still fails closed as before. The single-sign-on path (`verifyResponse`) always required a signature and is unaffected.

items.title: SAML SLO parse methods require a verify key by default
items.body: If you call `sp.parseLogoutRequest`, `sp.parseLogoutResponse`, `sp.parseLogoutRequestPost`, or `sp.parseLogoutResponseSoap`, supply `idpVerifyKey` (the IdP's public key) and `idpVerifyAlg` so the inbound message's signature is verified — the recommended configuration. If you intentionally accept unsigned SLO messages (for example an IdP that does not sign them, with integrity provided by another layer), pass `allowUnsigned: true` explicitly on the parse call. A call with neither now throws `auth-saml/slo-verification-required` instead of returning the parsed message.

releases.headline: Token and credential verifiers reject a non-finite expiry and an unknown critical header
releases.summary: A JSON number literal that overflows the double range (for example `1e400`) decodes to Infinity, and the JWT/JOSE, OpenID Connect, OpenID Federation, OpenID4VCI client-attestation, SD-JWT-VC, DPoP, and step-up-grant verifiers gated expiry with a plain numeric type check. Infinity is a number, so an `exp` of that shape passed the check and the `exp < now` comparison was always false: the token or statement never expired. The verifiers now require a finite RFC 7519 NumericDate for `exp` (and for the claims each freshness check reads), so a non-finite value is refused instead of read as never-expiring. The SD-JWT-VC key-binding JWT now refuses an unrecognized `crit` header, matching the issuer credential JWT and the OpenID4VCI proof JWT. `b.auth.dpop.verify` no longer lets a non-finite `now` disable the proof freshness window, and `b.auth.openidFederation.verifyEntityStatement` now applies its documented `now` override.

items.title: A non-finite expiry no longer reads as never-expiring
items.body: `b.auth.jwt.verifyExternal`, `b.auth.oauth` (ID token and client-attestation / attestation-PoP verification), `b.auth.openidFederation.verifyEntityStatement`, `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify`, and `b.auth.stepUp.grant.verify` gated `exp` with a `typeof value === "number"` check. A JSON `1e400` literal decodes to Infinity, which is a number, so the value passed the check and `exp + skew < now` evaluated to false — the token or statement was accepted at any time. Each verifier now requires `exp` (and the timestamp claims its freshness checks read) to be a finite NumericDate and refuses a non-finite value. A well-formed token with a finite `exp` is unaffected.

items.title: SD-JWT-VC key-binding JWT refuses an unrecognized crit header
items.body: `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify` (and `b.auth.oid4vp.verifyResponse`, which composes it) read the key-binding JWT header without checking `crit`. The issuer credential JWT and the OpenID4VCI proof JWT already refuse a JWS that declares an unsupported critical extension (RFC 7515 §4.1.11); the key-binding JWT now does the same, throwing `auth-sd-jwt-vc/unknown-crit`.

items.title: A non-finite now no longer disables the DPoP freshness window
items.body: `b.auth.dpop.verify` accepts a caller-supplied `now`. A non-finite value (for example a NaN produced by upstream date arithmetic) made the `Math.abs(now - iat) > window` comparison false, so a proof of any age passed the `iat` freshness check. `verify` now falls back to the current time when `now` is not a finite number, matching `b.auth.jwt.verifyExternal`.

items.title: b.auth.openidFederation.verifyEntityStatement applies its now override
items.body: The documented `now` option was ignored; the freshness check always read the wall clock. It now uses `now` when supplied (falling back to the current time when it is absent or non-finite), so a statement can be verified as of a specific time.

releases.headline: X.509 chain validation enforces dNSName and iPAddress nameConstraints
releases.summary: A CA certificate can carry basicConstraints nameConstraints (RFC 5280 §4.2.1.10) that restrict the names any certificate below it may bear, but node's X509Certificate does not evaluate them and neither does checkIssued, so a sub-CA restricted to one domain could still vouch for a leaf outside it. The chain-validating consumers now reject such a chain through the new `b.x509Chain.nameConstraintsSatisfied`, which accumulates each CA's permittedSubtrees and excludedSubtrees down the path and checks every certificate's subjectAltName against them.

items.title: b.x509Chain.nameConstraintsSatisfied enforces RFC 5280 name constraints
items.body: `b.x509Chain.nameConstraintsSatisfied(chain)` takes an ordered chain (leaf first, trust anchor last) and returns whether every certificate's subjectAltName satisfies the nameConstraints of the CAs above it. dNSName subtrees use the RFC 5280 add-labels rule (base `example.com` is satisfied by `example.com` and `host.example.com`, not `notexample.com`; a leading-dot base `.example.com` matches subdomains only), and iPAddress subtrees use the address/mask CIDR. Permitted subtrees accumulate as an intersection and excluded subtrees as a union. A malformed nameConstraints or subjectAltName extension, or a constraint of a subtree form this release does not evaluate (directoryName, rfc822Name, URI, otherName), fails closed.

items.title: Certificate chains are rejected when a leaf falls outside a CA's nameConstraints
items.body: basicConstraints nameConstraints (RFC 5280 §4.2.1.10) restrict the subject names a CA may certify below it, but were enforced nowhere: node's `X509Certificate` and `checkIssued` ignore the extension, so an intermediate permitted only `example.com` could issue a leaf with subjectAltName `evil.com` and the chain verified. The chain-validating consumers (`b.tsa.verifyToken`, `b.mdoc`, `b.mail.crypto.smime`, `b.mail.bimi`, `b.auth.fidoMds3`, `b.contentCredentials`) now reject a leaf whose dNSName or iPAddress subjectAltName is outside a CA's permittedSubtrees or inside its excludedSubtrees, with the constraints accumulating down the chain. Constraint and name forms not yet evaluated, and malformed extensions, fail closed rather than being ignored.

releases.headline: X.509 chain validation enforces the basicConstraints pathLenConstraint
releases.summary: node's X509Certificate does not expose a CA certificate's basicConstraints pathLenConstraint, so a certificate chain whose links each verified could still exceed a CA's stated path length: a CA with pathLen:0 vouching for an intermediate that in turn issues the end-entity. The framework's certificate-chain walkers now enforce the constraint through the new `b.x509Chain.pathLenSatisfied`, which reads pathLenConstraint from each certificate's DER and applies the RFC 5280 path-length rule. The token- and message-carried walkers also route through the new `b.x509Chain.resolveChain`, which builds the path by trying every candidate issuer, so a valid path is not rejected when a stricter interchangeable issuer appears first in the certificate bag.

items.title: b.x509Chain.resolveChain builds a certification path with path-length enforcement
items.body: `b.x509Chain.resolveChain(leaf, pool, anchors, opts)` searches for a path from a leaf certificate through a pool of candidate issuers to a trust anchor. Every node passes the caller's `validAt` predicate, every link passes `issued` (default `b.x509Chain.issuerValidlyIssued`), and the assembled path satisfies `pathLenSatisfied`. When one candidate issuer overruns a path-length constraint the search tries the remaining candidates. The result reports `reason` ("anchored", "pathlen", or "untrusted") and the first certificate that failed `validAt`. `maxDepth` caps the path length and `maxVisits` caps the search to bound work on a crafted certificate bag.

items.title: Certificate chains are rejected when they exceed a CA's pathLenConstraint
items.body: A CA certificate's basicConstraints pathLenConstraint (RFC 5280 §4.2.1.9) limits how many intermediate CAs may appear below it in a valid path. node's `X509Certificate` exposes the cA flag but not pathLenConstraint, so `X509Certificate.checkIssued` and the framework's per-link issuer test accepted a chain that violated it, for example a root asserting pathLen:0 that issued an intermediate CA which then issued the end-entity. The chain-validating consumers (`b.tsa.verifyToken`, `b.mdoc`, `b.auth.fidoMds3`, `b.contentCredentials`, `b.mail.bimi`, `b.mail.crypto.smime`) now reject such a chain. The check is the new `b.x509Chain.pathLenSatisfied(chain)`, which reads pathLenConstraint from each certificate's DER and applies the RFC 5280 §6.1.4 path-length rule over the ordered chain; a certificate that asserts no pathLenConstraint imposes no limit, and a chain too short to contain an intermediate is unaffected.

items.title: A valid path is no longer rejected when an interchangeable issuer appears first
items.body: When a timestamp token or mdoc certificate bag carried more than one issuer for a certificate (for example a CA reissued with a different pathLenConstraint), `b.tsa.verifyToken`, `b.mdoc`, `b.mail.bimi`, and `b.mail.crypto.smime` committed to the first matching issuer. A stricter issuer listed before an interchangeable one that would complete a within-limit path caused the token to be rejected. These walkers now build the path through `b.x509Chain.resolveChain`, which tries the alternative issuers.

releases.headline: OCSP evaluation always binds a response to the issuer of the certificate under validation
releases.summary: The RFC 6960 §4.1.1 CertID issuer binding in `b.network.tls.ocsp.evaluate` was enforced only when the caller supplied `issuerCertDer`; without it the response matched on serial number alone. A serial is unique only per issuer, so a signature-valid `good` for one issuer's certificate could be accepted for a different issuer's certificate with a colliding serial. The binding is now mandatory and always checks both the issuer name and key hashes, derived from `issuerCertDer` when given, otherwise from the issuer certificate in `issuerPem`.

items.title: The OCSP CertID issuer binding is mandatory, not opt-in
items.body: `b.network.tls.ocsp.evaluate` ran the RFC 6960 §4.1.1 issuerNameHash/issuerKeyHash binding only when `opts.issuerCertDer` was supplied. Without it, a response was matched to the certificate under validation on serial number alone. Because a serial number is unique only within one issuer, a signature-valid `good` produced for one issuer's certificate could be replayed as proof for a different issuer's certificate that happened to share the serial, for example a responder trusted across several CAs or a shared responder key. Evaluation now always binds the matched response to the issuer and checks both the issuerNameHash and the issuerKeyHash: from `issuerCertDer` when it is given, otherwise from the issuer certificate parsed from `opts.issuerPem`. Checking the name as well as the key is required because two issuers can reuse one public key under different subject names. `b.network.tls.ocsp.fetch` is unaffected because it already derives the issuer certificate from `issuerPem`.

items.title: evaluate and requireGood need the issuer certificate, not a bare public key
items.body: `b.network.tls.ocsp.evaluate` and `requireGood` now bind against the issuer's name and key, so the issuer identity must be available. Pass `opts.issuerCertDer` with the issuing CA certificate, or pass an `opts.issuerPem` that is the issuer certificate rather than a bare public key. A caller that verifies a response signed by a delegated responder must pass `opts.issuerCertDer` with the issuing CA certificate so the binding names the real issuer. A bare-public-key `issuerPem` with no `issuerCertDer` can no longer be bound and is refused; callers that previously relied on serial-only matching are now refused with a wrong-issuer or missing-issuer-identity error.

releases.headline: OCSP evaluation bounds the age of a response that omits nextUpdate and rejects trailing DER bytes
releases.summary: Two hardening fixes in the OCSP response verifier. A response that omits the optional nextUpdate field carried no expiry, so a signature-valid `good` predating a revocation could be replayed indefinitely; evaluation now bounds such a response to a maximum age measured from thisUpdate (default 24 hours, override with maxAgeMs). And the OCSP response decoder ignored bytes appended after the top-level structure; it now rejects trailing data, matching the CMS and timestamp decoders.

items.title: OCSP evaluation bounds the age of a response that omits nextUpdate
items.body: `b.network.tls.ocsp.evaluate` enforced the nextUpdate expiry window only when the response stated one. RFC 6960 §4.2.2.1 allows a responder to omit nextUpdate, and for such a response the verifier checked only that thisUpdate was not in the future, placing no upper bound on how old the response could be. A signature-valid `good` produced before a certificate was revoked could then be replayed forever. Evaluation now refuses a response that omits nextUpdate once thisUpdate is older than a maximum age, 24 hours by default, which a caller can widen or tighten with the new `maxAgeMs` option. A response that states a nextUpdate is unaffected and remains valid for its stated window.

items.title: OCSP response decoding rejects trailing DER bytes
items.body: `b.network.tls.ocsp.parseResponse` and `evaluate` parsed the first top-level DER structure and ignored any bytes after it, so an OCSP response could be padded with arbitrary trailing bytes and still parse. Decoding now requires the DER to be fully consumed and refuses trailing data (`tls/ocsp-trailing-data`), through the same `asn1.readNodeStrict` step used by the CMS and timestamp decoders. The signature covers only tbsResponseData, so trailing bytes forged no status; the padded form is now rejected so it cannot defeat a byte-exact equality or deduplication assumption or a stricter downstream parser.

releases.headline: TSA and CMS verification reject trailing DER bytes, and the timestamp verifier requires the contentType signed attribute
releases.summary: Two hardening fixes in the CMS and RFC 3161 timestamp verification paths. The timestamp verifier accepted a token whose signed attributes omitted the mandatory `contentType` attribute; it now requires it, matching the S/MIME verifier. And the CMS and timestamp DER decoders silently ignored bytes appended after the top-level structure; they now reject trailing data, so a signature or timestamp token cannot be padded.

items.title: Timestamp verification requires the contentType signed attribute
items.body: `b.tsa.verifyToken` refused a signed `contentType` attribute that disagreed with `id-ct-TSTInfo`, but accepted a token whose signed attributes omitted the attribute entirely. RFC 5652 §11.1 makes `contentType` mandatory when signed attributes are present, and the S/MIME verifier already enforced it. `verifyToken` now refuses a token missing the `contentType` attribute with `tsa/no-content-type-attr`. The token stayed bound to the caller's data through the messageImprint and messageDigest checks regardless, so this is a conformance and consistency fix rather than a substitution bypass.

items.title: CMS and timestamp decoders reject trailing DER bytes
items.body: `b.cms.decode` and the timestamp token and response decoders parsed the first top-level DER structure and ignored any bytes after it, so a CMS signature or an RFC 3161 timestamp token could be padded with arbitrary trailing bytes and still parse. The decoders now require the DER to be fully consumed and refuse trailing data (`cms/trailing-data`, `tsa/trailing-data`), through a shared `asn1.readNodeStrict` decode step. The bytes covered by the signature were never affected; the padded form is now rejected so it cannot defeat a byte-exact equality or deduplication assumption or a stricter downstream parser.

releases.headline: `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify` refuses a credential whose `nbf` (not-before) is in the future
releases.summary: `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify` validated a credential's `exp` (expiry) but did not check `nbf` (not-before), so an issuer-signed SD-JWT verifiable credential presented before its activation time verified as valid. It now refuses such a credential with `auth-sd-jwt-vc/not-yet-valid`, matching the not-before check the other token verifiers already apply.

items.title: sdJwtVc.verify enforces the not-before (nbf) claim
items.body: `b.auth.sdJwtVc.verify` checked `iat` (not in the future) and `exp` (not expired) but had no `nbf` (not-before) check, so an issuer-signed credential carrying a future `nbf` verified as valid before its activation time, including when reached through `b.auth.oid4vp` presentation verification. A credential whose `nbf` is more than the clock-skew tolerance in the future is now refused with `auth-sd-jwt-vc/not-yet-valid`, matching the not-before enforcement already in the JWT, external-JWT, and OIDC ID-token verifiers. A credential with no `nbf`, or one within the skew window, is unaffected.

releases.headline: The CSRF and fetch-metadata method exemptions normalize case, and expiry checks fail closed on a non-numeric timestamp
releases.summary: Two request-handling guards accepted malformed or non-canonical input instead of rejecting it. The CSRF and fetch-metadata middleware exempt safe methods by comparing the request method against an upper-cased list without normalizing the request method's case; over HTTP/2, which delivers the method verbatim, a request using a non-canonical case (such as `Post`) skipped the gate. Separately, the session, API-key, break-glass, and cluster leader-lease expiry checks used a NaN-blind numeric comparison, so a non-finite stored value (a missing or non-numeric timestamp from a custom store) read as never-expiring. Both are fixed to normalize and to fail closed.

items.title: CSRF and fetch-metadata method exemptions normalize the request method case
items.body: `b.middleware.csrfProtect` and `b.middleware.fetchMetadata` exempt safe methods from their checks by testing the request method against the configured protected-method list. The list is upper-cased at construction, but the request method was compared without normalizing its case. HTTP/1.1 rejects a non-canonical method case before the handler runs, but HTTP/2 delivers the method verbatim, so a state-changing request using a non-canonical case (for example `Post`) fell outside the protected list and skipped the gate, including the Origin and token / Sec-Fetch checks. The request method is now upper-cased before the exemption test, so a protected method is gated whatever its case; safe methods remain exempt.

items.title: Session, API-key, break-glass, and cluster-lease expiry checks fail closed on a non-finite timestamp
items.body: The session, API-key, break-glass grant, and cluster leader-lease expiry checks compared the stored expiry with `Number(value) < now`. When `Number(value)` is `NaN` (a missing key, or a non-numeric value such as an ISO date string returned by a custom store), the comparison is false, so the record read as not expired. A SQL NULL was already handled (`Number(null)` is 0), so the shipped stores were unaffected, but a custom `b.session.useStore` adapter or store returning a non-numeric expiry disabled expiry enforcement. These checks now treat a non-finite timestamp as already past, so a malformed expiry fails closed.

releases.headline: Object-store keys with a `.` or `..` path segment are refused across every remote backend
releases.summary: An object key containing a `.` or `..` path segment could resolve outside the configured bucket or container. Each backend percent-encoded the key per `/`-separated segment, joined the segments into a URL path, and parsed the result as a URL, and URL parsing collapses `.`/`..` dot segments. In path-style S3 addressing a key such as `../../other-bucket/object` reached a different bucket on the same endpoint, with a valid signature; virtual-hosted addressing rewrote the delivered key. Such keys are now refused across the SigV4, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob backends, matching the filesystem and generic-HTTP backends. Three presigned-URL correctness fixes ship alongside.

items.title: Object keys that would escape the bucket or container are refused
items.body: The object-store backends built the request path by percent-encoding each `/`-separated key segment and joining them, then parsing the result as a URL. A `.` or `..` segment survived the encoding and was then collapsed by the URL parser, so a key such as `../../other-bucket/object` resolved above the configured bucket: path-style S3 reached a different bucket on the same endpoint, and virtual-hosted addressing rewrote the delivered key. Because the request signature was computed over the already-resolved path, the server honored it rather than rejecting it. The SigV4, GCS, and Azure Blob object and presigned-URL paths, and the S3 object-lock retention and legal-hold operations, now refuse a key with a `.` or `..` path segment (or a null byte) with `objectstore/invalid-key`, the contract the filesystem and generic-HTTP backends already enforced. Keys with a dot inside a segment (`report.v2/data..bak`) are unaffected.

items.title: Presigned URLs and upload policies refuse a contentType with CR, LF, or NUL
items.body: A presigned URL or upload policy folds the caller-supplied `contentType` into the request signature and hands it back in the header map or form fields the caller is told to send. A CR, LF, or NUL in that value is a header-injection vector at that boundary and desyncs the sent value from the signed one. `presignedUploadUrl`, `presignedDownloadUrl`, and `presignedUploadPolicy` on the SigV4, GCS, and Azure Blob backends now refuse such a `contentType` with `objectstore/invalid-content-type`, matching the refusal already applied to presigned response-header overrides.

items.title: SigV4 wire query encoding matches the signature for `*` and `~`
items.body: The query sent on a SigV4 request encoded `*` and `~` differently from the canonical form the signature was computed over: `*` was left bare instead of `%2A`, and `~` was `%7E` instead of bare. A request whose query carried either character (a `list` prefix, a presigned response-header override) was rejected by the server with a signature mismatch. The wire query is now aligned to the canonical encoding on those characters, so the requests are accepted; a bare subresource token such as `?uploads` is unchanged.

items.title: Presigned-URL expiry refuses non-integer and non-finite values
items.body: `expiresIn` is bounded to 1 through 604800 seconds, but `NaN` passed the numeric bound (both comparisons are false) and a fractional value produced a fractional `X-Amz-Expires`. `expiresIn` must now be an integer within the range; `NaN`, `Infinity`, and fractional values are refused with `objectstore/invalid-expires`.

releases.headline: `safeSql.quoteIdentifier` doubles its quote character, and CORS refuses a stateful (g/y-flagged) RegExp origin
releases.summary: Two public security primitives had input-handling correctness gaps. `b.safeSql.quoteIdentifier` wrapped a name in quotes without doubling the quote character inside it, so a caller that admitted a quote through a custom validation pattern could break out of the quoting. `b.middleware.cors` accepted a RegExp origin carrying the global (g) or sticky (y) flag, which makes `.test()` stateful across requests and origin matching unreliable. Both are fixed.

items.title: safeSql.quoteIdentifier doubles the dialect quote character
items.body: `b.safeSql.quoteIdentifier` validated a name and then wrapped it in double quotes (SQLite/Postgres) or backticks (MySQL) verbatim, without doubling any occurrence of that quote character inside the name, as standard SQL identifier quoting requires. The default identifier shape excludes quote characters, so the built-in query builder (`b.sql`, `b.db`) was never exposed; but a caller passing a custom `opts.pattern` that admits a `"` or backtick could produce a quoted identifier that breaks out of the quotes. `quoteIdentifier` now doubles the dialect quote character inside the name (`"`→`""`, backtick→doubled backtick), so it quotes safely regardless of the pattern that admitted the name. `b.safeSql.quoteQualified` and `b.safeSql.quoteList` delegate to it and are covered.

items.title: CORS refuses a global- or sticky-flagged RegExp origin
items.body: `b.middleware.cors` matched a RegExp origin entry with `pattern.test(origin)`. A pattern carrying the global (`g`) or sticky (`y`) flag makes `.test()` stateful (it advances `lastIndex` between calls), so the same origin can match on one request and not the next, making a credentialed CORS decision unreliable. `cors` now refuses such a pattern at construction with `cors/stateful-pattern`; an unflagged RegExp origin is unchanged.

releases.headline: WebSocket bounds the number of fragments in a message and rejects RSV1 on control frames
releases.summary: A WebSocket message was reassembled under a byte cap applied to the running total, but a continuation frame with an empty payload never advances that total. A peer that opened a fragmented message and then streamed empty continuation frames without setting the final bit grew the buffered-fragment array without bound, exhausting memory. Both the server and the client now cap the fragment count per message in addition to the byte total. The server also rejects a control frame that sets the RSV1 bit, per RFC 7692 §6.1.

items.title: WebSocket caps a message's fragment count, not only its byte size
items.body: `b.websocket` reassembled a fragmented message under the `maxMessageBytes` cap applied to the running byte total. A continuation frame carrying an empty payload does not advance that total, so a peer that opened a fragmented message and then streamed empty (or one-byte) continuation frames without ever setting the FIN bit grew the array of buffered fragments without bound, exhausting process memory (CWE-770). The heartbeat does not intervene because the attacker interleaves valid PONG frames. The server (`b.websocket`) and the WebSocket client (`b.wsClient`) now cap the number of fragments per message in addition to the byte total. The server refuses an over-cap message with a 1009 close; the client raises a message-too-big error and closes the connection, the same way it already handles a message that exceeds `maxMessageBytes`. The cap defaults to a generous ceiling (derived from `maxMessageBytes`, with a floor that keeps finely-fragmented small messages valid) and is configurable through the `maxFragments` option. A message split into a reasonable number of fragments is unaffected.

items.title: WebSocket rejects the RSV1 bit on a control frame
items.body: RFC 7692 §6.1 forbids the RSV1 (per-message-deflate) bit on a control frame, even when permessage-deflate is negotiated for the connection. The server accepted a PING, PONG, or CLOSE frame that set RSV1; it now fails the connection with a protocol-error close (1002). Control-frame payloads were never routed through decompression, so this is a conformance fix with no exploit path.

releases.headline: IMAP accepts a quoted mailbox name that contains an escaped double quote
releases.summary: RFC 3501 §4.3 carries a double quote inside a quoted string as `\"`. The IMAP commands that split a leading mailbox name from the arguments after it matched the name with a class that stopped at the first quote, so a mailbox name holding both a space and a double quote was rejected with BAD even though it is a valid name. The name is now read across the escape and passed to the mail store intact.

items.title: IMAP reads a quoted mailbox name across an escaped quote
items.body: STATUS, GETMETADATA, SETMETADATA, APPEND, APPEND CATENATE, and SELECT with QRESYNC each split a leading mailbox name from the arguments that follow it. The name was matched with a quoted-string class that stopped at the first double quote, so an RFC 3501 §4.3 escaped quote (`\"`) inside the name ended the match early; with the rest of the command still to match, the command was rejected with BAD. A mailbox name that contains both a space and a double quote, such as the wire form `"a\"b c"` for the name `a"b c`, is a name `b.mail.server.imap` already accepts, so a conformant client could neither query nor append to it. The six commands now read the quoted name across the escape and hand the mail store the decoded name; a name without a space was already carried whole by the atom form, so only spaced quoted names change. GETMETADATA's untagged METADATA response also serializes the mailbox name as a quoted string, matching STATUS, so a name that carries a space or a quote stays parseable in the reply.

releases.headline: Sieve removes the leading dot from a text: block's first line, and ManageSieve refuses control bytes inside quoted script names
releases.summary: Two mail-scripting parsers mis-read hostile input. `b.safeSieve` removed RFC 5228 §2.4.2 dot-stuffing from every body line of a `text:` multi-line string except the first, so a first line beginning with a doubled dot kept its extra dot and the decoded script diverged from what a conformant Sieve engine executes. And `b.guardManageSieveCommand` skipped its control-byte screen inside a quoted string, so a control byte (ESC, DEL, or a C0) in a quoted script name passed on the wire, unlike the IMAP, POP3, and SMTP command guards. Both are fixed: the first `text:` body line is de-stuffed on the same rule as the rest, and a control byte anywhere on a ManageSieve command line, quoted or not, is refused.

items.title: ManageSieve refuses control bytes inside a quoted script name
items.body: `b.guardManageSieveCommand.validate` scans a command line for forbidden control bytes but skipped the scan inside a quoted string, so an ESC, DEL, or other C0 control byte in a quoted script name (for GETSCRIPT, PUTSCRIPT, RENAMESCRIPT, SETACTIVE, or DELETESCRIPT) passed the guard. The IMAP, POP3, and SMTP command guards scan the whole line and refuse such bytes; ManageSieve was the outlier. An accepted control byte reached the operator's storage-backend key, the audit metadata, and the byte-for-byte LISTSCRIPTS echo, where an ESC is a terminal or log escape-sequence injection (CWE-117 / CWE-150). The guard now refuses a control byte anywhere on the line, whether inside a quoted string or not.

items.title: Sieve text: dot-stuffing is removed from the first body line too
items.body: RFC 5228 §2.4.2 requires a Sieve `text:` multi-line string to have the extra leading period removed from every body line that begins with two periods, including the first. `b.safeSieve.parse` removed it only from the second line onward, so a first body line such as `..Junk` decoded to `..Junk` instead of `.Junk`, and the decoded string, which drives `fileinto` folders, `redirect` addresses, and match keys, differed from what a deployed Sieve engine such as Dovecot or Cyrus runs. The first body line is now de-stuffed on the same rule as the rest; a single leading period is still preserved.

releases.headline: IMAP un-escapes a quoted mailbox name, so a name containing a backslash or quote is not corrupted
releases.summary: `b.mail.server.imap` parsed a quoted mailbox name (and other quoted arguments) by stripping the surrounding double quotes but never reversing the RFC 3501 §4.3 backslash escaping the client applied. A name containing a backslash arrived at the mailStore with the backslash doubled, and a name containing a double quote arrived with its escaping backslash still attached, so SELECT, STATUS, APPEND, and the metadata commands operated on a different name than the client sent. The parser now un-escapes a backslash-escaped character, so the mailStore receives the name the client meant.

items.title: IMAP quoted mailbox names are un-escaped per RFC 3501 §4.3
items.body: An IMAP quoted-string escapes a `"` or `\` in its content with a backslash (RFC 3501 §4.3). `b.mail.server.imap` removed the surrounding quotes but left the escaping in place, so a mailbox name such as `a\b` reached the mailStore as `a\\b` and `a"b` reached it with the backslash still on the quote.
