SELECT, STATUS, APPEND, CATENATE, and GETMETADATA/SETMETADATA therefore keyed, created, or applied ACLs to a name that differed from the one the client sent. The parser now reverses the escaping, delivering the name the client intended. A mailbox name that embeds a literal double quote is still refused by the verbs that extract it with a plain quoted-string pattern; those names, which are unusual, are a separate conformance follow-up.

releases.headline: POP3 RETR and TOP dot-stuff a stored body against the CRLF endings a client parses
releases.summary: `b.mail.server.pop3` built its `RETR` and `TOP` multiline responses by dot-stuffing the stored message bytes with `b.safeSmtp.dotStuff`, which doubles a line-initial `.` only where the preceding line ended in a canonical CRLF. A message stored with bare-LF or bare-CR line endings, the form a Maildir or mbox maildrop keeps, therefore emitted any line consisting of a single `.` un-stuffed. A client that treats a bare LF or CR as a line boundary reads that `.` as the end of the message and the bytes after it as unrequested response lines, truncating the message and letting a sender who mails such a body smuggle content into the client stream. `RETR` and `TOP` now canonicalize the body to CRLF before dot-stuffing through the new `b.safeSmtp.dotStuffForWire`, so every line ending is CRLF and every line-initial `.` is doubled.

items.title: POP3 RETR/TOP dot-stuff a stored body against the line endings a client parses
items.body: A POP3 server transmits a message as CRLF-terminated lines and byte-stuffs any line beginning with the termination octet `.` (RFC 1939 §3). `b.mail.server.pop3` dot-stuffed the stored bytes with `b.safeSmtp.dotStuff`, which stuffs a line-initial `.` only where the preceding line ended in a canonical CRLF. A body stored with bare-LF or bare-CR line endings, the common Maildir and mbox form, left a line consisting of a lone `.` un-stuffed, so the RETR or TOP response carried a `.` line at a non-canonical boundary. A client that splits lines on a bare LF or CR, as several do for historical POP3 and mbox compatibility, reads that line as the end-of-message terminator: it truncates the message and parses everything the server sends after it as further response lines. This is the retrieval-side analog of the SMTP DATA-body smuggling refused in 0.20.8. RETR and TOP now canonicalize the body to CRLF before dot-stuffing, so the response is well-formed and every line-initial `.` is doubled. STAT, LIST, and RETR report the canonical wire octet count the `mailStore` provides for a message, and RETR delivers a body of exactly that size, so the advertised sizes are consistent across the three commands; a backend that stores messages with bare-LF endings reports the CRLF size, not the stored byte length.

items.title: `b.safeSmtp.dotStuffForWire` canonicalizes line endings before dot-stuffing
items.body: `b.safeSmtp.dotStuffForWire(buf)` canonicalizes every line ending in a message body to CRLF and then applies RFC 5321 §4.5.2 / RFC 1939 §3 dot-stuffing. `b.safeSmtp.dotStuff` on its own stuffs a line-initial `.` only at a canonical CRLF boundary and documents that its caller must canonicalize or refuse bare-LF first; this primitive composes that canonicalization with the stuffing, for a caller serving a stored body over the wire such as a POP3 RETR or TOP response.

items.title: `b.safeSmtp.canonicalizeEol` rewrites line endings to CRLF
items.body: `b.safeSmtp.canonicalizeEol(buf)` rewrites every line ending in a buffer to canonical CRLF: a bare LF and a bare CR each become CRLF, an existing CRLF is unchanged. It brings a stored message body to the wire form a POP3 or SMTP multiline response requires before dot-stuffing, and gives the octet count the peer receives.

releases.headline: The SMTP DATA-body smuggling check covers every non-canonical dot-terminator
releases.summary:
`b.guardSmtpCommand.detectBodySmuggling`, which the MX and submission listeners run on every DATA chunk and BDAT body, refused a `.`-alone-line terminated by `
.
`, `
.
`, `
.
`, or `.`, but let three more slip through: `.
`, `
.`, and `
.`. The last is the `<CR><LF>.<CR>` shape Exim accepted in the CVE-2023-51766 disclosure, so a hostile sender could still terminate a message in a way a lenient downstream relay reads as end-of-data and smuggle a second message after it. The check now refuses any `.`-alone-line whose surrounding line endings are not both canonical CRLF, matched across chunk boundaries, while still passing a lone bare LF or CR that is not such a terminator so a binary BDAT body is not refused for its content.

items.title: SMTP DATA-body smuggling detection covers every non-canonical dot-terminator
items.body:
SMTP smuggling (CVE-2023-51764 / -51765 / -51766) terminates a message with a `.` on a line whose line endings are not the canonical `
.
`, so a downstream relay that accepts the non-canonical form as end-of-data resumes parsing the next bytes as a second, unauthorized message. `b.guardSmtpCommand.detectBodySmuggling`, run by `b.mail.server.mx` and `b.mail.server.submission` on every DATA chunk and BDAT body, enumerated only four of the seven shapes and missed `.
`, `
.`, and `
.` (the `<CR><LF>.<CR>` form named in the CVE-2023-51766 Exim disclosure). It now refuses a `.`-alone-line whenever the line ending before or after the dot is a bare LF or bare CR rather than a canonical CRLF, deciding the same verdict whether the terminator arrives whole or split across two DATA chunks. A lone bare LF or CR that does not form such a dot-terminator is still accepted, so a binary BDAT body is not refused for carrying those bytes.

items.title: `b.guardTemplate` documents that it does not screen Pug source-code lines
items.body: `b.guardTemplate` refuses delimited template markers, including Pug `#{...}` / `!{...}` interpolation. Its docblock now records the boundary of that screen: an indentation-based engine (Pug, HAML) also compiles a buffered `=` / `!=` line, an unbuffered `-` line, a control keyword, an attribute expression, and a mixin call as code, and that code is un-delimited and syntactically indistinguishable from ordinary prose (a domain, a Markdown link, an `x = y` assignment), so a marker scan cannot flag it without refusing that prose. Untrusted input must therefore never be compiled as a Pug or HAML template, whatever this guard reports.

releases.headline: `b.guardGraphql` measures query depth across resolved fragment spreads
releases.summary: The GraphQL depth cap counted the selection-set nesting within each query definition in isolation, but the executor resolves `...fragment` spreads before it runs the query. A shallow operation whose fragment chain resolves deep passed the guard and reached the executor at its true depth. `b.guardGraphql` now resolves fragment spreads and inline fragments before measuring depth, so the cap sees the depth the executor will, and refuses a fragment spread that resolves back to itself as unbounded depth. Upgrading requires no code change; a query that amplifies its depth through fragments is now refused at the same cap as its inlined equivalent.

items.title: Depth cap resolves fragment spreads
items.body: The depth cap counted the selection-set nesting within each operation and fragment definition separately, so a fragment chain (an operation spreading `f1`, which spreads `f2`, ending in a deeply-nested fragment) reached an effective resolved depth far past `maxDepth` while no single definition nested past a few levels. The guard now walks the operation expanding each `...fragment` spread at its site and merging inline fragments, so the measured depth is the depth the executor resolves, and refuses it as `graphql.depth-exceeded` exactly as it already refused the inline-equivalent query. A fragment spread that resolves back to itself has unbounded resolved depth and is refused rather than passed to a resolver that would loop on it. The walker is iterative, so a deeply-nested query within the byte cap yields a depth finding rather than exhausting the call stack.

items.title: Alias-bomb count is the distinct aliases in one selection set
items.body: The alias-bomb cap counted every colon following an identifier, which included field-argument colons (`field(after: $x)`) and repeated alias names, so a field-argument-heavy selection set could be refused though it declares few aliases. The count is now the distinct alias names in a selection set, skipping arguments, and aliases in separate selection sets or in mutually-exclusive inline-fragment type conditions are not summed, which stops the over-refusal of argument-heavy and polymorphic queries while still refusing a genuine alias bomb concentrated in one selection set.

releases.headline: `b.guardJwt` refuses a JWT that repeats a header parameter or a claim
releases.summary: A JWT header and claims set are JSON, where a repeated member name is kept last by `JSON.parse` and read first by some verifiers, so a token with two `alg` values reads as one algorithm to the guard and another to a first-wins verifier, the algorithm-confusion smuggling shape. `b.guardJson` already refuses duplicate keys; `b.guardJwt` now refuses a JWT whose decoded header or payload repeats a member, reusing the same detector, exposed as `b.guardJson.detectDuplicateKeys`. Upgrading requires no code change; a token carrying a duplicate header parameter or claim is now refused at every profile.

items.title: `b.guardJwt` refuses a duplicate JOSE header parameter or claim
items.body: RFC 7515 §4 and RFC 7519 §4 require the member names of the JOSE header and the JWT claims set to be unique, but a JWT is accepted by many verifiers when they are not, and JSON readers disagree on which value wins: `JSON.parse` keeps the last, some streaming readers keep the first. A token whose header is `{"alg":"none","alg":"ES256"}` therefore reads as `ES256` (signature required) to a last-wins verifier and as `none` (no signature) to a first-wins one, the algorithm-confusion smuggling shape behind the `alg=none` CVE family. The guard decodes the header and payload and refuses a token that repeats any member name at one object level, with `jwt.duplicate-key`, at every profile. The detection is `b.guardJson`'s existing duplicate-key scan, so an escaped-equivalent key (`"alg"` and `"\u0061lg"`) collapses and is caught the same way the guard already catches an escaped `alg=none`.

items.title: `b.guardJson.detectDuplicateKeys`
items.body: `detectDuplicateKeys(jsonText)` returns the key names a JSON source string repeats at the same object nesting level, reading only key positions so a repeated key inside a string value is not counted. It is the scan behind `b.guardJson`'s `duplicate-key` finding, exposed so a sibling guard whose payload is JSON, such as `b.guardJwt`'s JOSE header and claims, refuses the same smuggling shape rather than reimplementing it.

releases.headline: `b.guardSql` reads a comment as a separator, so one placed before a dangerous function name no longer hides it
releases.summary: The raw-SQL guard's normalizer removed a comment by joining the text on either side of it into one token when both sides were identifier characters, modeling a claim that `LOAD/**/_FILE` reads as `LOAD_FILE`. A real engine does the opposite: a comment is whitespace, a token separator, so MySQL rejects `LOAD/**/_FILE` and reads `SELECT/**/LOAD_FILE(...)` as a call to `LOAD_FILE`. The guard's join turned `SELECT/**/LOAD_FILE` into the single token `SELECTLOAD_FILE`, and the `LOAD_FILE` the engine runs was hidden from the dangerous-function detector; the same shape hid `pg_read_file` from Postgres. A comment is now a separator everywhere, matching every engine and refusing what any of them would run. Upgrading requires no code change; a raw SQL fragment or statement that reached a dangerous built-in past a comment is now refused.

items.title: `b.guardSql` treats a comment as a token separator, not a joiner
items.body: The normalizer, which strips comments before the keyword detectors run, removed a `/* */`, `--` or `#` comment by concatenating the surrounding text when the characters on both sides were identifier characters. This modeled a comment as fusing two identifier fragments into one token, but no engine does that: a comment is whitespace. MySQL rejects `SELECT LOAD/**/_FILE('/x')` (it reads `LOAD` then `_FILE`, not `LOAD_FILE`) and accepts `SELECT/**/LOAD_FILE('/x')` (it reads `SELECT` then `LOAD_FILE`); both MySQL and Postgres PREPARE `SELECT/**/LOAD_FILE(...)` and `SELECT/**/pg_read_file(...)` as live calls to those file-reading built-ins. The guard's join produced `SELECTLOAD_FILE` from the first, so the `LOAD_FILE`/`pg_read_file` the engine runs was buried inside a longer token and no dangerous-function finding fired, at every profile. The normalizer now replaces every comment with a single space, so a dangerous function name preceded or abutted by a comment is read as its own token and refused; a comment placed inside what would be an identifier (`LOAD/**/_FILE`) is now two tokens, as every engine reads it, rather than being fused into a keyword the engine never sees. Verified against live MySQL 8.4 and Postgres 18 (statements PREPAREd non-executing): every comment-placed call to a dangerous built-in the engines accept is now refused.

releases.headline: `b.guardYaml` resolves a tag the way a parser does before it judges it
releases.summary: A YAML tag shorthand's suffix is percent-encoded, and a parser decodes it once before it resolves the tag: `!!%70ython/object/apply:os.system` is the PyYAML deserialization tag, and `!<tag:yaml.org,2002:python/object/apply:os.system>` is the same tag written out. The guard compared the raw source text against `!!python/`, and its scanner required a letter after the `!!`, so an escaped suffix and the verbatim form both passed strict validation with no finding and the gate served them. The guard now reads the tag as a parser resolves it, and the same escape no longer slips past the source-level tag ban in `b.parse`. Upgrading requires no code change.

items.title: `b.guardYaml` judges a tag by the name a parser resolves it to
items.body:
The deserialization-tag denylist (`!!python/`, `!!java.`, `!!ruby/`, `!!perl/`, `!!js/`, `!!cs/`, `!!net/`, `!!system.`, and the `!!apply` / `!!new` / `!!eval` / `!!exec` family) matched the raw `!!` shorthand, and the tag scanner recognized a tag only when an ASCII letter followed the `!!`. A tag suffix is percent-encoded for characters outside the URI set, and js-yaml, PyYAML and the `yaml` package all decode it once before resolving the tag, so `!!%70ython/object/apply:os.system` (with `%70` for `p`), `!!%65val`, `!!%6e%65w` and the verbatim `!<tag:yaml.org,2002:python/object/apply:os.system>` each resolve to a tag the guard means to refuse, yet each validated clean and was served at every profile.

The guard now reads the whole tag token, including a percent-escaped or verbatim form, decodes the suffix once as a parser does, and matches the resolved name against the denylist; a decoded deserialization tag is refused at every profile, and a percent-escaped tag that resolves to any other name is the custom-tag finding it would be if written plainly. A differential against js-yaml and the `yaml` package over 60,000 documents finds no tag that resolves to a denylisted family and validates clean.

items.title: `b.parse` refuses a percent-escaped tag as it refuses a plain one
items.body: The source-level YAML parser refuses a document that carries a tag, because a tag directs a downstream parser to construct a typed value. It recognized a tag only when a letter or `<` followed the handle, so `!!%73tr` passed where `!!str` was refused. It now recognizes a percent-escaped suffix as a tag, so the two are refused alike.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.7.45
items.body: The vendored bundle rises from 0.7.42 to 0.7.45. `pki.jose.verify` refuses, with `jose/private-key-material`, a JWS whose protected header embeds a JWK carrying any private member (`d`, the RSA CRT parameters, the symmetric `k`, or an AKP `priv`) before the signature is checked. `pki.cmp.build` fills an omitted header `transactionID` or `senderNonce` with sixteen random bytes, fills an omitted `sender` under signature protection with the signer certificate's subject (RFC 9483), binds a KEM-protected message's derivation to the filled `transactionID`, and refuses a `senderNonce` shorter than 128 bits; `pki.scep.build` refuses a `transactionId` carrying a character outside the RFC 8894 PrintableString set with `scep/bad-input`. The package continues to declare no dependencies and no install, prepare or prepublish scripts.

releases.headline: `b.guardCsv` reads a document under every delimiter a consumer might use, and its sanitize disarms or refuses
releases.summary: The CSV guard split cells on every delimiter it knows at once, while a consumer reads with one, so a formula cell that a comma reader or a tab reader sees could sit inside a cell the guard read as quoted. Each candidate delimiter is now its own reading and every finding any reading produces is reported. `sanitize()` never disarmed a formula cell and returned one the operator had set to refuse; it now disarms under a prefixing policy and refuses under `reject` and for a denylisted function. The profiles' default mitigation moves from a TAB prefix to the single-quote prefix, which holds under every delimiter reading. Upgrading requires no code change; a CSV emitted through the guard carries `'` where it carried a TAB in front of a formula-shaped cell, and `prefix-tab` remains selectable for tab-separated output.

items.title: `b.guardCsv` reads a document under each delimiter separately
items.body:
The cell walk treated `,`, `;`, TAB and `|` as delimiters at the same time. A consumer reads with one of them, and the two structures differ around quotes: to a comma reader `a;"x` followed by a newline and `""=1` is text, a record end, and then an empty quoted section with `=1` after it, which every RFC 4180 reader including `b.csv.parse` yields as the cell `=1`, a live formula. The guard split at the `;`, read the quote as opening a quoted cell, and carried that cell across the newline, so the formula rule never saw the cell and strict validation reported nothing. The same shape hid from the guard behind a TAB or a `|` a comma reader does not split on, and behind a comma a tab reader does not.

The guard now walks the document once per candidate delimiter (`,`, `;`, TAB, `|`, and the operator's own) and reports what any reading finds: a formula cell, a denylisted function, and the residual check that decides whether a sanitized document can be served. One cell is one finding however many readings expose it.

items.title: `b.guardCsv.sanitize` disarms a formula cell or refuses it
items.body:
`sanitize()` stripped characters and returned the document, so a formula cell came back as written, under `formulaInjectionPolicy: "reject"` too, and a denylisted `=WEBSERVICE(...)` came back as written at every profile, while the function's own documentation promised it never returns a class the operator asked it to refuse. It now refuses a formula cell under `reject`, a denylisted function, and mixed line endings under `dialectPolicy: "strict"`, each with the finding's rule id. Under a prefixing policy it disarms a formula cell the way the gate does: the document is re-parsed, re-serialized with the prefix inside a quoted field, and read again under every delimiter; a cell that is still a formula under one of those readings is refused rather than served. The gate serves what `sanitize` returns.

The mitigated form of a denylisted function is still the denylisted function. `"'=WEBSERVICE(...)"` and, under `prefix-tab`, `"<TAB>=WEBSERVICE(...)"` validated clean; Excel drops the leading apostrophe when it saves and re-opens the file, and the gate refuses a denylisted call even prefixed. The denylist walk reads through the guard's own prefixes now, in either order with the leading whitespace it also reads through.

items.title: A denylisted call anywhere in a formula cell is refused
items.body:
The denylist read the one word after the trigger, so `=SUM(HYPERLINK(A1))`, `=1+WEBSERVICE("http://x/")`, `=(WEBSERVICE(...))`, `="x"&WEBSERVICE(...)` and `= WEBSERVICE(...)` validated with only the formula finding, which a prefixing policy sanitizes rather than refuses, and `sanitize()` served them prefixed. The walk now reads the whole cell as the consumer decodes it under each delimiter reading, including the text after a closing quote and, under `quote: "'"`, the guard's own prefix written as a doubled quote, and reports the first denylisted call it finds anywhere in the cell, outside a string, a quoted sheet name or a structured reference. A call under Excel's `_xlfn.` or `_xlws.` namespace names the same function (`=_xlfn.WEBSERVICE(...)` is `WEBSERVICE`), and a tab or a line break between a name and its parenthesis is read as the space it is. A name that begins after a digit or a letter is still read as a call: no evaluator runs `=1HYPERLINK(...)`, and refusing it costs no formula that runs.

Under `formulaInjectionPolicy: "allowlist"`, a formula cell that only another delimiter's reading exposes cannot be re-serialized away, and the residual check exempted such a cell on its leading call alone, so `safe;=SUM(FOO(A1))` was served to a semicolon reader with only `SUM` allowlisted. The residual is now served only when every call in it is allowlisted, the rule `escapeCell` already applied to the cells it can rewrite.

items.title: `POSITIVE_NUMBER_OPTS` on every guard, and `positiveNumberOpts` on `b.gateContract.defineGuard` and `resolveProfileAndPosture`
items.body: A guard's ratio and threshold options are declared the way its integer caps are declared in `INT_OPTS`. The resolver holds each one to a positive finite number, with fractions allowed, and exempts it from the integer checks. `b.guardCsv` and `b.guardText` declare `sanitizeAmplificationCap`; `b.guardDomain` declares `dgaEntropyThreshold`. A guard built by `defineGuard` that names a `sanitizeAmplificationCap` field declares it without being asked.

items.title: `b.guardCsv.sanitize` re-parses a document under the guard's own caps
items.body: The disarm step re-parses through `b.csv.parse`, whose defaults (16 MiB of input, 1 MiB per field) are not the guard's (`maxTotalBytes` 1 GiB, `maxCellBytes` 64 KiB), so an export within the guard's limits failed with the parser's `csv/too-large` when, and only when, a formula cell required mitigation. The parser now runs under `maxTotalBytes`, `maxRows` and `maxCellBytes`, a cap it hits is reported as the guard's own `csv.total-too-large`, `csv.too-many-rows` or `csv.cell-too-large`, and a document the emitted dialect cannot parse is refused as `csv.formula-injection` rather than surfacing another module's error.

items.title: A line break inside a quoted cell is content, for the dialect rule and for the trailing-whitespace trim
items.body: `dialect-mixed-line-endings` counted every CR and LF in the text, so a CRLF document carrying a multi-line quoted cell, which `b.csv.parse` reads as one record, was refused as a mixed dialect; `b.guardCsv.detect` reported the same document as `mixed`. Both read record ends under the configured delimiter and quote now: a line break inside a quoted cell is content, and a quote in the middle of an unquoted cell is text, so the line break after it is still a record end. `trailingWhitespacePolicy: "trim"` split the text on LF alone, so on a CRLF document, the guard's own default line ending, the CR was the last character of every line and nothing was trimmed, while inside a quoted multi-line cell the content was trimmed and the junk after its closing quote was kept. The trim now strips the horizontal whitespace at the end of each record, under CRLF, LF or CR, and leaves the inside of a quoted cell alone.

items.title: `b.guardCsv.serialize` resolves its options once per document
items.body: Every cell merged the guard's defaults into a fresh options object before it was escaped. A 17 MiB export of three million cells spent 20 seconds in that merge; it now serializes in under one.

items.title: A ratio or threshold option refuses a value it cannot compare against
items.body: `sanitizeAmplificationCap` on `b.guardCsv` and `b.guardText` and `dgaEntropyThreshold` on `b.guardDomain` accepted `Infinity`, `NaN`, a string, a negative number and zero. Each comparison against such a value is false, so an infinite cap removed the limit and a `NaN` threshold switched the DGA heuristic off while the option stayed set. Each now throws the guard's `bad-opt` error at the call that sets it. The integer caps already refused these shapes, and the check that did so was derived from the shape of an option's default, which is why a fractional default was never checked and a whole-number default would have refused the fraction a ratio takes.

items.title: The profiles' formula mitigation is `prefix-quote`
items.body:
`strict`, `balanced` and `permissive` prefixed a formula-shaped cell with a TAB inside the quoted field. A TAB is the delimiter of a tab-separated reader, and such a reader of a comma document with more than one column takes the quote and comma before the TAB as text and splits at the TAB: `b.csv.parse` with `delimiter: "\t"` reads `"alice","<TAB>=cmd|x"` as the cells `alice,"` and `=cmd|x"`, a live formula. The single-quote prefix holds under every delimiter reading and is the mitigation OWASP lists first. OWASP also notes that Excel drops it when it saves and re-opens the file, so the TAB prefix remains selectable as `formulaInjectionPolicy: "prefix-tab"` for tab-separated output, where it holds. A document sanitized under `prefix-tab` that a tab-separated reading would still evaluate is refused rather than served as disarmed.

`|` is no longer a formula trigger: no spreadsheet evaluator opens a formula on it and it is on no published list, so a cell such as `|x` is emitted as it is and is not a finding. A leading TAB, CR or LF is read through to the character after it, as an importer that trims leading whitespace evaluates what follows: `<TAB>=cmd` is a formula and `<TAB>hello` is text, which also stops a tab-separated file whose first cell is an empty quoted section from being refused under the comma reading. Text after a closing quote is read as part of the cell, as the parsers read it.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.7.42
items.body: The vendored bundle rises from 0.7.39 to 0.7.42. `pki.smime.sign` refuses, with `smime/bad-signer-certificate`, a signer certificate whose `keyUsage` asserts neither `digitalSignature` nor `nonRepudiation` or whose `extendedKeyUsage` carries neither `emailProtection` nor `anyExtendedKeyUsage` (RFC 8550 sections 4.4.2 and 4.4.4); a certificate carrying neither extension still signs, as does a key-only signer. `pki.est.serverkeygen` proves a server-generated private key is the private half of the certificate it binds it to with the key itself and refuses a mismatch with `est/key-cert-mismatch`; `pki.crmf.build` proves the key enclosed in an `encryptedKey` proof of possession the same way and refuses with `crmf/bad-popo` a key that only states the template's public components. `pki.pkcs12.build` refuses a `{ key, cert }` pair whose key is not the private half of the certificate's public key, and a key bag and a certificate bag sharing a `localKeyId` whose key is not that certificate's, across every safe of the store, proving the pair with the private material rather than the public components a private key carries about itself; a store carrying one `localKeyId` on two key bags, more than 1024 certificate bags under one key, or more than 1024 safes is refused. A finite-field Diffie-Hellman key pair is proven by the public value its exponent generates in either encoding (PKCS #3 or X9.42), held to a 4096-bit group whose modulus and stated order are prime, and a store links at most 8 such pairs. The package continues to declare no dependencies and no install, prepare or prepublish scripts.

items.title: `b.guardCsv`'s `sanitizeAmplificationCap` is measured on the served output and defaults to 4
items.body: The cap was measured on the character-stripped text before the formula re-serialization, so an operator's cap did not bound the one transform that grows a document. It is measured on what `sanitize()` returns now. The re-serialization quotes every cell, which grows a document of one-character cells 2.25x and one of blank rows 3.25x, so the default moves from 1.5 to 4; a document that grows past the cap is refused with `csv/sanitize-amplified`, and the gate refuses rather than serves it. An operator who set the cap below 2 will see short-celled documents with a formula cell refused where they were served.

releases.headline: Every review marker states its whole reason, and the vendored PKI bundle moves to 0.7.39
releases.summary: A comment sweep in 0.19.0 removed the line before or after eighteen `allow:` review markers and five `drop-silent` statements, leaving each a half-sentence in shipped source. All twenty-three are whole sentences again, the comment gate now fails a block that ends on a comma or a semicolon, opens a parenthesis it never closes, or opens on the tail of a sentence before its marker, and the vendored `@blamejs/pki` bundle rises to 0.7.39. Upgrading requires no code change.

items.title: Twenty-three comments in `lib/` are whole sentences again
items.body: The 0.19.0 comment sweep kept a line that carries an `allow:` review marker or a `drop-silent` statement and removed the lines around it. Where the reason ran onto the next line the shipped file carried half of it: `crypto-field.js` ended its marker on "operator", `dsr.js` opened a parenthesis it never closed, and `app-shutdown.js`, `audit.js`, `db-declare-row-policy.js`, `metrics.js`, `middleware/attach-user.js`, `middleware/span-http-server.js`, `middleware/idempotency-key.js` and `network-smtp-policy.js` each ended on a comma, a semicolon or a noun the rest of the sentence was meant to follow. Where the marker's line began with the tail of the sentence the lines before it had carried, the shipped file opened on it: three markers in `audit-tools.js` began "clusterStorage rewrites it." or "columns + binds 'audit'.", and one each in `audit.js`, `break-glass.js`, `crypto-field.js` and `db.js` began "honored.", "keying.)", "through." and "literal names ARE the contract.". Five `drop-silent` statements in `error-page.js`, `http-client.js`, `pqc-agent.js`, `safe-decompress.js` and `session-device-binding.js` were cut the same way. Each is one sentence on one line now, with the same claim it made before the sweep; every marker's claim was re-read against the code it annotates and holds.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.7.39
items.body: The vendored bundle rises from 0.7.37 to 0.7.39. `pki.lint.certificate` grades six more RFC 5280 rules (policy mapping to or from anyPolicy, unique identifiers present, and four more its parser had read past), `pki.schema.x509.parse` returns `issuerUniqueID` and `subjectUniqueID`, and `pki.schema.ocsp.parseRequest` and `parseResponse` refuse a CertID whose issuer hashes are not the length of the digest they name, with the digest lengths shared through `pki.constants.NAMES.DIGEST_OCTETS`. The package continues to declare no dependencies and no install, prepare or prepublish scripts.

items.title: A comment block that ends on `,` or `;`, opens a parenthesis it never closes, or opens on the tail of a sentence before its marker fails the whole-sentence gate
items.body: The gate that keeps `lib/` comments whole sentences judged a block's last word against a list of function words, so a block cut after a noun passed, and it exempted a marker line from the opens-mid-clause test wherever the marker sat on the line. It now also fails a block whose last line ends on a comma or a semicolon, one that opens a parenthesis it never closes, and one whose first line carries prose before its `allow:` marker. On the tree before this release it reported eighteen of the twenty-three blocks above and nothing else; the other five ended on a noun and were found by comparing each marker with its text before the sweep.

releases.headline: Content guards inspect what the consumer sees, not what the source shows
releases.summary: Every guard in the `b.guard*` family has regions it treats as inert: a comment, a quoted value, a code span, a string literal, an escape. Where the guard's idea of such a region disagreed with the consumer that will actually read the document, a payload could sit in the gap. This release closes that gap in `b.guardHtml`, `b.guardSvg`, `b.guardSql`, `b.guardCsv`, `b.guardJson`, `b.guardJsonpath` and `b.guardMarkdown`, corrects two values in the shared entity decoder, and removes three ways to spend unbounded time or memory on a request body that is inside the configured size cap. Upgrading requires no code change. Operators who keep dangerous SQL inside `#` comments, or who rely on `guardSvg.allowedAttrs` being ignored, will see new findings; both are described under Changed.

items.title: `b.guardSvg` reads a prefixed `href` wherever it reads `href`
items.body: In an XML document a namespace prefix is a binding, not part of the name: with `xmlns:l="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"` declared, `l:href` is `xlink:href`. Every rule that reads `href` in the guard matched the two literal spellings, so a bound prefix was invisible to all of them. `<a l:href="javascript:alert(1)">` and `<image l:href="javascript:alert(1)">` reported no `dangerous-url-scheme` issue at any profile, `sanitize` returned them unchanged, and a `<use l:href>` chain was not an expansion edge. The guard does not track namespace bindings; any prefix on `href` is now read wherever `href` is, which is the stricter side, and when an element carries several spellings every one is read, so a prefix bound to nothing cannot stand in front of the one a renderer honors. The dangerous-scheme check, the profile scheme allowlist, the external-reference rule at strict, the sanitizer and the expansion graph all read them.

items.title: `b.guardHtml` and `b.guardSvg` decode CSS escapes before reading a style value
items.body:
CSS lets any character of a property name, a value or an identifier be written as a backslash escape, and a renderer resolves the escape before it acts on the declaration. The `style` attribute scan matched the literal keyword, so escaping one character of the keyword hid it: `style="\6a avascript:alert(1)"`, `style="width:e\78 pression(alert(1))"` and `style="\40 import url(x)"` each reported no `css-injection` issue and the gate served them, while their unescaped spellings were critical at every profile. One hex escape, of one character, in any of `expression`, `behavior`, `-moz-binding`, `javascript`, `vbscript`, `livescript`, `@import` or `@namespace` was enough.

A style value is now unescaped before the dangerous-token scan: one to six hex digits with the single following whitespace character consumed as the delimiter, a backslash before any other character standing for that character, and a null or out-of-range code point becoming U+FFFD. Both guards read CSS through the same function, so the two agree by construction. A backslash that escapes an ordinary character, as in `content:'\201C'` or `font-family:My\ Font`, is unchanged and still passes.

The same decoding applies to the functional references the SVG expansion analysis follows, so `fill="url(\23 ref)"` and `style="fill:u\72l(#ref)"` name the same element as `fill="url(#ref)"`.

A `<style>` element is refused as a non-allowlisted tag by `b.guardSvg` and as a dangerous tag by `b.guardHtml`, so the attribute is the only CSS either guard reads.

items.title: `b.guardHtml` reads a tag the way the HTML tokenizer reads it
items.body:
Three constructs ended the guard's tag scan where a browser continues, so markup after them was never inspected and the gate served it at every profile. The tag scan now follows the tokenizer's states. A quote opens a quoted attribute value only in "before attribute value" state, which is reached by an `=` after an attribute name. Anything else there opens an unquoted value, which runs to whitespace or `>`, and inside it a further `=` or a quote is data. Once a value has ended, or before any name has been read, an `=` starts an attribute name and a quote after it is name data, and the tag name itself is not an attribute name. The whitespace that separates these states is the tokenizer's own: tab, line feed, form feed, carriage return and space. A no-break space or any other Unicode space after `=` is the first character of an unquoted value, not a gap before one. The scanner treated any quote as an opener, so a quote inside an UNQUOTED value ran the scan to the end of the input: `

`, `

`, `

` and `

` each reported no issues at all. A `>` inside a genuinely quoted value still does not end the tag. `text/html` has no CDATA section. ``, so `]]>` carries a live `img` that a browser runs. The guard was skipping to `]]>` and stepping over it. A `/` or `=` where an attribute name should start is a parse error a browser recovers from before reading the rest of the attributes. The attribute reader stopped there, so `

` lost the handler. The reader used by the security guards now resumes past such a character. The reader used by the accessibility audit still stops, because inventing an attribute that is not in the document would report an accessible page as inaccessible; both are built on one parser.

items.title: `b.guardSql` reports syntax the engines read differently instead of guessing
items.body:
The guard takes no dialect option, and in two places the engines disagree about where an inert region begins or ends. Masking either reading hides live SQL from the other, so neither choice is safe and the disagreement is reported instead.

`#` opens a line comment in MySQL and is an operator elsewhere, and MySQL opens a `--` comment only when whitespace or end of input follows, so `SELECT 1--1` is arithmetic there. Masking those to end of line hid `SELECT 3 # 1 AS a; COPY t TO PROGRAM 'true'` and `SELECT 1--1; SELECT LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd')` from every detector including the floor rules. Not masking them would let a quote inside what SQLite and PostgreSQL do read as a comment open a literal that hides a following statement from them. Both forms now report `ambiguous-comment` as critical. `-- ` with a space, and `/* */`, are read identically by every engine and are unaffected.

A backslash before a quote inside a string literal ends that literal one character later on MySQL than on SQLite or on PostgreSQL with standard-conforming strings, so `SELECT '\''; SELECT VERSION()` and `SELECT '\'; DROP TABLE victim; -- '` each hide a stacked statement from one of them. This reports `ambiguous-literal-escape` as critical. A backslash anywhere else in a literal does not move its end and is unaffected, so an ordinary string such as `'a\b'` is accepted.

Separately, the leading-verb rules skipped only space, tab, carriage return and line feed, so a leading form feed defeated the `DO` / `CALL` / `EXECUTE` floor, the migration verb allowlist and verb-in-fragment. Vertical tab and form feed are skipped too.

items.title: `b.guardCsv` reads a cell's value, not the bytes in front of it
items.body:
A leading empty quoted section contributes nothing to a cell's value, so `""=WEBSERVICE("http://evil/")` parses to `=WEBSERVICE("http://evil/")`, a live formula, in every RFC 4180 reader including `b.csv.parse`. The formula rules decided whether a cell was quoted from its first byte and read the second quote as the trigger character, so nothing fired at any profile, and on the sanitize path the gate returned the formula unchanged in its own output. Cell values are now decoded the way a parser decodes them, including doubled quotes: a cell whose value genuinely begins with a quote is still not a formula. The delimiter after a closing quote ends the cell whether or not it is also a trigger character, so `""` followed by a tab is an empty TSV cell and not a cell beginning with one.

`formulaInjectionPolicy: "allowlist"` passes only functions it can identify as safe. It judged the leading function name and stopped, so a denylisted call reached by concatenation or by nesting rode through unmitigated: `=SUM(1)&WEBSERVICE("http://evil/")` and `=IF(1,WEBSERVICE("http://evil/"),2)` were returned as written. Every call in the cell is checked now.

items.title: `b.guardJson` compares the key the parser will see
items.body: JSON allows `\uXXXX` inside a key string, so `{"__prot\u006f__": …}` parses to `__proto__` while the source text contains no such string. The prototype-pollution scan and the duplicate-key rescan both read the raw slice between the quotes, so one escaped character hid the key from both: `validate()` returned `ok: true` with no issues and the gate returned `serve`, at every profile. Keys are now decoded before they are compared, which covers `\uXXXX` and the short escapes. A malformed escape leaves the key as written, which is input the parser rejects anyway.

items.title: `b.guardJsonpath` matches the construct rather than one spelling
items.body:
RFC 9535 writes a filter selector as `?` followed by a logical expression, with the parentheses of the older syntax optional. The detector searched for the two characters `?(`, so `$.store.book[?@.price<10].title` passed clean at every profile while the parenthesized spelling was critical, and `b.jsonPath.query` returns the same result for both. A `?` in selector position is a filter now, wherever the whitespace falls, and a `?` inside a quoted member name still is not.

The recursive-descent cap counted only `..*` and `..[*]`, so twenty `..name` descents scored zero against a limit of two. The descendant segment is `..` whatever selector follows it.

items.title: `b.guardMarkdown` extracts links a renderer resolves
items.body:
CommonMark gives a link title three delimiter pairs. The scanner knew only the double quote, so with a `'…'` or `(…)` title it found no closing parenthesis, dropped the opening bracket, and never handed the destination to the scheme check: `[x](javascript:1 'y')` validated clean and `sanitize()` returned it unchanged at every profile, while its double-quoted twin was critical. A backslash escapes a delimiter inside a title, so the scan takes the first unescaped one: `[x](javascript:alert%281%29 "a\"b")` is one link with an executable destination and is refused, where taking the escaped quote as the close had dropped it.

An angle-bracketed destination may contain spaces, which the destination scanner stops on, so `[x](<javascript:alert(1) >)` was claimed by neither the autolink reader nor the inline reader. It is read to its own closing bracket now.

The code-fence info string reaches a class attribute in renderers that interpolate it, and the rule fired only on a fence at column 0. CommonMark allows a fence up to three columns of indent inside whatever container holds it. Indentation is counted in columns, so a tab advances to the next stop of four, and one space after a `>` marker belongs to the marker rather than to the indent, so `>` followed by four spaces and a fence is a fence. Four columns opens an indented code block, where the backticks are literal text, and is still left alone.

A link reference definition and a fence sit after the container markers on their line, and their three-column budget is measured from the innermost container's content. The definition reader skipped `>` and whitespace only, so `- [x]: javascript:alert(1)` and `1. [x]: javascript:alert(1)`, which every renderer resolves, were never read, and a fence on a list marker line was not a fence. The guard now reads the block structure CommonMark reads: block quote markers and list markers each after up to three columns, a list item's content column set by its marker and the spaces after it, and the item held open across later lines by that column, by a blank line followed by enough indentation, or by lazy paragraph continuation, and closed by a line that opens a block or starts a new item. So `- item`, a blank line and a four-space `[x]: javascript:alert(1)` is a definition inside the item and is refused, while the same four spaces at the top level, or five after a `>`, or a `>` after four spaces, is indented code and is left alone. A definition cannot interrupt a paragraph, so one directly under paragraph text is that paragraph's text, consecutive definitions form one paragraph whose later lines keep no indentation, and a definition's title may follow on the next line and span lines until its closing delimiter. A definition that spans lines, a label to its closing bracket, a destination on the line after the label, a title closed lines later, is read as one scan, and a scan that fails hands every line it took back to the block reader: a fence between the lines of a would-be label is a fence, a title that never closes leaves the definition at its destination line and the text under it to be headed by a setext underline, and a title that opened on the destination line and never closed leaves the whole line as paragraph text. A bracket pair with a nested pair inside is not a label, and an angle bracket that never closes is not a destination, so each leaves its line as text a setext underline can head; the destination after a nested-bracket pair is still inspected. Fenced code holds no definitions and ends on a closing fence of its container or when that container closes; a fence-shaped line inside a differently fenced block is not a fence.

Renderers do not agree on HTML blocks or on what follows a definition. CommonMark treats `<div>`, a raw-text tag, a comment, a processing instruction, CDATA, a declaration or a complete tag alone on its line as a block that holds no definitions, cannot be lazily continued and ends on its own terms; a renderer with HTML disabled, which is markdown-it's default, treats those lines as paragraph text. CommonMark extracts a definition when its paragraph closes, so an empty bullet or a `9)` marker under a definition is text; markdown-it consumes the definition as its own block, so the marker starts a list, a line that follows the block does not continue a quote lazily, an indented line at a shallower depth closes an open quote, a `>` continues an open quote at any indentation, and a title left open runs through code-indented, outdented and underline-shaped lines until its closing delimiter. markdown-it with tables enabled, its default, also reads a GFM table, a header row holding a pipe over a delimiter row of dashes with one cell per header cell, whose rows run until a blank line or a line that opens a block, where any list marker opens one; a table interrupts a paragraph and a definition's title. Two of its indentation rules are read as well: a quote's lazy line is tested for a block start by the quotes nested inside it with its indentation erased, so a code-indented marker, break, heading or fence two quotes deep closes them and is code outside; and a line not indented enough for its list item is tested against the paragraph's terminators the same way, so a code-indented break, heading, fence or HTML block there closes the item's paragraph while a list marker there continues it. The guard reads the document five times, as CommonMark and as markdown-it with HTML on or off and tables on or off, and a document holding a Unicode line or paragraph separator is read again with the separator as a line ending, which no CommonMark renderer treats it as; it inspects every definition and every fence any reading produces, so a document is refused when any of those renderers would resolve an executable destination or interpolate a fence's info string from it.

items.title: `b.codepointClass` decodes two named references to the characters HTML assigns them
items.body: `‐` decoded to U+002D HYPHEN-MINUS instead of U+2010 HYPHEN, and ` ` to a plain space instead of U+00A0. The first manufactured a scheme out of a character that cannot form one, so `[a](view‐source:x)` was refused while `[a](view‐source:x)`, the text a browser actually produces, was accepted. Both now carry the code point the HTML named-character-reference table assigns, so an entity spelling and the character it names reach the same verdict.

items.title: Three ways to spend unbounded time or memory on an accepted request body
items.body:
`b.guardMarkdown` merged its two readings of a document by appending one to the other, leaving the combined list out of document order while the scheme reader walks it by position through a forward-only index. Every backward step rescanned. A document alternating a plain link with one whose opening bracket sits inside a code span, each destination carrying zero-width padding, took 7.1 seconds to validate at 896 KB and was ACCEPTED, so the work was done on behalf of a request that passes. The same document now validates in 163 ms and a growth test holds it linear. The scheme reader's memo of what normalization strips keeps one span per destination in a sorted list, and nested links visit their destinations at decreasing offsets, so each span went in at the front of the list: 64,000 nested links with entity-padded destinations spent 0.8 s shifting spans. The list grows room at its front, so a span below every other is one write.

`b.guardHtml`'s nesting cap reported one issue per tag past the limit with no bound on the list. A 2 MiB body, inside the strict profile's own `maxBytes`, produced 419,301 issue objects and 153 MiB of heap. `b.guardSvg`'s `<use>` cap had the same shape and reported one issue per following element, and so did every finding raised once per attribute, cell, key, tag or link: an event handler on each of 20,000 attributes, a `javascript:` URL on each of 20,000 links, a `HYPERLINK` in each of 20,000 cells, a `__proto__` key in each of 20,000 objects, a `!!python/object` tag on each of 20,000 items, each produced 20,000 issue objects for a verdict the first one decided, and `b.guardJson`'s tree walk raised its node-count cap once per node past the cap, so a 200 KB array of 100,000 zeros produced 91,809 of them. `b.guardHtml`, `b.guardSvg`, `b.guardCsv`, `b.guardJson`, `b.guardYaml` and `b.guardMarkdown` now report at most `b.gateContract.MAX_ISSUES_PER_KIND` (32) issues of any one kind, through one reporter, and the verdict is unchanged.

items.title: `b.guardHtml`'s nesting cap counts nesting
items.body:
`maxTagDepth` counted every opening tag and never discounted the ones that open nothing. A void element has no matching end tag, so a flat run accumulated depth that never unwound and 129 consecutive `
` was refused as a nesting attack at the strict profile. Only elements that can nest count now. A trailing slash does not close a container in text/html, so `
` still nests, and `
` does not unwind a real ancestor.

items.title: `b.guardSvg` bounds what `<use>` expands to rather than how it is written
items.body:
`maxUseDepth` counted `<use>` elements as they appeared in the source. That is not what a `<use>` costs: it renders the subtree it names, and that subtree may hold further `<use>` elements, so the quantity to bound is how far a reference chain reaches and how many instances it expands to. Counting source nesting measured neither. A sprite sheet of 17 sibling `<use/>` icons, which expands to 17 instances, was refused as recursion, while 25 group definitions each referencing the previous one twice, which is 1.4 KB describing roughly 33 million rendered instances, passed with no issues at the balanced and permissive profiles.

The guard now builds the reference graph and walks it, reporting `use-depth-cap` when a chain is deeper than `maxUseDepth`, when references form a cycle, when the expanded instance count outruns the number of references that take part in rendering it, counting only those reached from something painted so a definition nothing reaches cannot widen the allowance, and when the elements those instances draw reach 100,000. The last measure is what bounds a wide, shallow document: five thousand references to one five-thousand-element group is five thousand instances and twenty-five million rectangles. A document of independent icons expands to about one instance per element and is unaffected, and the walk memoizes, so a document built to be expensive to measure is not.

An edge is any reference a renderer follows, not only `<use href>`. `href` on `<pattern>`, `<linearGradient>`, `<radialGradient>`, `<textPath>`, `<mpath>` and `<feImage>` names the element they take their content from, and `xlink:href` is read when `href` is absent. A `url(#id)` is followed from the properties that take one, which are `fill`, `stroke`, `mask`, `clip-path`, `filter`, `cursor`, `color-profile`, `shape-inside`, `shape-subtract` and the `marker` family, written either as an attribute or as a declaration inside `style`. A `url(#id)` elsewhere, in a label or a data attribute, paints nothing and is not an edge. An animation the profile allows can set one of those properties, so the `from`, `to`, `by` and `values` attributes of an animation element are read the same way, and a prefixed `href` is read wherever an unprefixed one is.

Within those properties the guard does not work out which declaration wins. Deciding that takes a CSS cascade: declaration order and `!important`, custom-property scope, inheritance and shadowing, guaranteed-invalid values, and the tree a `<use>` instantiates. A partial implementation of those rules is a list of the references it does not follow, so every `url(#id)` written in a property that takes one, or in a custom property, counts. The cost is the other direction: a document that names a fragment in a declaration the renderer discards, such as `fill:red;fill:url(#p)` or a `--custom` property nothing reads, is treated as referencing it. Where that matters, remove the unused declaration or raise `maxUseDepth`.

A `<defs>`, `<symbol>`, `<clipPath>`, `<mask>`, `<marker>`, `<pattern>`, `<filter>` or gradient renders when something painted references it, and is left alone when nothing does, including its own attributes. Only what renders is walked, so a loop among definitions nothing references is not a finding.

A reference declared on a container is painted by every element inside it. `fill="url(#p)"` on a group of a thousand rectangles is a thousand paintings of the pattern, and a pattern of seventeen `<use>` elements naming a hundred-rectangle group is 1.7 million rectangles from a document of 1,122 elements. That reference was one edge, so the document was served; the same reference written on each rectangle was refused. A reference in an inherited property now counts once for the element and once for every element in its subtree, including the content a `<use>` inside it instantiates and the content a `<use>` carrying the reference instantiates, so the two spellings reach one verdict. The inherited properties are `fill`, `stroke`, the `marker` family, `cursor`, `color-profile` and every custom property; `clip-path`, `mask`, `filter`, `shape-inside` and `shape-subtract` apply to the element's composited result once and are counted once, so a thirty-primitive filter on a group of four thousand rectangles is thirty primitives. The guard does not work out which inner declaration wins, so a rectangle under nested pattern fills is counted as painting each of them; the multiplier is the elements in the subtree, not the elements those inner paints draw, so nested declarations add rather than multiply. An animation the profile allows sets the property its `attributeName` names on its parent, a `<use>` included, or on the element its `href` names, and a reference in an inherited property is inherited from there; an animated `style` value is read as declarations. A rule in a `<style>` element applies to whatever its selector matches, which the guard does not evaluate, so a reference in a stylesheet is counted as painted by every element in the document; the element is outside every shipped profile's `allowedTags`, and an operator who adds it gets the same `css-injection` finding on the sheet's text that the `style` attribute gets, and `sanitize` drops a dangerous sheet the way it drops a dangerous `style` attribute, and drops the sheet's text with the element when the element is not allowed.

Fragments are compared after XML character references are resolved, CSS escapes are decoded, percent escapes are decoded and tab, newline and carriage return are removed, so two spellings of one id are one node. The value is read as CSS rather than searched as text: a comment is ignored, a quoted argument runs to its own closing quote, and a declaration ends at a semicolon outside quotes and parentheses.

items.title: `b.guardSvg.allowedAttrs` governs the attributes it names
items.body: `allowedAttrs` is declared on every profile and documented as an option, and neither `validate` nor `sanitize` read it, so every attribute outside the list survived both. `validate` reports an attribute outside the list as `non-allowlisted-attr`, and `sanitize` drops it. Leaving the option unset keeps the profile's behaviour unchanged.

items.title: `b.guardFilename.sanitize` documents the floor it actually has
items.body: The block said its security floor always throws regardless of mode and profile, and listed NTFS alternate data streams among the classes. It does not: at the permissive profile `reservedCharPolicy` is `strip`, so the colons become underscores before the ADS check runs and sanitize returns the repaired name. The name it returns is safe, `validate` reports `ntfs-ads` at every profile and the gate refuses it, but the sentence an operator reads was wrong. The block now states the real floor, which is path traversal raw and percent-encoded, null byte, UNC path, overlong UTF-8 and the post-strip length cap.

items.title: `b.guardSql` refuses `#` and `--` comments that lack following whitespace
items.body: Statements using `#` as a comment introducer, or `--` with no whitespace after it, now report `ambiguous-comment` as a critical issue, because the supported engines do not agree on whether the rest of the line is code or a comment. SQL that previously passed with such a comment will be refused. Rewriting the comment as `-- ` with a space, or as `/* */`, removes the finding, and both forms are read identically by every engine.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.7.37
items.body: The vendored bundle rises from 0.7.9 to 0.7.37. Every object a signer reads refuses a field it does not read (`pki.ocsp.sign`, `pki.attrcert.sign`, `pki.csr.sign` and `pki.ct.signSct` refuse an unknown option or field by name), a signed OCSP request names its signer, and a requester nonce shorter than the 32 octets RFC 9654 requires is refused. The attribute-certificate signer holds its extensions and attributes to the RFC 5755 issuer rules, takes `crlDistributionPoints` and `authorityInfoAccess`, and emits the authority key identifier by default; the timestamp signer refuses a TSA certificate its verifier would refuse and keeps `genTime`'s fraction of a second; and the ASN.1 time builders read a `Date` through the accessors captured at load. HPKE encrypts to an ML-KEM public key: `pki.hpke.suites.KEM.ML_KEM_512`, `ML_KEM_768` and `ML_KEM_1024` bind FIPS 203 encapsulation into the base and psk modes with every KDF and AEAD, `HKDF_SHA384` joins the KDFs, a serialized HPKE private key is checked at one door for every suite, and a sender key supplied outside the auth modes is refused rather than left unused. `pki.x509.sign` issues the RFC 5280 key identifiers without being asked (a `subjectKeyIdentifier` derived from the subject key and an `authorityKeyIdentifier` naming the issuer's, so a spec with no extensions now yields a v3 certificate; `extensions: []` remains the way to a v1 one), `pki.crl.sign` places an `authorityKeyIdentifier` on every CRL, and `pki.x509.extension(name, value, opts)` encodes one extension from its plain value form. The OCSP signer refuses what its own lint grades an error: a revoked response for a non-issued certificate carries the extended revoked definition and may not carry CRL references, and a pre-encoded single extension is held to where RFC 6960 places it. Comparing public keys of different algorithms no longer leaves an OpenSSL fault queued that failed the next private-key import. It adds a CRL linting profile (`pki.lint.crl`, under the `rfc5280-crl` profile name) and an OCSP one (`pki.lint.ocsp`, under `rfc6960`, with `rfc5019` for the lightweight profile on request), and the issuing side gains every certificate extension the reading side understands, twenty-six in all: `certificatePolicies` with its CPS and user-notice qualifiers, an `authorityKeyIdentifier` that names the issuing certificate by name and serial, the five Microsoft template extensions, `issuerAltName` on a CRL, `subjectInfoAccess`, `subjectDirectoryAttributes` and `ocspNoCheck`, and a certificate request can carry the extensions its subject owns while one the issuing CA assigns is refused by name. Two fixes ride along. `pki.asn1.build.utf8` refuses ill-formed UTF-16 with `asn1/bad-utf8-string` rather than substituting U+FFFD, which had let a distinguished name be signed carrying a replacement character its issuer never wrote. `pki.ocsp.verify` decodes a delegated responder's `ocspNoCheck` extension rather than testing for its presence, so a responder certificate carrying a malformed marker is unauthorized instead of accepted. An OCSP single response takes and parses `archiveCutoff` and `crlReferences`, and every signing verb refuses a `Date` outside years 0000 to 9999 with its own code rather than letting it reach the DER encoder. `pki.key` and the Sigstore bundle verifier now decide with the built-in operations bound when the module loads, so a `Buffer`, `Object`, `Array`, `String`, `Number`, `BigInt` or `Date` method replaced after load is not consulted. The package continues to declare no dependencies and no install, prepare or prepublish scripts.

items.title: `b.guardCsv` allowlist judges every call in a cell
items.body: `formulaInjectionPolicy: "allowlist"` previously mitigated a cell only when its leading function name was outside the list. A cell whose leading call is allowlisted but which reaches a further call by concatenation or nesting is now mitigated as well. A cell whose calls are all allowlisted is left alone, as before.

items.title: `b.gateContract.makeIssueReporter` and `MAX_ISSUES_PER_KIND`
items.body: `makeIssueReporter(issues, maxPerKind?)` returns a function that appends an issue to `issues` until `maxPerKind` issues of that `kind` at that `severity` have been appended and drops further ones of that kind and severity, so a kind reported as a warning per instance and as critical for one instance keeps the critical one and the verdict it decides. `maxPerKind` defaults to `MAX_ISSUES_PER_KIND`, which is 32, and a value below one is refused with a `TypeError`. The six content guards that raise a finding per offense route every finding through it. A guard built on `b.gateContract.defineGuard` can do the same.

items.title: `b.codepointClass.decodeReferenceAt`
items.body: `decodeReferenceAt(s, at)` decodes the one character reference beginning at index `at` the way `decodeMarkupEntities` decodes it, which includes a named reference completed by a numerically written ampersand, so a caller walking a string by position reproduces the whole-string result. `decodeEntityAt` reads one reference in isolation and does not model that composition; its block previously claimed the equivalence and now points here for it.

items.title: `b.codepointClass.isAsciiWhitespace`
items.body: `isAsciiWhitespace(cc)` is true for tab, line feed, form feed, carriage return and space, and false for every other code unit including the no-break space and the other Unicode spaces. The HTML tag scanner in `b.markupTokenizer`, the raw HTML reader in `b.guardMarkdown` and the CSS value trimmer in `b.guardSvg` all read this one predicate.

items.title: `b.markupTokenizer.parseAttrsRecovering` and `b.htmlBalance.VOID_TAGS`
items.body: `parseAttrsRecovering(src)` reads attributes past a `/` or `=` in name position, which is what a guard needs, while `parseAttrs` still stops there, which is what a structural reader needs so it never reports an attribute the document does not contain. The recovering form is a loop over the existing parser rather than a second one. `VOID_TAGS` is the existing HTML void-element set, exported so the depth rules can ask one list which elements open nothing.

items.title: The gate contract is asserted over every content guard at every profile
items.body: The integration harness drove each guard's gate through its own fixtures at the strict profile and asserted only that hostile input was not served. That passes when the action is `sanitize` and the sanitized body still carries the payload. It now checks the body the gate hands back for critical issues, and does so at all three profiles, over the guard list rather than a fixed set, so a guard added later is covered without editing the harness.

items.title: The filename floor is compared against its own documentation
items.body: A test reads the floor sentence out of the source, asserts the prose names every class that really does always throw, asserts it does not name a class refused only by a policy an operator can opt out of, and drives each named class through `sanitize` at three profiles and both modes. A class added to the prose without being implemented, or dropped from the code without being removed from the prose, fails it.

items.title: Named entity values are pinned to the HTML table
items.body: Each entry in the shared named-reference table is asserted against the code point the HTML named-character-reference table assigns that name, which is what caught the two wrong values in this release.

releases.headline: The supported Node version is now 24.21.0
releases.summary: `engines.node` rises from `>=24.19.0` to `>=24.21.0`, the current patch level of the active LTS line. 24.21.0 carries OpenSSL 3.5.8 and the NSS 3.126 root store, both of which the framework's TLS paths read directly. Operators on 24.19.x or 24.20.x should upgrade Node before taking this release. npm treats `engines` as advisory unless `engine-strict` is set, so an install on a lower version prints a warning and then completes, leaving the framework running on a runtime it does not support. Set `engine-strict=true` to have the mismatch refused instead.

items.title: `engines.node` requires 24.21.0
items.body:
The floor moves to Node 24.21.0. It ships OpenSSL 3.5.8 and updates the bundled root certificates to NSS 3.126, so the trust store behind outbound TLS, certificate validation and the mail transports comes from that release. It also corrects a crash in `dns.setServers()` when a resolver is given port 0, tightens port-range validation in the same call, and stops `dgram` discarding bind errors when a callback is supplied.

The framework's own behaviour is unchanged by those three. `b.network.dns.setServers()` already refuses a resolver port outside [1,65535], including 0, before the call reaches Node, and the framework's UDP sockets bind implicitly and attach an error listener rather than passing a bind callback. The floor moves for the OpenSSL and root-store updates.

CI, the publish workflow and the release-container workflow now install 24.21.0, and the README and SECURITY.md requirement lines state it.

items.title: `b.codepointClass.decodeEntityAt`, `decodeNamedEntityAt`, `decodeReferenceAt` and `isUrlSchemeStrippable`
items.body: `decodeEntityAt(s, at)` decodes the one numeric or named entity reference that begins at index `at` of `s` and returns `{ text, next }`, or `null` when no reference begins there. `decodeNamedEntityAt(s, at)` reads a named reference behind a literal ampersand only, and returns `null` for a numeric reference at `at` whatever it decodes to. `decodeMarkupEntities` decodes numeric references in one pass and named references in a second pass over the result, so a numeric reference that yields an ampersand can complete a named reference with the text after it; `decodeReferenceAt(s, at)` reads one reference in that order, so a caller walking by position sees `&colon;` as `:`. `isUrlSchemeStrippable(cp)` reports whether a code point is one that URL-scheme normalization removes: a C0 control or space, tab, line feed, carriage return, or a zero-width character. Together they let a scheme be located by position in a document without copying or normalizing the whole of it, which is how `b.guardMarkdown` now reads link destinations.

items.title: An `xn--` label with no Punycode payload is refused on every runtime
items.body:
`b.safeUrl`, `b.mail.toAscii()` and `b.publicSuffix` read the runtime's URL machinery as a verdict on whether a host is well-formed. It maps rather than validates, and its answer for a payload-less ACE label moved between Node releases. On 24.21.0 `url.domainToASCII("xn--")` returns `"xn--"` unchanged and `new URL("https://xn--/")` is accepted with hostname `xn--`; on 26 the first returns the empty string and the second throws.

The effect was that the same input was accepted on one runtime and refused on the other. On 24.21.0 `b.mail.toAscii("xn--")` returned `"xn--"`, `b.publicSuffix` accepted it as a real domain after it passed the letter-digit-hyphen check, and `b.safeUrl.format("https://xn--/")` returned the URL instead of throwing. An operator's host validation depended on which Node they were running.

The framework now decides this itself. An `xn--` label must carry a payload that decodes to something other than itself, which refuses `xn--`, `xn--a`, `xn--zz` and `xn--.de` while leaving every well-formed A-label untouched. `b.mail.toAscii()` returns `null`, `b.publicSuffix` throws `public-suffix/invalid-domain`, and `b.safeUrl.parse()` and `b.safeUrl.format()` throw a typed `SafeUrlError`, identically on 24.21.0 and 26. The rule has one implementation, the new `b.guardDomain.aceLabelsCarryPayload()`. `b.guardDomain.validate()` and `.sanitize()` apply it too, under every profile: the guard already refused a bare `xn--` at high severity, and now reports `domain.punycode-undecodable` for a payload that decodes to nothing, so `xn--a.example.com` is refused where it was previously accepted at the balanced and permissive profiles. A well-formed A-label is unaffected, and the profile that refuses A-labels outright still does.

The guard also reads the label separators UTS 46 recognizes. It split on the ASCII dot alone, so a name written with the ideographic or fullwidth stop (`example。xn--a.com`) presented as a single label and every per-label rule was skipped for what followed the separator. All four separators normalize to the ASCII one before any rule runs, which is what keeps the whole-domain rules working too: `127。0。0。1` and `foo。localhost` are refused as the IP literal and special-use name they resolve to, and a trailing separator is the fully-qualified marker in whichever spelling it arrives.

Hosts reached through the other URL entry points are unaffected: the origin and host comparisons in CSRF protection, the SSRF guard and the WebSocket origin check match against expected values, so a malformed host fails them on both runtimes.

This was found by the release's own Node bump. The container leg runs the pinned floor, and two tests that pass on 26 failed on 24.21.0.

items.title: Two marker reasons in `lib/` ended mid-sentence
items.body: `lib/network-tls.js` and `lib/pqc-agent.js` each carry a suppression marker whose reason is the prose a reader weighs when re-checking why the exemption holds. Both ended on a dangling word, so neither stated its reason. The TLS one now records that the ECH feature probe's lookup aborts, so it negotiates nothing and has no posture to apply; the certificate one records that the context it builds is discarded and never serves a handshake.

items.title: A marker reason named a primitive that does not carry the pattern
items.body: The ISO-8601 instant literal is shared by three primitives. The reasons in `lib/ai-model-manifest.js` and `lib/metrics.js` named `mail-server-imap` as the third, which does not carry it. The three are `ai-model-manifest`, `metrics` text-render and `content-credentials`, and `lib/content-credentials.js` carried the literal with no reason at all. All three now state the same reason, and it is the operative one: none of the three imports `safe-schema`, whose `DATETIME_RE` also admits a numeric offset, so sharing that would pull a validation module into a hot-path sink for a 50-byte literal.

items.title: `b.guardMarkdown` inspects the destination of a link whose label contains brackets
items.body:
The inline-link scanner and the reference-definition scanner each took the first `]` as the end of a label. A label may contain balanced brackets, and a backslash escapes the character after it, so a linked image such as `[![alt](img.png)](javascript:...)`, a label with an inner bracketed run such as `[a [b] c](javascript:...)`, or an escaped bracket such as `[a\]b](javascript:...)` closed the label early. The outer destination was never extracted, the scheme policy never saw it, `validate()` reported no issue, and `sanitize()` returned the input unchanged, so a CommonMark renderer downstream produced a live link to the uninspected destination. Both scanners now honor nesting and escapes, and each of those shapes is refused under every profile. A benign nested or escaped label is unaffected. Brackets inside a code span take no part in matching, as in CommonMark, so a backtick-quoted bracket can neither close a label early nor turn an image into a plain link that escapes the image cap. Code spans are paired exactly as CommonMark pairs them: a backtick run opens a span only when a later run of the same length closes it, the earliest opener that finds a closer wins over any pair inside it, a run with no closer is literal text, and an escaped backtick cannot open a span but does close one, as in cmark, whose closer scan is raw. So a stray backtick in a label does not hide the link after it, and an inner pair inside a longer span does not leave the longer span unapplied. An autolink and a raw HTML tag bind tighter than a link too, so a bracket inside `<https://example.com/[>`, inside a tag attribute, or inside an HTML comment is literal as well, and the first of these constructs in text order wins: a backtick inside an autolink is literal, and an autolink inside a code span is literal. A code span binds tighter than a link in CommonMark, but a link-first renderer reads a backtick inside a destination as part of the URL, so a construct fabricated from that backtick would hide the hostile link after it; links and reference definitions are therefore extracted both with and without these constructs whenever one of them contains a bracket, and every match found either way is inspected. Where the two readings assign different destinations to one opening bracket, both destinations are inspected and the construct counts once, so `maxLinks`, `maxImages` and `maxRefDefs` are not spent twice on it. A link label and a code span may contain a line ending, and a blank line ends both, so `[x\ny](javascript:...)` is now extracted and refused where no earlier version extracted it. The pairing is one reverse pass and one forward pass over the backtick runs, and two further growth checks hold a document of back-to-back code spans, and code spans after thousands of unmatched run lengths, linear.

Verifying the report exposed a second gap in the same gate. `dangerousSchemePolicy`, `imageSchemePolicy`, `referenceLinkPolicy` and `autolinkSchemePolicy` grade the severity of a dangerous scheme in an inline link, an image, a reference definition or an autolink, and a value of `allow` also skipped the check entirely, so at the permissive profile `[ref]: javascript:...` and `<javascript:...>` passed with no issue. Each policy still sets the severity; a dangerous scheme is reported under every value, so `allow` now means not critical rather than not inspected.

Matching brackets correctly also exposed two quadratic paths. Nested labels close at decreasing offsets, so every link's destination is a suffix of the one before it. The extractor copied each label and each destination for every link, and the scheme check normalized each overlapping destination in full, so a 32 KB document of nested brackets took 1.3 seconds to validate at the permissive profile and 6.7 seconds at 64 KB. With entity-encoded control padding as the shared suffix the normalizing path could not be skipped, and 56 KB took 2.7 seconds. Bounding the inspected bytes would have been a bypass, since normalization strips unbounded leading control padding the way a browser does.

Label and destination text are no longer copied during validation; bracket mates are found in one pass and looked up; extraction stops once the link and image caps are exceeded; a destination whose first bytes are all printable ASCII with no entity reference or percent escape is classified from that prefix alone, since normalization would not change it; and otherwise the scheme is read by position through a memoized index of the next character that survives normalization, so shared padding is walked once for every link that starts inside it. Reading by position recognizes the same references the whole-string decoder does, in its order: numeric references are decoded first, and a named reference is then recognized even where its ampersand, its letters or its closing semicolon were written numerically, so `javascript&colon;alert(1)` and `javascript&colon;alert(1)` are both read as `javascript:`, while an ampersand a named reference produced does not begin a further one, so `javascript&colon;alert(1)` is not. A space inside a destination is kept, since normalization trims space only at the ends, so `java script:` is a relative path and not a scheme, while any amount of whitespace between a scheme name and its colon is passed over, as the scheme reader has always done, so a long run of encoded spaces there does not push the colon out of view. Each of these verdicts is asserted against the whole-string normalization rather than against a fixed expectation. The 64 KB document now validates in about 38 ms and the padded 56 KB one in about 61 ms. Three growth checks hold the scan linear at the permissive profile, whose caps do not truncate the input, for unmatched openers, nested destinations, and entity-padded overlap.

The indexes behind this hold one entry per run of characters actually walked rather than one per character or one per document position, so a document with no links allocates none of them and a single 4 MiB destination costs about 4 MiB. The bracket index is built once for links and reference definitions together, and it is bounded: a document with more than 65536 opening brackets is refused with `markdown.delimiter-cap` before any index is built, so a document of brackets alone can neither exhaust the heap nor smuggle a link through an unindexed scan as a clean verdict.

Reported by Dicky Mulia Fiqri (@dickymuliafiqri).

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.7.8
items.body:
